title: Log Measurements with Python
text:
I will be able to design a table for repeated measurements.

This is important because it enables me to turn observations from electrical and computer systems into evidence that can be checked and analyzed.
This advanced lesson extends the browser notebook pathway and optional local Jupyter setup. Complete those first if you are new to Python; do not repeat their introductory exercises here.

title: Log Measurements with Python
text:
Progression

Begin with a small teacher-provided dataset such as time, voltage, current, and temperature.
Identify the independent variable, dependent variables, units, expected ranges, and missing-value rule.
Write a Python program that appends one complete row to a CSV file.
Add a timestamp and a clear header row.
Reject values outside the teacher-approved range instead of silently saving them.
Open the CSV in a text editor and spreadsheet to confirm that the structure is portable.
Commit the program and a small non-private sample dataset.

Keep raw data unchanged. If you clean or transform it, save the result as a new file and document what changed.

text:
Evidence

Add command-line arguments for the output filename.
Record a sensor simulation at a fixed interval without connecting physical hardware yet.

title: Publish Your Quarto Site with GitHub Pages
text:
Publish safely
Before publishing, remove student numbers, private IP addresses, passwords, Wi-Fi information, tokens, and identifiable information about other students. Use a teacher-approved GitHub identity and repository.
Follow this progression:

Render and test the complete site locally.
Run git status and inspect every file that will be committed.
Commit the tested source.
Create or connect the GitHub repository.
Push the source branch.
Publish using the classroom Quarto GitHub Pages method.
Open the public URL in a private browser window and test every page.
Make one small improvement, commit it, push it, and confirm the public site updates.

The class will use one publishing method consistently. Do not switch between a docs folder, a gh-pages branch, and a GitHub Action unless the teacher changes the class workflow.
Publishing is optional. A local render or private classroom submission can demonstrate the same learning. Never require identifiable student work to be public.

title: Publish Your Quarto Site with GitHub Pages
text:
Verify the deployment
Record the source commit ID before publishing:
git status
git log -1 --oneline
quarto render
After deployment finishes, open the public URL in a private window. Test the navbar, project listing filter, category controls, sorting, site search, images, and changed links. Compare the public content with the recorded commit.

title: Publish Your Quarto Site with GitHub Pages
text:
The problem
The repository has the latest source, but the public site is old, blank, or missing an image.
The challenge: locate the failure in source, render, deployment, or browser cache and preserve evidence of the diagnosis.






TipProgressive hints






Check whether quarto render succeeds locally before investigating hosting.
Read the deployment log and the official Quarto GitHub Pages guide for the class publishing method.
Confirm the configured branch/folder, filename capitalization, base paths, latest commit ID, and .nojekyll requirements for the selected method.

title: Publish Your Quarto Site with GitHub Pages
text:
Common issues







Problem
Check




Build fails
Fix the first local Quarto error, commit the repair, and redeploy.


Public site is 404
Confirm Pages is enabled for the teacher-approved source branch or workflow and wait for the recorded deployment to finish.


CSS or images are missing
Test relative paths and exact capitalization on the rendered site. Do not use a local drive path.


Old content remains
Compare commit IDs, deployment time, and the private-window result before blaming cache.


Workflow lacks permission
Ask the teacher or repository owner. Do not broaden repository permissions without authorization.

title: Linux Offline Kit
text: The TEJ Linux Offline Kit lets students begin Computer Detective and Bashcrawl from a class USB drive without Internet. Students with Internet can download the same ZIP and follow the same steps.

title: Linux Offline Kit
text:
Start from a USB drive

Copy TEJ-Linux-Offline-Kit.zip from the class USB drive to Downloads.
Extract the ZIP. Keep the complete extracted folder together.
Open the extracted TEJ-Linux-Offline-Kit folder.
Double-click START-HERE.html.
Choose 3.1 Computer Detective or 3.2 Bashcrawl and follow the local instructions.

If Internet is available, download the ZIP above instead of copying it from the USB. Everything after the download is the same.

title: Linux Offline Kit
text:
What is included

3.1 Computer Detective: editable ODT and DOCX files, a PDF reference copy, and a plain-text answer sheet.
3.2 Bashcrawl: editable ODT and DOCX files, a PDF reference copy, and a plain-text answer sheet.
3.3 Sleek Out Linux Mint: editable ODT and DOCX files, a PDF reference copy, and a plain-text answer sheet.
Bashcrawl: the complete game, including its hidden rooms and GNU GPL v3 licence.
Cinnamon and Xfce appearance scripts: separate Windows-style and Mac-inspired starting layouts for each desktop. Never force one desktop’s script to run on the other.
Offline start page: a local HTML menu that works in a browser without a web server.
Printable Quick Start: a two-page, black-and-white handout with larger text and one command per step.

title: Linux Offline Kit
text:
Do students need LibreOffice?
Linux Mint normally includes LibreOffice Writer, so no portable office program should be needed on the classroom computers. Open the ODT version in LibreOffice when possible. DOCX is included for Microsoft Word and other compatible programs.
Check before going offline:
INPUT
libreoffice --version
If LibreOffice is missing, students can read the PDF and type their answers into the included TXT answer sheet using Linux Mint’s Text Editor. This kit does not include a third-party portable office executable.

title: Linux Offline Kit
text:
Terminal Quest without Internet
There are two separate ways to use these materials. At home, Terminal Quest works through Windows WSL, Windows Git Bash, Mac, a Chromebook Linux environment, Linux, Android Termux, or iPhone/iPad iSH. In class, it works without Internet after Linux Mint is installed or while Linux Mint is running from the bootable USB.
WSL, Git Bash, Chromebook Linux, Termux, and iSH must be installed while Internet access is available. Git Bash supplies Bash, Git, and common Unix-style commands on Windows, but it is not Linux or Unix. Windows still supplies the file system, permissions, processes, and system information, so some Computer Detective outputs and tools differ.
On a personal Chromebook or owner account, enable Linux through Settings > About ChromeOS > Developers > Linux development environment > Set up while Internet access is available. A school-managed Chromebook may block this feature. Do not use Developer Mode to bypass that restriction.
Using a phone is slower and more difficult than using a computer, but it works. Android uses Termux from F-Droid, and iPhone or iPad uses iSH Shell. A Bluetooth keyboard makes the work easier. Students waiting for a classroom computer or Internet connection can begin or continue the assignments on a phone instead of doing nothing.
Use top instead of trying to install htop. The account, file, system, process, and history commands do not need Internet access.

title: Linux Offline Kit
text:
Start Bashcrawl without Git
The ZIP contains the complete Bashcrawl folder, so students do not need git clone. The same game commands work in Linux Mint after installation or from the live USB. They also work through WSL, Git Bash, Mac, Chromebook Linux, Termux, or iSH after those environments are ready.

In the extracted kit, copy the entire bashcrawl folder.
In Files, open Home, create a folder named Games, and paste bashcrawl inside it.
Open Terminal with Ctrl + Alt + T in Linux Mint, including a live USB session.
Run one command at a time:

INPUT
cd ~/Games/bashcrawl/entrance
INPUT
cat scroll
Folders beginning with a dot are intentional hidden rooms. Copy the complete folder rather than selecting only the visible files.
Continue with ls, pwd, cat scroll, cd roomname, cd .., and ls -a. Do not type the $ prompt symbol shown in some examples.

title: Linux Offline Kit
section: Appearance scripts from the USB drive
text:
Appearance scripts from the USB drive
Identify the desktop first:
INPUT
echo "$XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP"
If the result includes Cinnamon, copy tej-cinnamon-style.sh to ~/Downloads. It previews the proposed changes, backs up every setting it changes, requires the student to type APPLY, and includes a Restore option:
INPUT
cd ~/Downloads
INPUT
less tej-cinnamon-style.sh
INPUT
chmod +x tej-cinnamon-style.sh
INPUT
./tej-cinnamon-style.sh
If the result includes XFCE, use the Xfce script below.
Copy tej-xfce-style.sh to ~/Downloads, inspect it, and then run it:
INPUT
cd ~/Downloads
INPUT
less tej-xfce-style.sh
INPUT
chmod +x tej-xfce-style.sh
INPUT
./tej-xfce-style.sh
The script changes only the current user’s Xfce settings and does not use sudo.

title: Linux Offline Kit
text:
Save now, submit later
Students save the completed ODT, DOCX, or TXT file locally. When Internet access returns, they upload that file to the matching Google Classroom assignment. Screenshots should be inserted into the editable document or saved beside the TXT answer sheet with clear filenames.
Do not record passwords, tokens, Wi-Fi credentials, student numbers, or other private information.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
text:
I will be able to identify the main hardware in my assigned computer.
I will be able to find the same information with graphical tools and terminal commands.
I will be able to explain the difference between installed hardware and current resource use.

This is important because it enables me to describe a computer accurately, decide whether software will run well, and notice when a system is under unusual load.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
text:
Start with the GUI
Open System Info from the Linux Mint menu. Record the operating system, Xfce version, processor, installed memory, graphics device, and storage information. Then open Task Manager and observe CPU and memory use while no large application is open.
Open a browser and Software Manager. Watch what changes. A computer can have 8 GB of RAM installed without having all 8 GB available because Linux and open applications are using some of it.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
text:
Confirm it in the terminal
Run one command at a time. Read the output before continuing.






NoteBegin with Terminal Quest



If you have not completed the cross-platform terminal basics, make a copy of Terminal Quest: WSL and Mac Basics. It explains how to open WSL, Linux Terminal, or macOS Terminal, run beginner commands, inspect processes, and paste a reviewed command history into one Google Doc.


lscpu
free -h
lsblk
df -h
lspci
ip address
Example free -h output:
               total        used        free      available
Mem:           7.7Gi       2.1Gi       3.8Gi          5.3Gi
Swap:          2.0Gi          0B       2.0Gi
Example lsblk output:
NAME   SIZE TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sda  238.5G disk
├─sda1  512M part /boot/efi
└─sda2  238G part /
Your device names and values will differ. Focus on what each column means rather than copying the example.
Use lscpu for processor information, free -h for memory, lsblk for storage devices, df -h for used and available space, lspci for internal hardware, and ip address for network interfaces.
Install htop from Software Manager if it is not already available, then run:
htop
Observe the processor meters, memory meter, process list, and load average. Press q to quit. Do not end a process unless your teacher approves it.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
text:
Submit
This is follow-up lesson evidence, not part of the three Explore Linux assignment submissions. If your teacher assigns it separately, include a two-column hardware inventory, one System Info screenshot, one htop or top screenshot, and a short comparison of what was easier to learn from the GUI and terminal. Follow the submission location and file count provided in Google Classroom.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
section: Everyday Python project: My Computer Report
text:
Everyday Python project: My Computer Report
Create a small Python program named computer_report.py. It should print the operating system, computer name, processor description, Python version, and total, used, and free space in your home drive. Begin with Python’s built-in platform and shutil modules so the program also works in WSL and on a Mac.
Run it from the terminal and compare its answers with System Info and the Linux commands above. Add the program to your Git repository later. Your report must not include passwords, serial numbers, public IP addresses, access tokens, or private information about another student.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
text:
Extend your learning

Read the Linux Mint user guide.
Explore the htop project documentation.
Investigate one unfamiliar device listed by lspci and explain its purpose.

title: Know Your Linux Computer
text:
Review and reflect
You identified CPU, RAM, storage, graphics, and networking information in two ways. Which measurement changed while you opened applications, and which hardware facts stayed the same?

title: Files, Folders, Terminal, and Permissions
text:
Safe practice workspace
Sign in to your own account and create one practice directory:
mkdir -p ~/linux-labs/files-practice
cd ~/linux-labs/files-practice
pwd
Use pwd before every group of commands. Practise with ls, mkdir, touch, cp, mv, cat, less, and rm. Use rm only on teacher-approved practice files. Do not use sudo, wildcards with rm, or commands copied from an unknown site.
Compare the same folder in Thunar File Manager. Turn on hidden files and find .bash_history. Do not edit or submit private information.

title: Files, Folders, Terminal, and Permissions
text:
Permissions
Create a file, then inspect it:
touch team-notes.txt
ls -l team-notes.txt
Learn what the read, write, and execute positions mean for the owner, group, and others. Use chmod only on the practice file and verify the result with ls -l.

title: Files, Folders, Terminal, and Permissions
text:
Evidence
This follow-up lesson is separate from Terminal Quest. If your teacher assigns evidence for it, provide a short command transcript, a screenshot showing the same folder in the terminal and GUI, and an explanation of why checking pwd reduces mistakes. Follow the submission location and file count provided in Google Classroom. Do not add this evidence to Terminal Quest unless your teacher explicitly asks.

title: Files, Folders, Terminal, and Permissions
section: Everyday Python project: Downloads Folder Helper
text:
Everyday Python project: Downloads Folder Helper
Write a Python program using pathlib that reads a teacher-approved practice folder and reports how many files have each extension. Add a dry-run mode that prints proposed moves without changing any files. Only after reviewing the output should the program organize copies inside the practice folder.
Never test a new file-management program on your real Downloads folder, shared folders, or another student’s files. A safe automation shows what it plans to do and stays inside a clearly bounded location.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
text:
A Linux distribution, or distro, is a complete operating system built around Linux. Distros are a little like different flavours: they share many ingredients, but each has its own installer, desktop, software choices, update system, and community. No flavour is best for everyone, although people often have strong preferences. Some distributions are also based on other distributions.
For example:
Debian
└── Ubuntu
    ├── Ubuntu Desktop
    ├── Xubuntu
    ├── Lubuntu
    └── Linux Mint
        ├── Cinnamon edition
        ├── MATE edition
        └── Xfce edition
Debian is a long-running, community-built distribution known for stability. Ubuntu is based on Debian and aims to make Linux practical for a wide range of users. The African word ubuntu is often translated as “I am because we are.” Xubuntu and Lubuntu are Ubuntu flavours. Linux Mint is Ubuntu-based and provides Cinnamon, MATE, and Xfce editions.
A distribution packages the operating system, installer, software sources, update policy, and support community. A desktop environment supplies the graphical workspace, menus, panels, and common tools. Linux Mint is a distribution; Xfce is one desktop environment it can use.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
text:
Our choice: Linux Mint Xfce
We will use Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” Xfce Edition because it works well and is easy for students to begin using. Xfce is the desktop interface. Its layout feels a little like older versions of Windows, and it runs quickly on our older computers with less than 8 GB of RAM. It starts simple, but we can improve and personalize the way it looks later.
Lubuntu is another good lightweight flavour to explore. If you want to compare many possibilities, try the questions at Distrochooser.

title: Choosing a Linux Distribution
section: Release styles: a stable base or the newest software
text:
Release styles: a stable base or the newest software
Ubuntu publishes a new version every six months, usually in April and October. Its version number shows the year and month: 24.04 means April 2024. Releases also have names, such as Ubuntu 24.04 “Noble Numbat.”
Every two years, the April release is an LTS, or Long Term Support, release. LTS versions receive updates for much longer than the releases between them, making them a dependable base for a classroom or everyday computer. Linux Mint 22.3 “Zena” uses the Ubuntu 24.04 LTS package base and is supported until April 2029. We can keep an LTS-based system for work and experiment with a faster-moving distribution on another computer, in a virtual machine, or later as part of a dual-boot setup.
Arch uses a rolling-release model instead of publishing separate LTS versions on a fixed timetable. You install it once and update it continuously, so new software arrives quickly. This gives you current software and a great deal of control, but it also asks you to read update notices, make decisions, and troubleshoot more often.
Arch Linux is the most difficult option discussed here. It expects you to assemble and configure much more of the system yourself. That makes it a poor first classroom installation, but a valuable future challenge if you want to become a system administrator and understand or control every part of a Linux system.
In my classes, students who chose Arch and persisted through its difficulties have often gone on to considerable success in computer engineering, including major scholarship and job opportunities. Arch itself is not a shortcut to those outcomes. The persistence, research, troubleshooting, and systems thinking required to make it work are excellent preparation.
For this lab, our choice is Linux Mint Xfce. In a future lab, we will choose another operating system and install it alongside Windows to create a dual-boot computer.

title: How Wi-Fi and Ethernet Connect
text:
Wi-Fi is not the Internet. Ethernet is not the Internet. Both are ways to join a local network.
Figure 1. One local network can use Wi-Fi and Ethernet at the same time. Open image source and licence.

title: How Wi-Fi and Ethernet Connect
text:
Switch or router?





Five-port Ethernet switch.



Switch: same local network
Learns which device is on each port and forwards Ethernet frames using MAC addresses. It gives the class more Ethernet ports. It does not normally create the Internet connection.
Figure 2. Classroom-style switch. Open source and licence.



Router: between networks
Forwards IP packets between different networks. The school router or gateway connects the classroom network toward the Internet.
A home Wi-Fi router combines several jobs in one box: router, switch, Wi-Fi access point, DHCP, NAT, and firewall.

title: How Wi-Fi and Ethernet Connect
text:
Classroom path
COMPUTER → ETHERNET CABLE → CLASS SWITCH → SCHOOL ROUTER/GATEWAY → INTERNET SERVICE

Access point: provides the Wi-Fi radio link.
DHCP: gives a device local network settings.
DNS: translates a name such as example.org into an IP address.
Modem or ONT: connects a customer network to cable, DSL, fibre, or another provider link.

Quick check: if Wi-Fi connects but websites do not load, test local IP settings, gateway reachability, DNS, and Internet service separately.
Next: choose an Ethernet cable

title: Build and Test an Ethernet Cable
text: This is the complete step-by-step sequence from the classroom presentation.
crumbs: 3. Build and Test an Ethernet Cable

title: Build and Test an Ethernet Cable
text:
Procedure


0

Measure and cut
Leave enough cable for a gentle route and a small service loop.



1

Remove the outer jacket
Strip about 25 to 40 mm. Cut lightly. Do not nick the eight insulated conductors.



2

Inspect every conductor
If copper is exposed or insulation is cut, remove the damaged section and start again.



3

Untangle and flatten
Separate the four pairs. Untwist only the length needed to reach the plug.



4

Arrange T568B
Place all eight conductors in the colour order shown above.



5

Trim to an even 13 mm
Pinch the order between your fingers. Cut the ends straight and even.



6

Insert and verify
Clip down, gold pins up, white-orange on the left. Every wire reaches the front. About 6 mm of jacket enters the plug.



7

Crimp
Insert the plug fully into the correct crimper slot. Squeeze completely using the demonstrated tool procedure.



8

Inspect the termination
All contacts sit evenly. The strain relief grips the jacket. Gently tug the cable.



9

Finish the other end and test
Use T568B again. A good tester shows pins 1 through 8 in the same order at both ends.








Outer jacket being removed from an Ethernet cable.



Steps 1 and 2
Remove only the jacket, then inspect the inner insulation.
Figure 3. Open source and licence.

Step 3
Separate the pairs and keep the untwisted length short.
Figure 4. Open source and licence.






Ethernet conductors aligned before entering the modular plug.



Steps 4 to 6
Order, flatten, trim, insert, and check through the clear plug.
Figure 5. Open source and licence.






A photo sequence showing an 8P8C plug being inserted and crimped.



Steps 7 and 8
Crimp fully. Check contact height and strain relief before testing.
Figure 6. Public-domain visual sequence. Open source.






Network cable tester used for modular Ethernet cables.

Test for correct order, opens, shorts, reversals, crossed pairs, and split pairs.

title: Component Foundations 1: Circuits and Schematics
Component Foundations 1: Circuits and Schematics
Component Foundations 1: Circuits and Schematics
text:
Lines, nodes, and junctions
A line normally represents a conductor. Every uninterrupted set of connected lines is one node, so all points on that node have the same ideal voltage.

A visible dot marks a junction when several lines connect.
Crossing lines without a junction dot should be treated as not connected unless the drawing standard states otherwise.
Ground is the chosen 0 V reference for voltage measurements. It is not automatically the Earth.
A component interrupts a wire because current must pass through that component between two nodes.

title: Component Foundations 1: Circuits and Schematics

Read a first schematic



Figure 2. The resistor and LED are in one path. Closing the switch completes the circuit.


Trace from the positive source terminal through \(S_1\), \(R_1\), and \(D_1\), then back to the source through ground. The resistor is not optional decoration: it limits current to protect the LED.

title: Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design
text: This lesson turns the charging curve into a design tool. Start with a target time, choose \(R\) and \(C\), then check the actual result.
crumbs: 5. Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design

title: Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design
text:
The time constant
For a simple resistor-capacitor circuit:
\[
\tau=RC
\]
where:

\(\tau\) is time in seconds;
\(R\) is resistance in ohms;
\(C\) is capacitance in farads.

Useful unit combinations are:
\[
\mathrm{k\Omega}\times\mathrm{\mu F}=\mathrm{ms},
\qquad
\mathrm{M\Omega}\times\mathrm{\mu F}=\mathrm{s}
\]
crumbs: 5. Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design

title: Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design
text:
Worked example using GUESS
A circuit uses \(R=15\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(C=47\,\mu\mathrm{F}\). Calculate the time constant and the practical charging time.
Given
\[R=15\,000\,\Omega,\qquad C=47\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}\]
Unknown
\[\tau=?,\qquad 5\tau=?\]
Equation
\[\tau=RC\]
Substitute and solve
\[
\tau=(15\,000\,\Omega)(47\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F})=0.705\,\mathrm{s}
\]
\[
5\tau=5(0.705\,\mathrm{s})=3.525\,\mathrm{s}
\]
Statement
The time constant is \(0.705\,\mathrm{s}\), and practical charging takes about \(3.53\,\mathrm{s}\).
crumbs: 5. Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design

title: Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design
section: Use the time scale on the graph
text:
Use the time scale on the graph



Figure 1. If \(\tau=0.705\,\mathrm{s}\), then the marks are \(0.705\,\mathrm{s}\), \(1.41\,\mathrm{s}\), \(2.12\,\mathrm{s}\), and \(3.53\,\mathrm{s}\) at \(1\tau\), \(2\tau\), \(3\tau\), and \(5\tau\).
crumbs: 5. Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design

title: Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design
text:
Solve for a part value
If the target time and capacitance are known:
\[
R=\frac{\tau}{C}
\]
If the target time and resistance are known:
\[
C=\frac{\tau}{R}
\]
The exact answer may not be a standard part value. Choose an available part and recalculate the actual time constant.
Example: a target of \(2.00\,\mathrm{s}\) with \(R=22.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) requires:
\[
C=\frac{2.00\,\mathrm{s}}{22\,000\,\Omega}=90.9\,\mu\mathrm{F}
\]
A \(100\,\mu\mathrm{F}\) part gives:
\[
\tau=(22.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega})(100\,\mu\mathrm{F})=2.20\,\mathrm{s}
\]
State both the ideal calculated value and the actual value from the selected part.
crumbs: 5. Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design

title: Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design
text:
Optional calculus bridge
You do not need calculus to complete this lesson. The full ideal equations are:
\[
v_C(t)=V_S\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right)
\]
for charging, and:
\[
v_C(t)=V_0e^{-t/RC}
\]
for discharging.
Differentiation describes how fast voltage changes. Integration connects current over time to stored charge. Later, an op amp can build practical integrators and differentiators.
crumbs: 5. Capacitors 3: RC Time Constants and Design

title: Component Foundations 6: Operational Amplifiers
text:
What is an op-amp?
An operational amplifier, or op-amp, is a high-gain differential amplifier. Its basic relationship is:
\[V_{OUT}=A_{OL}(V_+-V_-)\]
\(V_+\) is the non-inverting input, \(V_-\) is the inverting input, and \(A_{OL}\) is open-loop gain. Because open-loop gain is very large, useful circuits normally apply feedback rather than operate the amplifier open loop.
An op-amp also needs power-supply connections. The triangle symbol often omits those rails to keep a schematic readable, but the physical circuit cannot operate without them.

title: Component Foundations 6: Operational Amplifiers
section: Negative feedback and a voltage follower
text:
Negative feedback and a voltage follower



Figure 1. Negative feedback makes the closed-loop goal \(V_{OUT}\approx V_{IN}\) while the output remains within real device limits.


In the ideal negative-feedback model:

input currents are approximately zero;
the output moves so that \(V_+\approx V_-\) when the amplifier is operating normally;
the output cannot exceed the available supply and output-swing limits.

These are model assumptions, not universal facts. They fail during saturation, excessive input difference, missing power, instability, wiring faults, or operation outside the datasheet.

title: Component Foundations 6: Operational Amplifiers
Component Foundations 6: Operational Amplifiers
text:
Real limitations
A real op-amp has limited input range, output swing, current, bandwidth, slew rate, offset, and power dissipation. The XL741 guide’s first suggested follower test uses \(+15\) V and \(-15\) V rails and keeps \(V_{IN}\) within \(\pm13\) V. Any physical test must follow the current manufacturer documentation and a teacher-approved current-limited dual supply.

title: Component Foundations 6: Operational Amplifiers
text:
Five-question starter

Identify \(V_+\), \(V_-\), \(V_{OUT}\), and the two supply rails in Figure 1.
Explain what the expression \(V_+-V_-\) means.
Trace the feedback path and explain why the circuit is called a voltage follower.
Predict ideal \(V_{OUT}\) for inputs of \(-5.0\) V, 0 V, and \(+5.0\) V, then state two real limitations omitted by the prediction.
A follower simulation gives \(V_{OUT}=V_{IN}\) but a physical XL741 does not. Propose an evidence-based diagnostic order covering supplies, common reference, input range, terminal assignment, assembly, saturation, and measurement setup.

title: Component Foundations 4: Diodes and LEDs
text:
What is a diode?
A diode is a two-terminal semiconductor component that conducts much more readily in one direction than the other. Its terminals are the anode and cathode.
In the schematic symbol, the vertical bar marks the cathode side. Many cylindrical diodes place a physical stripe near the cathode. A stripe, flat edge, or lead length must be interpreted using the correct part documentation rather than a rule borrowed from another package.

title: Component Foundations 4: Diodes and LEDs
text:
A beginner model

Forward biased: the diode can conduct after its forward voltage is reached.
Reverse biased: the diode normally blocks current until a reverse limit is exceeded.

The diode is not a perfect one-way switch. Forward voltage changes with current, temperature, construction, and device type. Reverse voltage and current ratings must not be exceeded.

title: Component Foundations 4: Diodes and LEDs
text:
LEDs
An LED is a light-emitting diode. It still requires correct polarity and current limiting.



Figure 1. The resistor limits LED current; the LED is not connected directly across the source.


For a first estimate:
\[R=\frac{V_S-V_F}{I_{LED}}\]
Then choose an available standard resistance that stays within the LED, resistor, and source limits.

title: Component Foundations 4: Diodes and LEDs
text:
The XL741 connection
The available XL741 v2.0 kit uses two BAT85 diodes. The kit documentation explains that they help the discrete circuit match characteristics of the original integrated 741 more closely. Students should identify diode polarity and understand forward and reverse operation before assembling the kit.

title: Component Foundations 4: Diodes and LEDs
text:
Five-question starter

Name the two diode terminals and identify the cathode on the schematic symbol.
Explain forward bias and reverse bias without calling a diode a perfect switch.
A diode-mode test shows a plausible forward reading in one direction and overload in the other. What does that evidence suggest, and what does it not prove?
Calculate a first resistor estimate for a 5.0 V source, a 2.0 V LED, and 10 mA target current. Choose a nearby standard value conservatively.
A student reverses the LED and then removes the resistor because it does not light. Identify both reasoning errors and propose a safe diagnostic sequence.

title: Component Foundations 4: Diodes and LEDs
text:
Jupyter and lab pathway
Use Notebook 1 or a copied engineering-calculator notebook to compare candidate LED resistors and calculate resistor power. A circuit simulator can compare polarity and available values before a physical build.
For physical work, use a protected low-voltage source, retain the current-limiting resistor, and use diode mode only with power removed. Do not use a student breadboard for mains rectification.

Circuit analysis
Analyze voltage, current, resistance, power, and energy in computers, vehicles, batteries, sensors, motors, and robots. Start with Series Circuits to apply Ohm’s law, then use the circuits package sequence for parallel, mixed, Kirchhoff, and matrix methods.
Textbook reference: Grob’s Basic Electronics, supported by the Problems Manual and Experiments Manual. Public pages cite chapters and problem families without publishing scans.

Measurement and data
Record repeatable measurements with units, uncertainty, and enough metadata to interpret the test later. Use Python Measurement Logging and Python Analysis and Curve Fitting.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
section: Jupyter as the start-now engineering workspace
text:
Jupyter as the start-now engineering workspace
Students can begin computational work before every component, instrument, or soldered kit is available. The Jupyter Electronics Lab provides a complete progression through circuit calculations, parameter sweeps, KCL/KVL systems, graphs, CSV analysis, RC transients, op-amp models, and numerical calculus.
The required evidence is the hand prediction, reproducible notebook, independent check, graph, interpretation, and honest model limitation. Circuit simulation and physical measurement are later validation layers. A student must not label a numerical or simulated result as measured, but the absence of an optional kit does not prevent completion of the modelling outcomes.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
section: Signals, op-amps, and a bridge to calculus
text:
Signals, op-amps, and a bridge to calculus
After capacitors, RC response, diodes, and transistor fundamentals, an optional discrete XL741 op-amp project can make later mathematics visible in a real circuit. Calculus is not a prerequisite for the build. Start with average slope, area under a voltage-time graph, finite differences, and running sums; then compare those numerical results with measured integrator and differentiator outputs.
An ideal differentiator models rate of change,
\[
V_{\text{out}}=-RC\frac{dV_{\text{in}}}{dt},
\]
while an ideal integrator models accumulation,
\[
V_{\text{out}}=-\frac{1}{RC}\int V_{\text{in}}\,dt.
\]
The core TEJ goal is to explain the observed input and output waveforms using circuits, measurements, graphs, and numerical approximations. Derivatives, integrals, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and RC differential equations form an optional university-preparation extension. A strong investigation compares the same signal four ways: a hand estimate, a Python numerical result, a circuit simulation, and a measured XL741 output.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Computing and control
Connect operating systems, networking, programming, sensors, outputs, and feedback in recognizable systems. Continue through the Linux and Operating Systems path while the dedicated robotics and control packages are developed.

title: Engineering Preparation Track

Ontario course collaboration opportunities
TEJ3M and TEJ4M provide the computer-engineering context. SPH3U can support energy, measurement, and motion; SCH4U can support batteries and material systems; SBI4U can support sensor investigations where the electronics are the instrument, not a substitute for the biology. These connections identify useful collaboration, not course equivalencies.

title: Assignment: Python and NumPy Foundations
text:
2. Begin with named quantities
voltage_V = 9.0
resistance_ohm = 1000.0
current_A = voltage_V / resistance_ohm
current_mA = current_A * 1000

print(f"Current: {current_mA:.2f} mA")
The part before = is a variable name. The part after = is evaluated and stored. Python does not automatically know that 9.0 is a voltage, so include the unit in the name.
Comments begin with #:
resistance_ohm = 2200.0  # 2.2 kΩ written in base ohms

First checkpoint
Change the resistance to 2200.0. Run the code. Add an assertion that checks the current is positive.

title: Assignment: Python and NumPy Foundations
text:
3. Store several values
A Python list stores an ordered collection:
resistor_values_ohm = [1000.0, 2200.0, 3300.0, 4700.0]

print(resistor_values_ohm[0])   # first item
print(resistor_values_ohm[-1])  # last item
print(len(resistor_values_ohm))
Python starts indexing at zero. A loop repeats an operation:
for value_ohm in resistor_values_ohm:
    current_mA = 9.0 / value_ohm * 1000
    print(value_ohm, current_mA)

title: Assignment: Python and NumPy Foundations
text:
4. Meet NumPy
NumPy arrays store numerical data and support vectorized operations: one expression can calculate every item.
import numpy as np

voltage_V = np.array([1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6.0, 7.5, 9.0])
resistance_ohm = 2200.0
current_mA = voltage_V / resistance_ohm * 1000
This produces six currents because the division is applied to all six voltages.
Inspect the data before interpreting it:
print(type(voltage_V))
print(voltage_V.shape)
print(voltage_V.dtype)
print(voltage_V)
print(current_mA)
Useful array operations include:
current_mA[0]                 # first result
current_mA[-1]                # last result
current_mA.min()
current_mA.max()
current_mA.mean()
current_mA[current_mA < 3.0]  # Boolean filter
NumPy will later store matrix rows, but this lesson uses only one-dimensional arrays. You should understand the data before using a linear-algebra solver.

title: Assignment: Python and NumPy Foundations
text:
5. Write a reusable function
def calculate_current_mA(voltage_V, resistance_ohm):
    """Return resistor current in milliamperes."""
    return np.asarray(voltage_V) / resistance_ohm * 1000
Call and verify the function:
test_current_mA = calculate_current_mA([3.0, 6.0, 9.0], 3000.0)

assert np.allclose(test_current_mA, [1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
An assertion is a check, not the main calculation. np.allclose is used for decimal calculations because computers may store a result such as 0.3 as a number that is extremely close to, but not exactly, 0.3.

title: Assignment: Python and NumPy Foundations
text:
6. Read the documentation
Start with the object you are using:
help(np.round)
In Jupyter, this also opens help:
np.round?
Read the function signature, then the parameter descriptions, return value, and examples. Do not guess parameter names.

Read an error from the bottom
When Python shows a traceback, start with the last line. Then look one line above it for the code that failed.








Last line says
Meaning
Check




missing required positional argument
The function needs another value
Compare your call with the function signature


unexpected keyword argument
The keyword name is not accepted
Copy the exact parameter name from the documentation


AssertionError
A check was false
Print both values; use np.allclose for decimal arrays



For a larger library, search the official documentation for the function name. Compare the signature with your line of code from left to right. Fix one mismatch and run the cell again.
The notebook contains this intentional error behind a switch:
trigger_documentation_error = True

if trigger_documentation_error:
    rounded_current_mA = np.round(current_mA, digits=2)
Read the final exception line. Open the official numpy.round documentation, find the correct keyword, repair only that keyword, and rerun the cell until it prints the rounded array.
Use the full documentation and help-request lesson when the first lookup does not solve the problem. That lesson also covers Google searches, Stack Overflow, minimal reproducible examples, and the evidence required when asking the teacher.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot(voltage_V, current_mA, marker="o")
plt.xlabel("Voltage (V)")
plt.ylabel("Current (mA)")
plt.title("Current through a 2.2 kΩ resistor")

Why this is useful
Two loops share one component, so the current through the shared component depends on both loop currents. A matrix does not replace the circuit reasoning. It organizes the equations after the arrows, signs, units, and KVL equations are correct.
This bridge has two parts. Question 4 is the fully worked teaching example. Question 5 is the independent transfer task: the helper questions reveal the process, but not the completed coefficients, matrix, or currents.

title: Assignment: From Two Loops to a Matrix
text:
Part A: Worked Question 4
Follow the complete example once. Each line performs one algebra move, so you can reuse the method without reusing the numbers.

1. Use Kirchhoff’s Current Law to define the three currents




Figure 1. Read the current arrows before reading the equations. The top centre junction connects all three current paths. #



Kirchhoff’s Current Law at the junction
At the top centre junction:


\(I_1\)entersfrom the left


\(I_2\)leavesto the right


\(I_3\)leavesdownward



current entering = current leaving
\[
I_1=I_2+I_3
\]
\[
I_1-I_2-I_3=0
\]
\[
\boxed{I_3=I_1-I_2}
\]



Use clockwise mesh currents \(I_1\) and \(I_2\). Define \(I_3\) downward through the shared resistor, as shown. Keep the arrows and the equation \(I_3=I_1-I_2\) visible beside the work.


2. Derive Equation 1 from Loop 1




Figure 2. Isolate Loop 1 before writing its KVL equation. Only the three components crossed by this loop are shown. #



Turn the circuit into signed terms


\(V_{S1}\)source rise\(+10\)


\(R_1\)with \(I_1\)\(-3I_1\)


\(R_3\)with \(I_3\)\(-2I_3\)



\[
+10-3I_1-2I_3=0
\]



Use the printable guide and record each signed KVL term:








Element
Signed term
Reason




\(V_{S1}=10\,\mathrm{V}\)
\(+10\)
source rise


\(R_1=3.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\)
\(-3I_1\)
travel with \(I_1\)


\(R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\)
\(-2I_3\)
travel with the defined \(I_3\)



Do not replace the resistor-voltage symbols with numbers in one jump. Show the complete chain:
\[
+10-V_{R1}-V_{R3}=0,
\]
\[
V_{R1}=I_1R_1=3I_1,\qquad V_{R3}=I_3R_3=2I_3,
\]
\[
+10-3I_1-2I_3=0,
\]
\[
+10-3I_1-2(I_1-I_2)=0,
\]
\[
+10-3I_1-2I_1+2I_2=0,
\]
\[
+10-5I_1+2I_2=0,
\]
\[
-5I_1+2I_2=-10,
\]
\[
\boxed{5I_1-2I_2=10}.
\]
The second-last line subtracts \(10\) from both sides. The final line multiplies the complete equation by \(-1\) so the leading coefficient is positive.


3. Derive Equation 2 from Loop 2




Figure 3. Isolate Loop 2. This loop crosses the shared resistor in the direction opposite the defined \(I_3\) arrow. #



The shared-resistor sign changes


\(V_{S2}\)source rise\(+6\)


\(R_2\)with \(I_2\)\(-5I_2\)


\(R_3\)against \(I_3\)\(+2I_3\)



\[
+6-5I_2+2I_3=0
\]



Loop 2 travels through the shared resistor against the defined direction of \(I_3\). Its resistor term is therefore positive.








Element
Signed term
Reason




\(V_{S2}=6.0\,\mathrm{V}\)
\(+6\)
source rise


\(R_2=5.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\)
\(-5I_2\)
travel with \(I_2\)


\(R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\)
\(+2I_3\)
travel against the defined \(I_3\)



Again, begin with resistor-voltage symbols and show one algebra move per line:
\[
+6-V_{R2}+V_{R3}=0,
\]
\[
V_{R2}=I_2R_2=5I_2,\qquad V_{R3}=I_3R_3=2I_3,
\]
\[
+6-5I_2+2I_3=0,
\]
\[
+6-5I_2+2(I_1-I_2)=0,
\]
\[
+6-5I_2+2I_1-2I_2=0,
\]
\[
+6+2I_1-5I_2-2I_2=0,
\]
\[
+6+2I_1-7I_2=0,
\]
\[
2I_1-7I_2=-6,
\]
\[
\boxed{-2I_1+7I_2=6}.
\]
Multiplying the complete equation by \(-1\) does not change its solution.


4. Build the matrix
State the variable order before entering any coefficients:
\[
[I_1,I_2].
\]

Common issues

The shared resistor has the wrong sign
Loop 1 travels with the defined \(I_3\), so its term is \(-2I_3\). Loop 2 travels against \(I_3\), so its term is \(+2I_3\).


The matrix solves the wrong equations
Check the variable order and read each row back as an equation. A solver cannot recognize that a coefficient was copied into the wrong column.


SymPy is not installed
If you see ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sympy', use the current course JupyterLite environment or install the provided requirements in the local virtual environment:
python -m pip install -r requirements-jupyter.txt


A negative current appears
A negative current means the real current is opposite the arrow selected before solving. It is not automatically an error.

title: Jupyter Electronics Lab
section: Why Jupyter comes before the hardware
text:
Why Jupyter comes before the hardware
Physical components, instruments, soldering time, and kits may not be available at the same moment for every student. Jupyter provides meaningful engineering work while students wait. It can repeat calculations, sweep component values, solve systems, model change over time, analyze data, and expose assumptions.
Jupyter does not prove that a circuit was wired correctly or that hardware is safe. Until a physical test occurs, describe results as calculated, modelled, or simulated, never measured.






ImportantThe evidence ladder



Calculate by hand → Model in Jupyter → Simulate the circuit → Measure when available → Compare → Verify
Each layer answers a different question. Agreement builds confidence; disagreement creates a troubleshooting investigation.

title: Jupyter Electronics Lab
Jupyter Electronics Lab
section: Read the documentation before asking for the fix
text:
Read the documentation before asking for the fix
Coding lessons deliberately include two kinds of faults:

an error that stops the program and produces a message;
a plausible wrong answer that runs without an error but fails a units, residual, conservation, or limiting-case check.

The sequence always starts from success and increases gradually: run known-good code, repair one incorrect keyword, diagnose an array-shape error, and finally find a silent unit error that produces a believable result.
Use this routine before asking for line-by-line help:

Reproduce: run the smallest cell that still shows the problem.
Read: copy the exact error message, or state which verification check failed.
Inspect: print the relevant values, types, shapes, and units.
Research: try help(function_name), function_name?, or an exact-phrase web search containing the library and function name. Prefer the official documentation.
Repair: change the smallest possible part of the code and explain the documented requirement behind the change.
Verify: restart the kernel, run from the first cell, and use an independent check to show that the result is now trustworthy.







NoteRequired debugging evidence



Submit the original symptom, the search terms used, the documentation source, the requirement you found, the repair, and the verification result. Copying a finished solution without this evidence does not complete the debugging task.


Use Find Documentation and Ask for Programming Help for the full pandas, official-documentation, Stack Overflow, minimal-example, and teacher-help protocol.

title: Jupyter Electronics Lab
text:
A repeatable class cycle

Day 1: understand and calculate
Read the matching electronics notes, draw or interpret the schematic, identify variables and units, and complete one representative hand calculation.


Day 2: model and verify
Run the working notebook, change only the assigned values, and add an independent check.


Day 3: investigate
Sweep one component or condition across a justified range. Use a graph to identify a pattern, threshold, trade-off, or sensitive region.


Day 4: simulate or analyze evidence
Compare the numerical model with a circuit simulator or a supplied dataset. Record differences without forcing them to agree.


Day 5: verify and prepare for hardware
Finish the evidence table, run every check, and identify the physical measurement to add when equipment is available.

text:
The help ladder
Use the first level that can answer the question. Record what you learned before moving down the list.

Read the last line of the error and the line that caused it.
Reproduce the issue in the smallest possible cell.
Inspect values, types, shapes, column names, units, versions, and file locations.

The goal is not to avoid asking for help. The goal is to make the question answerable.

title: Find Documentation and Ask for Programming Help
text:
1. Reproduce the issue
Save the notebook, restart the kernel, and run from the first cell. Then make a small copy that still produces the same problem.
import sys
import pandas as pd

print(sys.executable)
print(sys.version)
print("pandas", pd.__version__)
For a pandas problem, also inspect the data structure instead of guessing:
print(type(data))
print(data.shape)
print(data.columns.tolist())
print(data.head())
print(data.dtypes)
Copy errors as text. Do not submit a photograph of code or an error when the text can be copied.






ImportantProtect information before sharing



Remove names, student numbers, tokens, passwords, private file paths, and confidential data. Replace a large or private dataset with a few invented rows that still reproduce the behaviour.

title: Find Documentation and Ask for Programming Help
text:
2. Ask Python and Jupyter first
Use the object you are actually calling:
help(pd.read_csv)
In a Jupyter cell, a question mark shows the signature and documentation:
pd.read_csv?
For a method on a DataFrame:
data.dropna?
Read the signature, parameters, returns, raises, and examples. Check whether the documented requirement matches your input type, array shape, column name, path, or unit.

title: Find Documentation and Ask for Programming Help
text:
3. Search the web deliberately
A useful search normally contains:
library + function + exact error or unexpected behaviour
Examples:
pandas read_csv FileNotFoundError Jupyter relative path
numpy linalg solve matrix must be square
matplotlib plot x and y different first dimension
Put a distinctive error fragment in quotation marks when the search is too broad:
pandas read_csv "No such file or directory" Jupyter
Limit a search to an authoritative site when needed:
site:pandas.pydata.org pandas read_csv usecols
site:numpy.org numpy linalg solve shape
site:docs.python.org pathlib current working directory
site:stackoverflow.com pandas KeyError column name
Do not paste the first result into the notebook. Compare it with the installed package version, understand which line changes, and verify the result independently.

5. Search Stack Overflow
Search before posting. Start with the exact error, language, library, and function. Read more than the accepted code snippet:

Does the question describe the same input and goal?
Which package and Python versions were involved?
Is the answer old enough that the API may have changed?
Do comments or newer answers identify a limitation?
Can you explain the suggested change before running it?

Stack Overflow community answers are leads, not authority. Confirm important details in the current official documentation and test the proposed fix on the minimal example.

title: Find Documentation and Ask for Programming Help
text:
6. Create a minimal reproducible example
Stack Overflow calls this an MRE: minimal, reproducible example.

Minimal: remove unrelated imports, cells, files, and data.
Complete: include every import, variable, and small input needed to run it.
Reproducible: restart and verify that the example produces the reported result.

Example small dataset:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "voltage_V": [2.0, 4.0, 6.0],
        "current_mA": [2.1, 4.0, 6.2],
    }
)

print(data["current_ma"].mean())
The example is short, contains its own data, and reproduces the column-name problem without requiring somebody else to download a private CSV file.
Read Stack Overflow’s official guidance on asking a good question and creating a minimal reproducible example before posting.

### Goal

### Actual result
Instead, ...

### Exact error or failed check
Paste the complete final exception line or the incorrect output as text.

### Minimal code and input
Paste the smallest runnable example.

### Environment
Operating system:
Python version:
Package versions:
Jupyter kernel/interpreter path:

### What I tried
1. I ...
2. I ...

### Sources I checked
- Documentation or question link:
- Relevant requirement or example:

### My current hypothesis
I think the problem may be ... because ...

### Focused question
What assumption, input, or documented requirement should I check next?
This lets the teacher see your reasoning, reproduce the issue, and teach the missing idea instead of guessing what happened.

Before you start

Open Tinkercad Circuits in a current school-approved browser.
Have your calculation and the matching circuit-analysis schematic ready.
Use only simulated low-voltage direct-current circuits in this activity.

Tinkercad is an external Autodesk service. Availability, sign-in rules, and saved work depend on the school browser and account policy. If it is unavailable, use a teacher-approved physical build or another approved simulator and record which tool you used.






NoteJoining a Tinkercad Classroom



Your teacher may give you a class link or class code. A teacher can also create a lightweight class seat and assign a nickname that does not require personal information. Use only the nickname and joining method your teacher provides. Never place a class code in a public screenshot, notebook, or portfolio.

title: Build and Measure Circuits in Tinkercad
text:
1. Create the circuit

Open Circuits and choose Create new Circuit. Rename it with the teacher’s required filename pattern.
Find each part in the components panel. Drag the source, resistors, breadboard if required, and Multimeter into the work area.
Select each component and set its value and unit. Check Ω, kΩ, volts, and source polarity before wiring.
Click one terminal, then the destination terminal, to draw a wire. Use clear wire routes and colour consistently. A wire that only crosses another wire is not automatically a junction.
Trace the finished path from the positive source terminal back to the negative terminal. Compare every node with the course schematic.

This is an actual Tinkercad Circuits workspace. The incomplete starter contains the parts but does not give away the wiring.



Actual Tinkercad Circuits workspace with two power supplies, three resistors, a multimeter, the Components panel, and Start Simulation button.


Clicking a resistor opens the real settings panel. Type the number in Resistance and confirm the unit menu before wiring.



Actual Tinkercad resistor settings panel with a Resistance field and kilohm unit menu.


Use Schematic view to check the finished topology. The starter below is still unwired, so its components appear without connection lines. After you wire the circuit, the lines should match the source schematic.



Actual Tinkercad Schematic view of the unwired starter with two supplies and three labelled resistors but no connection lines.

title: Build and Measure Circuits in Tinkercad
text:
2. Simulate and measure
Choose Start Simulation. Stop the simulation before moving wires or changing values.

Voltage: set the multimeter to voltage and place its probes across two nodes. This is a parallel connection.
Current: open the branch and place the meter in the current path. This is a series connection. Never place an ammeter directly across a source.
Resistance: stop the simulation and remove power before measuring across the part or equivalent network.

Record the sign as well as the magnitude. A negative voltage or current often means the probes or assumed direction are reversed; it is evidence to interpret, not a value to hide.

title: Build and Measure Circuits in Tinkercad
text:
3. Compare the evidence
Use full precision for the calculation, then round the reported values to sensible significant figures.










Quantity and location
Predicted
Simulated
Absolute difference
Percentage difference




Voltage (V)






Current (mA)






Resistance (Ω)






Power (mW)







Calculate absolute difference with
\[
\Delta x=\left|x_{\mathrm{simulated}}-x_{\mathrm{predicted}}\right|.
\tag{1}\]
When the predicted reference is not zero, calculate
\[
\%\text{ difference}=\frac{\Delta x}{\left|x_{\mathrm{predicted}}\right|}\times 100\%.
\tag{2}\]
If the predicted value is zero, percentage difference is undefined. Report the absolute difference and explain whether the simulated value is small enough for the purpose.

title: Build and Measure Circuits in Tinkercad
text:
The problem
Your simulated measurement does not match your prediction closely enough to trust the result.
The essential skill: compare one node, one value, and one meter connection at a time.
The challenge: locate the cause, correct it, and preserve one screenshot or note showing what changed.
The stumbling block: a circuit can look similar while one wire ends in the wrong breadboard row, a resistor uses the wrong unit, or the ammeter bypasses a load.
The investigation: use Tinkercad’s built-in tutorials and search its component panel by the exact component name. Ask: What do you know, what do you need to find out, and how will you know when you are right?






TipHint 1: concept clue





Check whether the mismatch affects the whole circuit or only one branch. That tells you where to begin tracing.









TipHint 2: documentation clue





Review Wiring Components, Editing Components, and Ohm’s Law from the official Tinkercad Circuits page. Search for the exact meter mode you need.









TipHint 3: technical clue





Stop the simulation. Confirm source polarity, resistor units, shared breadboard rows, and every meter connection. Restart and test one known node before rebuilding the circuit.

The simulated topology and labels match the source schematic.

Voltage is measured across two nodes; current is measured through a branch.

title: Series Circuits
text:
Series and parallel
A series circuit has one path, so the current is the same everywhere. A parallel circuit has branches that share the same two nodes, so each branch has the same voltage.



Figure 1. Series-circuit reference schematic. The same current passes through every component. #


Opening any component stops current everywhere.

title: Series Circuits
text:
General rules
\[
I_k = I_T
\tag{1}\]
\[
R_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} R_k
\tag{2}\]
\[
V_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} V_k
\tag{3}\]
\[
P_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} P_k = V_T I_T
\tag{4}\]
\[
I_T = \frac{V_T}{R_T}
\tag{5}\]
\[
V_k = I_T R_k
\tag{6}\]

How sigma notation works
\[
R_T=R_{eq}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}R_k=R_1+R_2+\cdots+R_n
\tag{7}\]
\[
V_T=\sum_{k=1}^{n}V_k=V_1+V_2+\cdots+V_n
\tag{8}\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(R_T\) or \(R_{eq}\)
total or equivalent resistance


\(R_k\) or \(V_k\)
the value at position \(k\)


\(k\)
the index variable; it changes through \(1,2,3,\ldots,n\)


\(n\)
the fixed last index; the sum stops here



\(\Sigma\) means add each term while \(k\) runs from \(1\) to \(n\). The final expanded term is \(R_n\) or \(V_n\). Keep full calculator precision until the final answer.
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n} V_k \overset{?}{=} V_T
\tag{9}\]
Use Equation Equation 9 to check the voltage drops. Also check power ratings.

title: Series Circuits
text:
Worked solutions
Questions 2 and 4 are provided as student models. Complete the other questions independently using the same GUESS structure.






NoteQuestion 2: Complete series analysis





Given: \(V_T=15.0\,\mathrm{V}\), \(R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=2.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_3=3.3\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\).
\[
R_T=R_1+R_2+R_3=6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
\tag{10}\]
\[
I_T=\frac{V_T}{R_T}=\frac{15.0\,\mathrm{V}}{6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}=2.307692\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}
\tag{11}\]
Using \(V_k=I_TR_k\) gives \(V_1=2.307692\ldots\,\mathrm{V}\), \(V_2=5.076923\ldots\,\mathrm{V}\), and \(V_3=7.615385\ldots\,\mathrm{V}\).
Final answers: \(R_T=6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(I_T=2.3\,\mathrm{mA}\), \(V_1=2.3\,\mathrm{V}\), \(V_2=5.1\,\mathrm{V}\), \(V_3=7.6\,\mathrm{V}\), and \(P_T=35\,\mathrm{mW}\).
Check: Use the unrounded values: \(V_1+V_2+V_3=15.0\,\mathrm{V}\).









NoteQuestion 4: Choose a dropping resistor





Given: a \(6.0\,\mathrm{V}\), \(80\,\mathrm{mA}\) lamp on a \(9.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source.
\[
V_R=V_T-V_L=9.0\,\mathrm{V}-6.0\,\mathrm{V}=3.0\,\mathrm{V}
\tag{12}\]
\[
R=\frac{V_R}{I}=\frac{3.0\,\mathrm{V}}{80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}}=37.5\,\Omega
\tag{13}\]
\[
P_R=V_RI=(3.0\,\mathrm{V})(80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A})=0.240\,\mathrm{W}
\tag{14}\]
Final answer: the calculated value is \(37.5\,\Omega\). Choose the next common 5% value, \(39\,\Omega\), rated for at least \(0.5\,\mathrm{W}\).
Key note: A \(0.25\,\mathrm{W}\) resistor is too close to the calculated \(0.240\,\mathrm{W}\) load.

Linear Algebra for Circuits
text:
Solve and check
Use substitution or elimination for a small system. Use a simultaneous-equation or matrix solver for a larger system. Keep the variable order and units consistent, then substitute the answer into the original equations or calculate the residual:
\[
\mathbf{r}=A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}
\tag{4}\]
\[
\mathbf{r}\approx\mathbf{0}
\tag{5}\]
A large residual can flag a wrong sign, wrong measurement, or wiring fault.

Worked solutions
On the course calculator, the Casio fx-991ES PLUS C, press MODE, then 5 for EQN. Press 1 for two unknowns or 2 for three unknowns. Enter each coefficient in equation order and press = after every value; after the final coefficient, each additional = displays the next solution. This sequence is verified against the official Casio fx-991ES PLUS C equation guide.






NoteQuestion 2: Solve a two-by-two system





Enter the rows \((10,-4,6)\) and \((-4,12,3)\).
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & -4 \\
-4 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
I_1 \\ I_2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
6 \\ 3
\end{bmatrix}
\tag{6}\]
Final answers: \(I_1=0.808\,\mathrm{mA}\) and \(I_2=0.519\,\mathrm{mA}\).
Substitution into both original rows gives a residual of approximately zero.









NoteQuestion 4: Solve a three-by-three system





Enter the coefficient rows \((10,-2,0,5)\), \((-2,12,-3,6)\), and \((0,-3,9,4)\). The zeros keep the variable columns aligned.
Final answers: \(I_1=0.657\,\mathrm{mA}\), \(I_2=0.786\,\mathrm{mA}\), and \(I_3=0.706\,\mathrm{mA}\).
Substitute the three currents into all three original rows to check the solution.

Significant figures
Significant figures show the precision of a measured or stated value. Keep full calculator precision and round once, at the end.
0.00420 has three significant figures.
\(6.23 \times 1.23 = 7.6629\), reported as 7.66.
For multiplication and division, use the same number of significant figures as the least precise input. For addition and subtraction, use the least precise decimal place.

\(27\,000 = 2.7 \times 10^4 = 27 \times 10^3 = 27\,\mathrm{k}\) \(0.00047 = 4.7 \times 10^{-4} = 470 \times 10^{-6} = 470\,\mu\)

title: Circuits
text:
Ohm’s law and power
Ohm’s law connects voltage, current, and resistance.
\[
V = IR \qquad I = \frac{V}{R} \qquad R = \frac{V}{I}
\tag{1}\]
Equation Equation 1 gives the three general forms of Ohm’s law.
Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer:
\[
P = VI \qquad P = I^2R \qquad P = \frac{V^2}{R}
\tag{2}\]
Use Equation Equation 2 only after identifying the known quantities.
Use volts (V), amperes (A), ohms (\(\Omega\)), and watts (W). Convert prefixes before substituting, then report the final answer with the appropriate prefix and significant figures.

title: Circuits
text:
GUESS method
Put each part on its own line.
G: Given: list each known value with its symbol and unit.
U: Unknown: list each value you must find.
E: Equation: choose a general equation.
S: Substitute: rearrange first, then substitute values with units.
S: Solve: show the unrounded result, check it, then round once.
For a Casio calculator, enter one calculation per line. Use EXP for powers of ten. Write units beside the result, not in the calculator.

        Solve simultaneous circuit equations by substitution, elimination, and matrices.
        The method prepares students for college and university network analysis.
        Slides Current Problem Set Quick Reference Teacher Answers, restricted
      
    
    
      
        14. Build and Measure Circuits in Tinkercad▾
        Build a low-voltage circuit, run the simulation, measure it, and compare the evidence with a calculation.
        Simulation provides a safe, repeatable bridge between schematic analysis and physical measurement.
        Tinkercad Circuits
      
    
  


  
    6. Computer Systems2 lessons
  
  
    
      
        1. Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts▾
        Use power and static precautions, identify the main internal parts, and compare HDD, SATA SSD, and M.2 storage.
        Safe part recognition prepares students to inspect and service a desktop computer.
      
    
    
      
        2. USB, Peripherals, and Cable Management▾
        Recognize USB connector shapes, check USB-C capabilities, connect common peripherals, and route cables cleanly.
        A serviceable workstation is easier to use, inspect, and troubleshoot.
      
    
  


  
    7. Linux and Operating Systems12 lessons
  
  
    
      
        1. Choosing a Linux Distribution▾
        Compare distribution families, desktop environments, hardware needs, software, and support.
        A good choice matches the computer and the work instead of following a brand name.
        Slides
      
    
    
      
        2. Install Linux Mint▾
        Prepare installation media, protect data, install Mint, and verify the result.
        The procedure supports computer recovery and prepares a system for later projects.
        Slides Linux Mint Installation Reflection
      
    
    
      
        3. Explore Linux▾
        Complete Computer Detective, explore Bashcrawl, and customize the Linux Mint desktop using separate submission contracts.
        The activities build confidence before students administer or program the system.
        Slides 3.1 Computer Detective 3.2 Bashcrawl 3.3 Sleek Out Linux Mint Linux Offline Kit
      
    
    
      
        4. Know Your Linux Computer▾
        Record hardware, operating-system, storage, and device information.
        A verified inventory supports troubleshooting, upgrades, and performance comparisons.
      
    
    
      
        5. Files, Terminal, and Permissions▾
        Navigate paths, inspect files, and use permissions safely.
        These skills are essential for administration, automation, and development.
      
    
    
      
        6. Git Version Control▾
        Record, inspect, and share changes with a safe Git workflow.
        Version control protects project history and supports collaboration.
      
    
    
      
        7. Build a Quarto Website▾
        Turn Markdown, code, and media into a small technical website.
        A website makes project evidence and explanations easy to review and share.
      
    
    
      
        8. Publish with GitHub Pages▾
        Publish a reviewed static site without exposing secrets or private files.
        Deployment turns local documentation into a durable public portfolio.
      
    
    
      
        9. Python Measurement Logging▾
        Write a small Python program that records measurements with units and timestamps.
        Logging supports sensor tests, performance studies, and repeatable experiments.
      
    
    
      
        10. Python Analysis and Curve Fitting▾
        Inspect recorded data and fit a simple model.
        Analysis connects observations to engineering decisions and predictions.
      
    
    
      
        11. Networking, SSH, and tmux▾
        Diagnose a network connection and manage a remote Linux session safely.
        Remote administration is common for servers, Raspberry Pi systems, and lab equipment.
      
    
    
      
        12. Power and Raspberry Pi Bridge▾
        Connect computer power concepts to a future Raspberry Pi build without inventing a lab.
        The calculation bridge prepares students to reason about supplies, loads, and interfaces.
      
    
  


  
    8. Networking3 lessons
  
  
    
      
        1. How Wi-Fi and Ethernet Connect▾
        Trace data through an access point or cable, a switch, a router, and Internet service.
        Separating the jobs of Wi-Fi, switching, and routing makes network faults easier to locate.
      
    
    
      
        2. Ethernet Cable Categories and Speeds▾
        Compare Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6A, and Cat8 and identify the 8P8C plug commonly called RJ45.
        Cable labels and limits help students choose an appropriate connection instead of guessing by colour.
      
    
    
      
        3. Build and Test an Ethernet Cable▾
        Terminate both ends in T568B order, inspect the crimp, and verify all eight conductors with a tester.
        A complete build-and-test procedure turns cable theory into reliable classroom work.
      
    
  


  
    9. Computational Engineering9 lessons
  
  
    
      
        1. Python Engineering Notebooks with JupyterLite▾
        Open, run, edit, save, download, and submit engineering notebooks in a browser.
        The browser workflow works without a local install or new account when the school permits JupyterLite.
        Notebook Bundle
      
    
    
      
        2. Circuit Quest: Power the Grid▾
        Rotate circuit tiles, complete three paths, light lamps, and see how a branch carries power.
        A short clickable game gives students an immediate success experience in Jupyter before the longer circuit assignment.
        Circuit Quest Notebook
      
    
    
      
        3. Assignment: Python First Steps▾
        Start from zero with notebook cells, printing, calculator operations, variables, four basic types, lists, and one small NumPy array.
        Students learn the minimum Python and Jupyter vocabulary needed before the larger NumPy and circuit notebooks.
        Python First Steps Notebook
      
    
    
      
        4. Run Python and Jupyter on Your Own Computer▾
        Choose a Jupyter route for Windows with WSL, macOS, Linux, native Windows, or Google Colab.
        Local Jupyter gives students more control over files, packages, and hardware; Colab remains a no-install fallback.
        Notebook Requirements Google Colab
      
    
    
      
        5. Assignment: Python and NumPy Foundations▾
        Continue from Python basics to NumPy arrays, plotting, documentation lookup, and evidence-based debugging before circuit linear algebra.
        Students complete a resistor investigation with vectorized calculations, a reusable function, assertions, a graph, Markdown explanations, and one documentation-driven repair.
        Python and NumPy Notebook NumPy Documentation
      
    
    
      
        6. Find Documentation and Ask for Programming Help▾
        Reproduce a problem, search official documentation and Stack Overflow, and ask a complete technical question.
        Students learn to provide minimal code, exact errors, environment details, attempted fixes, sources, and a reasoned hypothesis when requesting help.
        Stack Overflow: How to Ask pandas Documentation
      
    
    
      
        7. Assignment: From Two Loops to a Matrix▾
        Derive two signed KVL equations, arrange them in matrix form, and solve the same system numerically and symbolically.
        The guided bridge teaches the missing step between loop traversal and a reproducible computational solution without creating another five-question package.
        Printable Two-Loop Guide Two-Loop Matrix Notebook Notebook Bundle
      
    
    
      
        8. Jupyter Electronics Lab▾
        Complete a simulation-first electronics pathway while components, instruments, or soldered kits are unavailable.
        Students apply documentation, debugging, calculations, models, graphs, checks, and investigations before adding physical validation.
        Notebook Bundle RC and Op-Amp Calculus Notebook
      
    
    
      
        9. Life Checkpoint Upgrade: Jupyter + Tinkercad▾
        Digitize and correct the Life Checkpoint, solve it with NumPy, and verify the same circuit in Tinkercad.
        The two-day reassessment joins the existing checkpoint, LaTeX, Python, matrices, simulation, and measurement in one opportunity to improve the checkpoint mark to 100%.
        Student Notebook Tinkercad Circuits
      
    
  


  
    10. Robotics and Control Systems1 lesson
  
  
    
      
        1. Robotics and Control Sequence (planned)▾
        The public package sequence is planned.
        It will connect diagrams, code, measurements, and physical tests.
      
    
  


  
    11. Engineering Preparation1 lesson
  
  
    
      
        1. Engineering Preparation Track (planned)▾
        Use the concise track overview, including the optional XL741 signal-and-calculus bridge, with its current notes and problem sets.
        The page connects existing packages to recognizable engineering systems and introduces calculus through measured circuit behaviour.
