title: Accessible Design
text:
Graphics Accommodation Guide



Accessible design is not a separate style. It is the work of making sure the idea survives small type, colour changes, busy backgrounds, printing, projection, and fabrication.
These four lessons use the explanations and examples from the original guide, reorganized into a shorter path for students.






A serif capital H beside a sans serif capital H. Decorative strokes are marked around the serif letter.





Hue, saturation, and value shown as three separate colour scales.





High-contrast black and white text above two low-contrast colour combinations.

title: Accessible Design
text:
Accessible design is not a separate style. It is the work of making sure the idea survives small type, colour changes, busy backgrounds, printing, projection, and fabrication.
These four lessons use the explanations and examples from the original guide, reorganized into a shorter path for students.

title: Accessible Design
text:
Zoom out before choosing
Check the design at its real output size and from the expected viewing distance before choosing a font, colour, line thickness, or level of detail.


See it
Can the important parts be found quickly?


Read it
Do size, spacing, and letter shapes hold up?


Understand it
Does the message work without colour alone?


Make it
Will the design survive print, projection, or fabrication?

title: Accessible Design
text:
Follow the guide





Google Docs showing the Alt text panel for a selected image.



Lesson 1

Access & Alt Text
Decide what an image contributes, then describe that purpose for someone who cannot see it.







The words Properly stroked, Properly outlined, Thickly stroked, and Thickly outlined show how line weight changes letter shapes.



Lesson 2

Fonts & Text Effects
Choose readable type and use backgrounds, outlines, and shadows only when they help the letters stay clear.







A colour wheel shown in full colour and in greyscale. Several different hues become similar grey values.



Lesson 3

Understanding Colour
Separate hue, saturation, and value, then connect them to RGB, CMYK, opacity, and output.







Three panels label red with green text and blue with lighter blue text as bad choices, and green with pale yellow text as a good choice.



Lesson 4

Contrast, Emphasis & Output
Measure contrast, add a second cue beside colour, and test the actual screen, print, or fabricated result.





Source and approach. The sequence applies the BBC guidance for visually and hearing impaired audiences, including clear contrast, useful labels, alt text, and explaining essential visual information in the page text. New graphics are used only when the website needs a clearer or more flexible explanation.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
I can use colour for emphasis without making colour the only cue.
I can measure text and graphic contrast.
I can test the final screen, print, or fabricated result and revise it.







Note



The lesson applies the BBC guidance for visually and hearing impaired audiences. WCAG 2.2 ratios are added so students have a measurable test as well as a visual comparison.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
I can use colour for emphasis without making colour the only cue.
I can measure text and graphic contrast.
I can test the final screen, print, or fabricated result and revise it.







Note



The lesson applies the BBC guidance for visually and hearing impaired audiences. WCAG 2.2 ratios are added so students have a measurable test as well as a visual comparison.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Why this is useful
“Looks different” is not a reliable contrast test. Two colours can have different hues and still be almost the same lightness. Measure the pair, then test the real output.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Use a measurable minimum


Clear contrast
12.6:1 · comfortably above the minimum


Minimum contrast
4.5:1 · passes for normal-size text


Weak contrast
2.0:1 · fails for text and essential graphics


Large text, at least 24 px regular or about 18.5 px bold, can use 3:1. Essential icons, controls, and graphic boundaries also need 3:1. Do not round: 4.49:1 does not meet 4.5:1.
These are WCAG 2.2 Level AA thresholds for digital content. They are a starting point, not a promise that every person or output device will find the result easy to use. Aim higher when you can.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Compare the guide’s examples




Black text on white and white text on black are labelled good contrast. Pale green on yellow and pale grey on light grey are labelled bad contrast.



Light-dark difference matters
The top two pairs have a large value difference. The bottom pairs do not. Source noted in the guide.






Six colour pairs place bad contrast examples in a left column and better contrast versions in a right column.



Hue is not enough
Changing the background value makes each word easier to separate, even when the hue remains similar. Source noted in the guide.






Green text on red and pale blue text on blue are labelled bad choices. Pale yellow text on dark green is labelled a good choice.



Some pairs interfere
Red-green and similar-blue pairs can fail for different reasons. The final pair adds a clear light-dark difference. Source noted in the guide.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Do not use colour alone
If colour communicates a status, category, warning, or selected state, add another cue.


Add a label
Write Pass and Revise, not just green and red dots.


Add a shape or pattern
Use different marker shapes, line styles, or fill patterns in a chart.


Add position
Keep categories in a stable order and label them directly.


Add emphasis
Use weight, size, an icon, or a border together with colour.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Test the real result

Check the design at its final size, not only while zoomed in.
Use a contrast checker for digital text and essential graphics.
View a greyscale copy.
Test on the target projector, printer, material, cutter, or engraver.
Show it without explaining it. Ask what the person noticed first and what was difficult to understand.
Revise and test again.

For fabrication, make a small sample before the final piece. Check thin lines, small gaps, inside spaces, surface finish, and lighting.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Check your work

Normal-size text meets at least 4.5:1.
Large text and essential non-text graphics meet at least 3:1.
Colour is never the only signal.
Text over a photograph has a dependable background or a tested halo.
The real output has been checked from the expected viewing distance.

title: Contrast, Emphasis & Output
text:
Summary
Measure contrast, add a second cue, and test the actual output. Return to the Accessible Design guide and use the four checks before publishing.
Sources: W3C Understanding Contrast Minimum, W3C Understanding Non-text Contrast, and W3C Understanding Use of Color.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
text:
Finished organizers

    Portable utility-knife organizer
    A full-size annotated photo shows why the organizer is easy to carry, easy to use and able to stand on a bench. The page also shows the drawing, two documented iterations and a possible one-sided French-cleat version.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
section: What makes a good tool holder?
text:
What makes a good tool holder?







Design criterion
What a student should be able to show




Visible inventory
Every tool or part has a visible position. A missing item can be noticed quickly.


Clear labels
Names, sizes, outlines or colour-independent symbols show where each item belongs.


Easy access
A user can see the handle, grip it and remove or return the tool without moving neighbouring tools.


Secure fit
The holder supports the tool without being so tight that normal removal becomes difficult. Sharp or fragile parts are protected.


Freestanding stability
The holder stands on its own and does not tip when a tool is removed from an outside position.


Wall option
The design can include a tested wall interface, such as a French cleat, while still allowing safe removal or service. Mounting hardware must suit the actual wall and load.


Stacking or modularity
Modules can align, connect or stack without hiding labels, blocking tools or becoming unstable.


Simple construction
Parts, joints and fasteners are understandable, buildable and replaceable.



Not every holder needs every feature. Choose the criteria that matter for the tools, user and location, then test those claims.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
text:
A practical test

Glance test: Can another student identify every tool and notice what is missing?
Reach test: Can the user remove and return each tool with a natural grip?
Tip test: Does the organizer remain stable when the heaviest outside tool is removed?
Carry test: Can it be moved without loose tools falling out or the structure flexing?
Mount test: If it hangs, can it be attached, removed and loaded without pulling away, rotating or lifting off accidentally?

Record the result of each test. A claim such as “wall-mountable,” “portable” or “stable” is not complete until the actual interface has been built and tested.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
text:
From measurements to a prototype

Compare the finished examples and decide which features fit the real tools and user.
Measure the real tools, including handles, collars, tapers and the hand clearance needed for removal.
Draw the concept using orthographic views and an isometric or assembly view.
Use the Fabrication Plate Builder for plates, rings and repeated holder holes.
Use the Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder when the organizer needs a freestanding base, legs or a rear support.
Browse the Laser-Cut Gallery for reusable geometry and design directions.
Make a small fit test before building the complete prototype.
Photograph the build, collect feedback and record the next revision.

title: Tool Organizer Gallery
text:
Add a future build
Each new organizer page should include a full finished photo, the original drawing, the problem, key dimensions, materials, fabrication method, what worked, feedback, the next revision, downloads where appropriate and a clear validation status.
Do not mark a design “validated” merely because a file renders or a digital assembly looks plausible. Distinguish drawing available, dimension-tested, fit-tested, shop-tested and photo documented. If evidence is missing, say so instead of filling the gap with a stock or generated image.

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text: This browser tool makes repeatable plate geometry. It opens in inches. A millimetre toggle remains available when a machine or material specification needs it; changing the unit converts the current values instead of changing the physical size. The downloaded SVG keeps the selected physical unit. The tool does not choose safe material, machine settings, joints, mounting hardware, or a final fit.

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text:
What the downloads contain

Cut SVG: the actual full-size plate outline and circular or rectangular openings. Open this in Inkscape or compatible laser software. Red paths are cut geometry. Optional guides, including the A-D corner labels, are not cut paths.
Settings JSON: a text record of every builder value. It is useful for documentation or troubleshooting, but it is not a laser-cut file and this version of the builder does not import it.
Share link: the current settings stored in the web address. Send or bookmark this when you want the builder to reopen the same design.


Circle and rectangle dimensions, without the jargon

For a circle, set Outer diameter. The tool calculates its radius as half the diameter.
For a ring, set Outer diameter and Ring wall thickness. The ring’s inner opening is the outer diameter minus twice the wall thickness.
For a rounded rectangle, set Width, Height, and Corner radius. Corner radius affects only the four outside corners.
For centre and repeated pattern openings, choose Circle or Rectangle. Every opening in that pattern uses the same shape and dimensions. Circle patterns can size from a measured object plus clearance or use a direct finished diameter.
Turn off Add centre or repeated pattern openings when you want only the plate outline. The optional A-D corner openings are controlled separately and can remain on or off.
Pattern rectangle width runs left to right and length runs top to bottom. Rows, grids, radial layouts, perimeter layouts, centre spacing, validation and SVG export all work with either pattern shape.
For corner openings, choose Circle or Rectangle for all four at once, then override any labelled corner if needed. Rectangle width runs left to right; rectangle length runs top to bottom.
Shape centre measures from each adjoining plate edge to the centre of the opening. Nearest edge of shape measures the remaining material between the cutout and those straight edges. The preview labels the corners A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right) and D (bottom left).

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text:
What happens next


1 · BuilderSet the base, measured opening, pattern and spacing. Resolve every red validation message.


2 · InkscapeOpen the SVG at 100%, confirm the document units and dimensions, then add labels, slots or project-specific geometry.


3 · Test couponUse the laser fabrication library to test the actual stock, machine and fit.


4 · OnshapeUse CAD when the design depends on 3D joints, motion, assemblies, toleranced interfaces or more than one plane.


The laser fabrication library is the idea and part library. This builder generates repeated plate geometry. Inkscape is the 2D finishing environment. Onshape is the better tool for assemblies and 3D relationships. These are complementary workflows, not interchangeable buttons.
Need supports for the plate? Open the Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder to generate straight, angled, triangular, cross-foot or rear-easel parts with measured slots.
Planning the complete holder? Use the Tool Organizer Gallery and design criteria to check visibility, labels, access, stability, wall mounting and modularity.

title: Tinkercad Faux-Enamel Logo Earring or Brooch
text:
New to Tinkercad? Start here
Complete this short introduction before beginning the logo. Keep Tinkercad open in one window and this lesson or the video open beside it. Pause whenever you need to copy an action.






Watch and follow

Watch the interface tour beginning at 4:45.
At 7:40, open a new design and follow along with the first build.
At 28:47, watch how an STL is exported for 3D printing.

Open Autodesk’s guided 3D-design basics Open the complete video



Five-minute practice build
Before using your logo, prove that you can control a simple shape:

Create a new 3D design and rename it lastname-tinkercad-practice.
Drag a Cylinder onto the workplane. Set its length and width to 30 mm and its height to 3 mm.
Orbit, pan and zoom until you can inspect the top, front and side.
Duplicate the cylinder. Make the copy 24 × 24 × 1 mm and raise it 3 mm above the workplane.
Select both cylinders, choose Align, and select the two centre dots.
Group the parts, then undo once so you know how to recover from a mistake.
Export the practice object as an STL.

You are ready when you can view, size, raise, align, group, undo and export without guessing. Autodesk also provides a printable Tinkercad getting-started and keyboard-shortcut guide.
Do not copy a company, team, game, social-media or clothing logo. Use the logo you created in Photopea, or create another original, teacher-approved design.
Read this as a third-angle orthographic drawing: the top view is above the front view, and the right-side view is placed to the right. The exterior views establish the shape and dimensions; section A–A shows how the two colour fills sit above the 3 mm base and between the 1 mm raised walls.

text:
Step 3: Add the outer rim

Import circle-rim.svg at the same diameter as the base.
Set its Height to 1 mm.
Raise it 3 mm above the workplane. Press Ctrl + Up Arrow three times.
Confirm that the rim sits on the base and creates an enclosed pocket. It must not hang past the edge.

title: Tinkercad Faux-Enamel Logo Earring or Brooch
section: Step 4: Import and size the logo
text:
Step 4: Import and size the logo

Select Import and choose your original SVG logo.
Use the target logo width from the dimension table.
Keep the logo centred inside the rim.
Remove tiny details that create narrow, fragile walls or pockets that a nail-polish brush cannot reach.

For the AA arrow, use the simpler arrow/lettermark without small text. For the Technology Commons example, use the circular lighthouse emblem without the words around it. Make that version a 50–60 mm brooch, not an earring.



Import the SVG: the reference uses a heart, but your project uses the circular base and your original logo. Confirm that the imported lines are clean before continuing. Screenshot: kura_kura / Instructables, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

title: Tinkercad Faux-Enamel Logo Earring or Brooch
text:
Step 5: Make the logo fillable
For the preferred full faux-enamel version:

Select the imported logo.
Open Fill Mode.
Choose Inner Line so the boundary becomes a wall and the logo becomes a recessed pocket.
Adjust the line width until every wall is at least 1.2 mm wide.
Set Height to 1 mm.
Raise the logo 3 mm above the workplane with Ctrl + Up Arrow three times.

For the easier one-colour-fill version, leave Fill Mode at Default, set Height to 1 mm, and raise the logo 3 mm.



Duplicate before editing: keep one copy for the raised detail and use the other to create the solid base. Separating the copies temporarily makes it easier to see which part you are changing. Screenshot: kura_kura / Instructables, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.





Change the fill mode: use Inner Line to create raised boundaries. Use the solid version for the flat base. Check the preview closely before aligning the parts. Screenshot: kura_kura / Instructables, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

title: Tinkercad Faux-Enamel Logo Earring or Brooch
text:
Step 6: Align and inspect

Select the base, rim and logo.
Select Align.
Use the two centre alignment dots so all three parts share the same centre.
Orbit the view and inspect the model from the top, side and bottom.
Confirm that every polish area is completely enclosed.
Confirm that the back is flat and uninterrupted.
Select all parts and press Ctrl + G to group them.

Do not continue if a cavity leaks through the rim, a wall is extremely thin, or a pocket is too small to fill cleanly.



Align and inspect: centre the raised detail on the base, set the upper feature to 1 mm and orbit to a low side view. Your circular version should have the same flat base and clearly enclosed pockets. Screenshot: kura_kura / Instructables, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

title: Tinkercad Faux-Enamel Logo Earring or Brooch
text:
Step 7: Export for printing

Select the grouped model.
Select Export.
Choose The selected shape.
Choose .STL.
Name the file lastname-logo-earring.stl or lastname-logo-brooch.stl.
Open the STL in the class slicer and inspect every layer before printing.

Print the badge flat with the decorated face upward unless the teacher approves a different orientation.

title: Tinkercad Faux-Enamel Logo Earring or Brooch
text:
Finish the faux enamel

Let the printed part cool completely and remove any loose strings.
Test the polish on a failed print or sample first.
Place a small drop of polish into a cavity.
Guide it to the edges with the brush or a toothpick. Do not cover the raised walls.
Apply two or three thin coats, allowing each coat to dry.
Let the finished piece cure fully before gluing hardware or wearing it.

Use only teacher-approved polish and finishing products, with the ventilation and protective procedures required by the school.

title: Tinkercad Faux-Enamel Logo Earring or Brooch
text:
Glue on the finding

Earring
Use an 8–10 mm stainless-steel flat-pad earring post with a matching back. The post pad must fit completely on the flat rear surface.


Brooch
Use a 20–25 mm glue-on bar pin with a flat base.
Lightly roughen only the glue area and remove dust. A teacher may apply a small amount of Loctite Super Glue Gel Control or another school-approved adhesive after testing it on the printed material. Five-minute epoxy is a stronger, more gap-filling option but requires more mixing, curing time and handling controls. Hot glue is not a durable jewellery attachment.
Do not wear the product until the polish and adhesive are completely cured. Do not claim that an earring finding is hypoallergenic unless the supplier documents the exact material.

Follow your school board’s safety guidelines and the course-specific information provided by your teacher; students in Mr.� Andrade’s classes can find it in Google Classroom.



The project moves from an original sketch to an editable Onshape model, slicing and orientation, printing and finishing, then evidence-based revision.

title: Parametric Faux Enamel Pin / Jewellery | Later Onshape Project
text:
Design-to-revision process


Sketch or choose an original graphic. State the meaning and intended wearer/viewer.


Simplify it for small-scale production. Remove tiny counters, narrow islands and details that will not survive printing or finishing.


Rebuild/model it parametrically in Onshape. Use constrained sketches and intentional dimensions instead of importing a finished 3D answer.


Create raised or recessed regions. Make boundaries appropriate for the intended visual effect and finishing process.


Confirm dimensions and thicknesses. Inspect overall size, base, details, holes and any attachment interface.


Export STL or 3MF. Retain the editable Onshape source and identify the exported version.


Slice. Inspect every layer, walls, top/bottom layers, infill, travel and estimated time/material.


Decide print orientation. Compare visual face quality, layer direction, supports, adhesion and strength.


Print. Use the course-specific process provided by your teacher.


Finish and colour. Use only teacher-approved methods and allow coatings/adhesives to cure fully.


Evaluate. Check legibility, surface finish, colour boundaries, comfort, attachment and durability.


Revise the source model. Tie at least one change to measured or observed evidence.

title: Parametric Faux Enamel Pin / Jewellery | Later Onshape Project
text:
Minimum-detail and test strategy
Do not copy a universal minimum feature size. It depends on nozzle, layer height, orientation, material, slicer, finishing method and printer condition. Place several representative line widths, gaps or colour wells in a small test piece before committing to a full class batch.



The same badge printed flat or upright creates different face-quality, support, layer-direction and adhesion questions.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
Parametric / solid CAD
Mesh / artistic modelling




Sketches, constraints, dimensions and feature history describe design intent.
Vertices, edges and faces describe the visible surface.


Best default for holes, brackets, patterns, mating parts and predictable revision.
Excellent for organic, sculptural, character, rendering and animation work.


Primary classroom tool: Onshape.
Primary artistic tool: Blender.






Parametric CAD uses constraints, dimensions and features for predictable change; mesh modelling uses vertices, edges and faces to shape visible form.


Blender can make printable models, but it is not the default for dimension-driven mechanical or fabrication parts. Onshape is the primary fabrication-modelling tool because a student can change a dimension and inspect how the whole model updates.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
Additive manufacturing
Unlike subtractive processes that remove material or forming processes that reshape it, additive manufacturing creates a part layer by layer. The model must become a printable toolpath, so model, slicer, machine, material and orientation all influence the result.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
Model with intent
Begin from a measured need in Onshape. Use fully considered sketches, geometric constraints, exact dimensions and named variables where useful. Build features in a sequence another person can understand and revise.
Core operations include extrude, remove, hole, fillet/chamfer, pattern and mirror. Use each because it describes the intended geometry, not merely because it produces the visible shape once. Change one controlling dimension and confirm that related features update predictably.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
section: Keep the source; export for the next job
text:
Keep the source; export for the next job

Editable source modelSTEP when solid interchange is neededSTL or 3MF for slicingSlicer project + toolpathPrinter


STEP can transfer solid geometry between compatible CAD systems.
STL carries a triangulated surface but normally no units, colour or feature history.
3MF can carry units and richer manufacturing information; support depends on the software and printer workflow.

An exported mesh is not the editable master. Retain the Onshape document/source model and record which version produced the manufacturing file.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
First modelling task
Model a small identity badge or labelled spacer with controlled width, height, hole diameter, wall thickness and edge treatment. Use constraints rather than visual guessing. Change one parameter and confirm the model updates predictably. Export STL or 3MF for slicing while retaining the editable source.

Is the body watertight and intended as one part or several?
Are walls and small features plausible for the selected process?
Can critical dimensions be traced to a measurement or requirement?
Is the part oriented in CAD for clarity, even if print orientation changes later?
Is the editable source saved alongside the exported manufacturing file?

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Bill-of-material and parameter routine
For any selected reference:

Measure at least three bottles: body diameter, cap diameter, height and any taper.
Choose the controlling diameter and required radial clearance.
Calculate opening = largest measured body + 2 × radial clearance.
Set centre spacing from cap diameter, hand access and remaining material, not appearance alone.
Update part dimensions and BOM before nesting.
Cut an opening coupon, record actual fit, then revise the source.
Dry-assemble; test insertion, removal, labels, tipping and collisions.

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Physical-test record
All five files currently have status unverified. Do not change that label because the SVG opens correctly. Record the material, measured thickness, machine, settings reference, date, tester, actual opening, fit result, load and revision before promoting a design to fit-tested or shop-tested.

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Reference systems worth studying
The sketches below are original Technology Commons diagrams, not copied product images. Follow each source to inspect the actual system and its licence. Borrow a principle only after checking dimensions, load, access, fabrication method and the source’s current terms.






French cleat


Principle: a continuous angled interface makes modules movable while the lower stand-off controls tilt.


Adapt: add an anti-lift or anti-slide feature where impact is possible.


Source: Wikipedia contributors · page content CC BY-SA · reference link · original schematic here is AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Gridfinity


Principle: a shared pitch lets containers move without redesigning the whole storage field.


Adapt: use a consistent centre spacing or interface datum across shop modules.


Source: Zack Freedman / Voidstar Lab and Kenneth Hodson’s rebuild · MIT · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







openGrid


Principle: a regular wall field separates the mounting interface from each accessory.


Adapt: document one interface and test light- and heavy-duty versions separately.


Source: David D / openGrid contributors · core parts CC BY · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Pegstr


Principle: parametric holders begin with the object and the host-board standard.


Adapt: measure both; do not assume imported inch pegboard dimensions match local stock.


Source: MGX3D · CC BY-NC · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







5S shadow board


Principle: a visible home position makes missing or misplaced items obvious.


Adapt: labels and silhouettes should support return, counting and inspection, not decoration.


Source: National Highways visual-management standard · Crown publication, linked for reference; no source media reused · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Flexible fabrication workshop


Principle: organize around workflow, shared infrastructure and reconfigurable work zones.


Adapt: map where material arrives, work happens, parts wait and completed work leaves.


Source: Open Source Ecology contributors · open-source project; linked page terms govern reuse and no source media is copied · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only









Warning



Wall mounting is not a decorative SVG problem. The wall substrate, anchor, fastener, backer, load, impact and inspection routine must be approved by the responsible instructor. A laser-cut plate is not a rated anchor.

title: Design & Fabrication Capstone | Complete a N.I.C.E. Design Cycle
text:
Required design record

Situation and need: user, context, facts, assumptions, requirements, restrictions, necessities, and priorities.
Inquiry: useful questions, credible sources, existing solutions, comparisons, and opportunities to borrow, combine, adapt, or improve.
Alternatives: distinct concepts with reasons, not cosmetic variations of one idea.
Selected concept: labelled communication, dimensions, materials, process plan, and identified uncertainties.
Prototype: a purposeful model or test for the highest-risk question.
Fabrication: versioned files, settings, material records, safe process, and assembly decisions.
Feedback and testing: observations from realistic use, measurements, and user response.
Evaluation and iteration: evidence compared with the need and a documented next version.

title: Design & Fabrication Capstone | Complete a N.I.C.E. Design Cycle
text:
Assessment emphasis
Assess the quality of decisions, evidence, communication, responsible process use, and revision, not only the polish of the final artifact. Reward students who discover a problem early, explain it clearly, and improve the design.
Use the N.I.C.E. classroom resource collection to support the design record and the Laser Fabrication Library for editable test geometry and component starting points.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Adaptable to TIJ1O and to project-based expectations in TDJ, TMJ, TCJ, TTJ, TEJ, and TGJ where the chosen need, design communication, materials, processes, and testing authentically fit the course.

Continue with the planned 3D Printing and Additive Manufacturing module, or begin another N.I.C.E. iteration.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Use the process that best suits each function. Thin laser-cut Baltic birch is valuable for precision faces, tool openings, slots, holes, dividers, shadow-board fronts, engraved labels, retainers, spacers, alignment aids, and drilling templates. It is not automatically the right structural rail or load-bearing backer.
Use 1/2 inch or 3/4 inch plywood, conventional lumber, commercial fasteners, dowels, or other approved materials where stiffness, impact resistance, screw holding, or load capacity matters.

text:
Use the process that best suits each function. Thin laser-cut Baltic birch is valuable for precision faces, tool openings, slots, holes, dividers, shadow-board fronts, engraved labels, retainers, spacers, alignment aids, and drilling templates. It is not automatically the right structural rail or load-bearing backer.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Assembly vocabulary

Floor and walls: establish the main volume and load path.
Tabs and slots: locate parts and transfer forces when sized for actual material.
Pins and dowels: align, hinge, retain, or reinforce.
Screws: allow removable mechanical assembly when the receiving material is suitable.
Glue: bonds compatible surfaces but should not compensate for a poorly fitted or unsafe structure.
Spacers and laminations: create controlled offsets or thicker local features.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Hybrid template strategy
A laser-cut face can act as a drilling or placement template for a thicker plywood backer. Clamp the template safely, locate holes accurately, transfer the pattern, then attach the precision face to the structural part. This preserves repeatability without pretending a thin sheet should carry every load.
Use joinery and French-cleat components as measured starting points and validate every interface physically.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Strong connections to TMJ2O, TCJ2O, TDJ2O, and TIJ1O through material selection, assemblies, joinery, fasteners, manufacturing planning, prototyping, and evaluation.

Next: apply these decisions to a useful holder using the Tool Organizer Gallery and design criteria.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text: Create a simple holder for measured classroom objects such as markers, pencils, screwdrivers, drill bits, or small electronics tools. The openings must come from real measurements, not a generic file or guessed diameter.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text: Create a simple holder for measured classroom objects such as markers, pencils, screwdrivers, drill bits, or small electronics tools. The openings must come from real measurements, not a generic file or guessed diameter.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Measure the object
Use calipers correctly and record units. Measure more than one example when nominally identical objects may vary. Identify the controlling dimension: outside diameter, widest body, collar, taper, handle shape, or removal clearance.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Build the layout

Create one opening from an exact measured dimension.
Decide what clearance the task requires; do not silently treat a nominal measurement as a finished fit.
Duplicate the opening into a controlled row or array.
Set centre-to-centre spacing and edge margins numerically.
Align labels and openings consistently.
Check that the remaining material between openings is strong enough for the intended use.

Use circles, holes, slots, rulers, and spacing templates as editable references. The source geometry is a starting point; the student’s measured object determines the final design.
For the first controlled organizer exercise, compare the Hole, Slot and Organizer palettes. Copy named groups, enter dimensions numerically, and make every repeated opening from one checked original.
Draw front, top and side views on the planning worksheet before building the digital layout. Use the Paper-to-Inkscape workflow for datums, grouping, alignment and preflight.
For a row, grid, staggered, radial or perimeter layout, the Fabrication Plate Builder can turn the checked measurements into a reproducible true-size SVG. It validates boundaries and overlap, but the calibration lesson is still required to decide the finished fit.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Evidence
Submit a measurement table, dimensioned layout, fabrication file, fit observation, and one revision. A visually even layout is not enough if tools bind, fall through, or cannot be removed easily.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Useful for TIJ1O, TMJ2O, TDJ2O, TCJ2O, TEJ2O, and TTJ2O contexts involving measurement, precision, layout, repeated geometry, tool organization, and prototype evaluation.

Next: learn why the measured opening and the cut result can differ in Material Fit + Calibration.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
Why this is useful
The tutorial showed you where the tools are and how they work. A designer must also make choices. This project asks you to use the same basic steps with your own name, your own logo, and your own layout.
You are designing for a real object. Good spacing, readable letters, and clean files make the name tag easier to understand and easier to manufacture.






ImportantThis is the task after the Andrade tutorial



Finish Photopea Lesson 3 and its video first. The ANDRADE file is a worked example, not your submission. Save a new copy and replace the example with your own design.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
Design brief
Create an original name tag for a teacher-approved 11 × 4 inch blank. Put a personal logo in the left area and your name in the remaining space. The name must be readable from about 2 metres away. Keep everything away from the edges and prepare clean files for teacher approval.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
What you will submit
Submit these three versions of the same design:

PSD: the editable master with clearly named layers.
PNG: a transparent preview or engraving image at 3300 × 1200 pixels.
SVG: the vector version with the logo and name visible.

Use clear filenames:

studentnumber-lastname-name-tag-master.psd
studentnumber-lastname-name-tag.png
studentnumber-lastname-name-tag.svg

Every filename must begin with your student number, followed by your last name. Replace studentnumber and lastname with your own information. Example: 123456789-Smith-name-tag-master.psd.
Your teacher will tell you which file the machine workflow needs. A PNG can be used for raster engraving. An SVG can carry paths for scoring, cutting, plotting, or another fabrication process.

3. Make a new working copy

Open your completed file from Photopea Lesson 3.
Choose File > Save as PSD immediately.
Give the copy your own filename.
Keep the canvas at 11 × 4 inches and 300 pixels per inch.
Keep the background transparent.
Add a 0.25 inch safe margin on every side.

At 300 pixels per inch, the document is 3300 × 1200 pixels and the 0.25 inch margin is 75 pixels.

Lesson 2B: Trace a multi-layer logo
Lesson 3: Combine the logo and name

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
4. Try fonts before choosing
Type your own name in at least three fonts. Keep the examples at the same size so you can compare them fairly.



The name Andrade shown in four font styles: balanced sans serif, serif, heavy and narrow, and script.


Choose the version that is easy to read in two seconds, has open letter shapes, and is thick enough to engrave. Do not stretch the letters to make them fit.






TipQuick test



Show the three versions to another person for two seconds. Use the one they can read first, unless another choice has a strong reason.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
5. Replace the example logo
Use the logo you traced in Lesson 2 or another teacher-approved personal mark.

Place the SVG or transparent PNG on its own layer.
Keep the width-and-height link turned on.
Resize from a corner so the logo does not stretch.
Keep the logo inside the left 4 × 4 inch area.
Leave visible space around the logo.

If your logo replaces the first letter of your name, check that the complete word is still obvious. Match the logo’s thickness and baseline to the letters.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
6. Make the layout look intentional
Check the complete design, not one layer at a time:

Safe margin: nothing crosses the 0.25 inch guide.
Logo area: the logo stays in the left 4 × 4 inch space.
Alignment: the logo and name feel centred from top to bottom.
Gap: the logo and name are connected but do not collide.
Hierarchy: your name is the first or equal reading target.
Balance: the empty space on one side does not make the design feel as if it is falling over.
Distance: the name is readable from about 2 metres away.




Small Technology Commons emblem beside extra-large ANDRADE text.


The simple version works best because the full name is easy to read.
Hide the guides and ask another person what they notice first. If they cannot read the name in two seconds, revise the size, font, spacing, or logo.

title: Your Turn: Design Your Own Name + Logo Name Tag
text:
7. Export and check every file

PSD

Keep the text and logo editable.
Name important layers.
Save the full 11 × 4 inch document.



PNG

Hide the background and guides.
Export at 3300 × 1200 pixels.
Reopen the file and check its transparency, spelling, and crop.



SVG

Make sure the logo and text are vectors, not missing smart objects.
Export with raster graphics turned off.
Reopen the SVG and check that the complete design appears.







WarningCheck the SVG before submitting



Photopea may leave a placed SVG smart object out of an SVG export. If the logo disappears, open the logo SVG, copy its vector layers, paste those layers into the name-tag file, hide the smart-object copy, and export again.

If Photopea downloads a file with the wrong name, rename it before you submit it. Keep the file ending, such as .psd, .png, or .svg.

Step 2: Make a simple complete draft
Start with one whole-logo PNG. Get the full sequence working before adding more parts.

Open smooth.video.
Choose Add media and import your logo.
Click the logo once. White handles should appear around it.
Choose Animate > In > Scale. Use Fade or Slide if it suits your logo better.

Choose Animate > Out > Fade.
Drag the Out point so the fade begins near 5.3 s and ends near 6.0 s.
Press the space bar. The logo should enter, hold still long enough to read, and fade out.

Step 3: Add a custom keyframe change
A keyframe is a diamond on the timeline. It saves an object’s position, size, rotation, opacity, or colour at one moment.

Click the logo or one logo part.
Move the playhead to the moment when the custom movement should start.
Click the small hollow diamond on the selected object’s timeline row.
Move the playhead later.
Move, resize, or rotate the object. A new diamond should appear automatically.
Press the space bar to watch the movement between the diamonds.




The black vertical line is the playhead. Each diamond on an object’s timeline row is a keyframe.








WarningNo diamond appeared?



Select the object, move the playhead away from the first frame, and then change its position, size, rotation, opacity, or colour.

Common issues






TipThe animation is too fast





Move timeline points farther apart. Add a one- or two-second hold after the complete logo appears.

Use the largest clean PNG or layered PSD you have. Do not enlarge a small image far beyond its original size.

Put each moving part on its own named layer in Photopea. Save a layered PSD, then import the PSD into smooth.video. Each layer should appear on its own timeline row.

1. Choose an audience and three emotions
Decide who should notice your graphic. Examples include a future employer, a co-op supervisor, a client, a club, or a creative community.
Choose three emotions you want that audience to feel. Use specific words when you can. For example, change happy to energized, welcomed, or proud.

text:
2. Choose what you want to make
Choose one short build-first tutorial. Make a banner, thumbnail, logo, or another screen graphic inspired by the tutorial. Follow the techniques, then change the result so it serves your audience and your three emotions.

Gaming or Roblox character logo

Add the most important message first.

Use colour and type to support all three emotions.
Name the important layers.
Save the working PSD before you continue.

your audience;

one design move you used for each emotion;

title: Sadness
text:
Back to all emotions
Sadness slows us down when something has been lost, ended, or mattered deeply.

title: Sadness
section: It can give us the urge to
text:
It can give us the urge to

slow down;
withdraw; or
cry.

title: Sadness
text:
It may be telling us

we may have lost something;
we may need support; or
something mattered to us.

title: Sadness
text:
What can help

Name the loss and acknowledge the pain.
Cry if it helps.
Rest and reach out.
Take one small action.

title: Sadness
text:
Design connection
Soft colour, flowing type, and familiar stories can communicate reflection, comfort, and nostalgia.
Examples: Kleenex, Pixar, and Build-A-Bear.
Previous: Love | Back to all emotions

title: Jealousy
text:
Back to all emotions
Jealousy is often about fearing that we could lose a relationship, role, place, or attention.

title: Jealousy
section: It can give us the urge to
text:
It can give us the urge to

hold on;
protect; or
control.

title: Jealousy
text:
It may be telling us

we may fear losing a relationship;
a role or status matters; or
trust feels uncertain.

title: Jealousy
text:
What can help

Check the facts.
Ask directly.
Name what you need.
Build trust without testing people.

title: Jealousy
text:
Design connection
Friendly, group-oriented symbols can communicate connection and belonging.
Examples: Snapchat and Discord.
Previous: Envy | Next: Guilt

title: Happiness
text:
Back to all emotions
Happiness draws us toward experiences, people, and actions that feel rewarding or meaningful.

title: Happiness
section: It can give us the urge to
text:
It can give us the urge to

continue;
share; or
connect.

title: Happiness
text:
It may be telling us

something feels rewarding;
a need may have been met; or
something is working.

title: Happiness
section: What can help: Big W? Don’t scroll past it
text:
What can help: Big W? Don’t scroll past it

Clock the win.
Actually enjoy it.
Share the good vibes.
Keep cooking.

title: Happiness
text:
Design connection
Bright colour, rounded forms, and playful imagery can create energy and delight.
Examples: LEGO, Nintendo, and Crocs.
Previous: Shame | Next: Love

title: Fear and Anxiety
text:
Back to all emotions
Fear and anxiety can be useful superpowers. They help us notice danger, uncertainty, and the need to prepare.

title: Fear and Anxiety
section: They can give us the urge to
text:
They can give us the urge to

escape;
avoid; or
freeze.

title: Fear and Anxiety
text:
They may be telling us

there may be danger;
something feels uncertain; or
we may need protection or preparation.

title: Fear and Anxiety
text:
What can help

Protect yourself if danger is real.
Check the facts.
Ask for help or support.
If it is safe, take one brave step.

title: Fear and Anxiety
text:
Design connection
Rounded forms and calm colours can reduce visual threat. Strong forms can communicate safety and durability.
Examples: Volvo, Headspace, and Calm.
Next: Anger

title: Disgust
text:
Back to all emotions
Disgust can help us move away from something unsafe, harmful, or deeply against our values.

title: Disgust
section: It can give us the urge to
text:
It can give us the urge to

reject;
move away; or
protect ourselves.

title: Disgust
text:
It may be telling us

something may be unsafe;
something may be harmful; or
a value may have been violated.

title: Disgust
text:
What can help

Name the exact problem.
Check the evidence.
Step back if needed.
Reject harmful behaviour without dehumanizing people.

title: Disgust
text:
Design connection
Clean geometry, cool colour, and clear type can signal order, control, and cleanliness.
Examples: Mr. Clean, CeraVe, and Lush.
Previous: Anger | Next: Envy

1. Situation

What is happening? What are you being asked to design, improve, or solve?

text:
2. User or stakeholder

Who is this for? What matters to the people affected?

3. Facts and questions
Separate what you know from what you still need to learn. Avoid treating guesses as facts.




Facts I know


Questions or information I still need

title: User Needs
text:
4. Needs, requirements, and restrictions
A need is something the solution must address. Requirements and restrictions are conditions the solution has to work within.




Need, requirement, or restriction


Why it matters


Evidence or source

title: User Needs
text:
5. Necessities and nice-to-haves
Necessities are required for the solution to work. Nice-to-haves could improve the solution but are not required.




Necessities


Nice-to-haves

title: User Needs
text:
6. Most important needs
Choose the needs that matter most before you begin Inquiry.




Priority need


Why it matters most

title: User Needs
text:
7. Need statement
Complete this in one or two sentences:

The user needs ___ because ___ while considering ___.

“We need a laser-cut name tag” already chooses the product. “A new classmate needs to identify who they are speaking with quickly and from a useful distance” keeps the problem open.

title: User Needs
text:
Review and reflection

What did you learn or make?
What evidence shows that your work is complete and correct?
What will you improve next time?
What extra idea, test, improvement, or related topic did you investigate?



Complete and submit the worksheet as directed by your teacher.

Make a worksheet copy

title: Rank the Priorities
text: I can rank nice-to-haves and explain which improvements should guide the design first.

title: Rank the Priorities
text: I can rank nice-to-haves and explain which improvements should guide the design first.

title: Rank the Priorities
text:
Use the 1-10 scale

10: necessity; the design fails without it.
7-9: high-value improvement.
4-6: useful improvement.
1-3: minor preference.

Give each nice-to-have a score and one short reason. Do not give every item a 9. Ranking only helps when it shows real trade-offs.

title: Rank the Priorities
text:
Compare two ideas
Check every idea against all necessities first. Then compare how well each idea addresses the highest-ranked nice-to-haves. The score supports a decision; it does not replace judgement or user feedback.
Complete the priorities section of the N.I.C.E. Needs Worksheet.

title: Investigate & Inquire
text:
I can generate several ideas, investigate existing solutions, and choose an idea using evidence.



Figure 3. Research starts with a useful question, not a random search.

title: Investigate & Inquire
text:
I can generate several ideas, investigate existing solutions, and choose an idea using evidence.



Figure 3. Research starts with a useful question, not a random search.

title: Investigate & Inquire
text:
Go wide, then investigate
Brainstorm several different possibilities before researching. Use quick sketches, changed materials, different orientations, and borrow, combine, adapt, improve prompts.
Then ask four questions:

What do we need?
What already exists?
What could work for us?
What would we change?

Record what is good, what is a problem, and what still needs to be checked. Name the sources you used.
Use the N.I.C.E. Inquiry Worksheet.

title: Evaluate, Improve & Repeat
text:
I can use evidence to decide what to keep, change, remove, or test next.



Figure 5. Use feedback patterns and test evidence to decide what changes.

title: Evaluate, Improve & Repeat
text:
I can use evidence to decide what to keep, change, remove, or test next.



Figure 5. Use feedback patterns and test evidence to decide what changes.

title: Evaluate, Improve & Repeat
text:
Compare evidence with the plan
Check the original situation, facts, assumptions, user needs, necessities, and ranked nice-to-haves. Group repeated feedback into patterns instead of obeying every individual comment.
For each important part, choose:

Keep: evidence shows it works.
Change: evidence points to a specific improvement.
Remove: it adds complexity without enough value.
Test: there is not enough evidence yet.

Finish this sentence: The evidence changes our understanding of , so the next cycle will .
Use the N.I.C.E. Evaluate Worksheet.

title: Land Lettermark
text:

title: Land Lettermark
text:

title: Land Lettermark
text:
The design jam
Combine three things:

one of your initials;
one careful observation of land, water, light, roots, paths, texture, or movement; and
one Good Life value that matters to you.

title: Land Lettermark
text:
Observe before drawing
Go outside and record three specific observations. Slow down. Observe or photograph, leave living things in place, and notice relationships such as water and soil, roots and paths, or light and shadow.

title: Land Lettermark
text:
Sketch three options
Make three quick lettermarks. Change the shape, spacing, direction, or relationship between the letter and the observation. Notice the approach of Indigenous artists without copying an artist’s style or cultural symbols.
Beside your strongest sketch, write:

Value: the idea you want the mark to carry;
Land observation: what you noticed; and
Design choice: how the shape communicates both.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
text:
FROM THE ARCHIVE
Originally published on andrewandrade.ca. This version is included in Lore because it captures the kind of learning record this section is meant to preserve: teaching, history, identity, community, and the things carried forward.
View the source history on GitHub
It’s been years since I last wrote here. I started this blog back in fourth-year engineering while job hunting, before I joined Palantir, before robotics labs and late-night debugging sessions, before teaching, before all the twists that came after.
This week, Remembrance Day brought me back.
I had the honour of playing trumpet with our school band, not the Last Post; I’m still working to be good enough for that, but enough to stand with the group in something meaningful. Instruments in hand, everything paused for a moment, and it pulled me right back to my time in army cadets.
Even now, that first year is burned into my memory: awkward uniform, barely any badges, trying to figure out what leadership meant. Luckily we had mentors to guide us.
Cadets taught me that rank wasn’t the patch; it was the work behind it.
As we approached Remembrance Day this year, I found myself thinking about the small rituals that shaped me. Raising the flag was one of them.
Sometimes it was early, cold, or rushed, but it mattered. And I wasn’t alone.
Music also became part of those mornings, including our national anthem.
Fast-forward to high school robotics, coding, and engineering, different worlds entirely, but the same threads of discipline and responsibility ran through them.
I didn’t stay long enough in cadets to stack up badges like the mentors I admired, but the two years I spent there were full. Varied, intense, and formative, but I still loved computers.
This year, as part of preparing for our ceremony, I learned more than I expected, thanks entirely to the Student Activity Council, who did all the research.
That’s where I discovered the story of George Cardozo, one of the “Port Credit Boys.”

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
section: The Bugler They Didn’t Let Become an Officer
text:
The Bugler They Didn’t Let Become an Officer
George’s story starts decades before mine, but strangely close to home.
He was a Jamaican-born teacher, educated in Port-au-Prince and Kingston, who came to Canada and enlisted with the 4th Battalion, Canadian Expeditionary Force, on 22 September 1914.
One of the first recruits at Valcartier.



George standing


His attestation paper recorded only the essentials: his trade or calling, his date of birth, and his place of birth. Beyond those brief entries, the rest of George’s life, identity, and service must be reconstructed through the surviving evidence gathered from archival and family research.
A fuller picture, his experiences as a Jamaican-born bugler, his movement through the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and the context surrounding his enlistment, comes from the sources compiled in the project’s research. These include My Jamaican Family’s biography They Shall Grow Not Old: George Cardozo, a Casualty of …, the Canadian Virtual War Memorial entry for George Cordozo from Veterans Affairs Canada, and his digitized service file in Library and Archives Canada’s Personnel Records of the First World War.
Together, these sources allow us to understand George far more deeply than the minimal information captured on the photo.



George’s attestation paper


According to Dorothy Kew from the My Jamaican Family Blog, he was:

Five foot five
Dark complexion
“Coloured”
Roman Catholic
Teacher

With his education and background, he should have been an officer.
But because of his colour, he wasn’t given that chance.
Instead, they made him a bugler.



George sitting


Today, the role is ceremonial.
Back then, buglers woke before everyone else, played Reveille in the cold, roused officers, and handled the morning chores no one else wanted.
George still trained hard, at Ravina Barracks, on the SS Tyrolia to England, and finally to the Western Front.



Port Credit Boys


He died sometime between April 22 and 26, 1915, during the Second Battle of Ypres, the first time poison gas was used in the Great War. His body was never found.
His name is carved on the Menin Gate Memorial in Belgium with over 55,000 others who have no known grave.



Memorial


Every evening at 8 p.m., beneath his name, they still sound the Last Post.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
section: Bugles, Flags, and the Things We Carry Forward
text:
Bugles, Flags, and the Things We Carry Forward
This year I raised my trumpet high,
Not for the Last Post’s mournful cry,
But with a deeper, steadier sight
Of all the threads that shaped my flight.
I thought of flags I used to raise,
The badges missed in younger days,
The mentors’ paths I didn’t tread,
And those who served and marched instead.
I thought of George, so much like me,
A teacher-learner meant to be,
Who left to fight through smoke and flame
And never made it home again.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
text:
We Remember

“They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old…”
- For the Fallen, Lawrence Binyon

This post is both a return and a reminder, of the past we inherit, the stories we uncover, and the unexpected ways they shape our present.
This Remembrance Day, I played the trumpet for our school.
But I also played it for George.
And I’m honoured to remember him here.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
I teach and learn Technological Education at Port Credit Secondary School. Teaching is more than content: knowledge helps us build skill, judgement, and practical wisdom so we can grow in capability, live well, and learn through experience. This site shares lessons, assignments, slides, experiments, and revisions so others can adapt them, learn by doing, and follow the way in their own work.
The resources are organized around Ontario’s Technological Education curriculum, with connections to other curricular and co-curricular learning where they are useful. Across the courses, the resources also connect with Port Credit’s SciTech Regional Program and can support Ontario’s Specialist High Skills Major (SHSM) in Manufacturing, including sector-focused learning, certifications, experiential learning, career exploration, reach-ahead experiences, and sector-partnered experiences.








NoteWork in progress and public contributions



This site is a living collection of teaching materials. It may contain errors, omissions, outdated information, and areas with significant room for improvement. If you find something that can be corrected or improved, please open an issue or submit a pull request.
The GitHub repository, issues, pull requests, comments, and commit history are public. Do not post student information, personal information, confidential school or board information, account information, or other sensitive material. Review and redact your contribution before publishing it. Contributors are responsible for the information they choose to place in a public GitHub contribution; this project cannot protect information that someone has chosen to publish publicly.





SOS: Search Oriented Shortcut: A playful way to turn a question into a shareable Google search. View the source.
Class Instants: A classroom-friendly soundboard with search, favourites, keyboard shortcuts, and 37 bundled sounds. View the source.
Technological Education Resources: Open notes, assignments, slides, tools, and classroom materials. View the source.
Blog: Articles about technology, learning, work, and projects.
CV and project history: Work, education, talks, publications, projects, and community activity.
GitHub: Current public code and project repositories.




Before teaching at Port Credit, I worked at Palantir, ran a startup called PetroPredict, and completed internships at Facebook, Suncor, and several smaller technology companies. Earlier, while I was still in high school, I worked as a lifeguard and deck supervisor with the City of Mississauga and in a machine shop after a co-op placement.
Outside work and school, I was a sponsored kiteboarder for Switch Kites and have been an avid box lacrosse player. Kiteboarding was a major part of my life and shaped how I think about practice, judgement, risk, feedback, equipment, weather, failure, and learning from people who have different skills, knowledge, and wisdom from you.



After moving back to Mississauga following time living abroad, kiteboarding became something I could realistically do only a few times a year. I needed other ways to keep learning with people, contributing to communities, and doing things that require practice.
I now volunteer, guest speak, and run workshops with a variety of organizations, but I spend the most time contributing to my local parish in Mississauga. I am of Goan Catholic heritage, and I have helped with children’s programs including First Holy Communion and with liturgy involving exceptional individuals.
I take my own beliefs seriously while also trying to study other philosophies and religious traditions with respect. That helps me understand more of the people I teach and work with, and gives me more ways to think about learning, discipline, community, service, attention, and human well-being. More recently, I have been training in Gong Fu and Qigong with the Chung Wah Kung Fu International System and the Human Wellness and Recuperation Centre.



The goal is simple: useful teaching and learning material is open-source, free to access, and easy to adapt. Learners, educators, and anyone else who can use it can access basic knowledge without a paywall or dependence on a single classroom, platform, or account.
This approach is influenced by open education projects such as Tony R. Kuphaldt’s Socratic Electronics, which emphasizes learning through questions, research, discussion, explaining ideas to others, and developing the ability to teach yourself.
The material here is meant to be used, questioned, adapted, improved, and shared again.



Many religions and philosophies contain ideas that can sound similar, much as versions of the Golden Rule appear across different traditions. Similarity does not make them identical. I do not want to flatten distinct histories, beliefs, languages, or practices into one system. These are short ideas I find useful to keep nearby when thinking about teaching, learning, practice, and community.

The Way: I use the Way here in a broad, non-doctrinal sense: being present with things as they are, without judgement, and letting the path become clearer through practice. The focus is on being rather than constantly reaching for the next outcome: doing one thing mindfully, acting effectively, accepting what is present, and working without attachment to a particular result. This also connects to well-being as something lived and practised across the physical, mental, spiritual, and emotional parts of a person. Different traditions use the idea of a way or path differently, and those differences matter.
Spirit: Spirit can describe something carried within a person, but also something strengthened between people: school spirit, team spirit, community spirit. It can grow through belonging, responsibility, shared effort, service, and the feeling that your work is connected to something larger than yourself.
Paul Cormier / Indigenous learning methodology: Kinoo’amaadawaad Megwaa Doodamawaad, translated by Cormier as “they are learning with each other while they are doing.” I want that idea to shape these notes: students learn with one another while doing real work, and the documentation grows from that work.
Confucianism: learn something, then practise it. Learning is not complete when something has merely been heard or read.
Daoism: a long journey begins beneath your feet. Large work starts from what is small and present, and care at the end matters as much as enthusiasm at the beginning.
Stoicism: Epictetus treats education as more than book knowledge; character and judgement are developed through repeated practice and self-correction.
Epicureanism: Epicurus places unusual weight on friendship as part of a good life. Learning is easier to sustain when people enjoy doing worthwhile things together.
Hindu tradition: the Bhagavad Gita 2:47 distinguishes action from attachment to its results: do the work carefully without letting the outcome become the only reason for doing it.
Buddhism: the Dhammapada 76 compares a wise person who points out your faults to someone revealing hidden treasure. Good correction can be a gift.
Jewish tradition: Pirkei Avot 4:1 asks, “Who is wise?” and answers: the person who learns from every person.
Christian tradition: “Iron sharpens iron” is a useful image for people improving one another through honest contact, practice, challenge, and care.
Islamic learning tradition: “Seek knowledge from the cradle to the grave” is a widely repeated educational maxim. It is worth carrying for its meaning, while being careful not to present it as a verified Prophetic hadith. The Qur’an also gives the concise prayer, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge”.
Ubuntu: “A person is a person through other persons.” The idea of umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu keeps learning connected to relationship, dignity, and community.
“Each one, teach one.” Knowledge becomes more useful when it moves through people instead of stopping with the first person who receives it.
OSSTF/FEESO: “Let us not take thought for our separate interests, but let us help one another.”
Port Credit: Lux numquam desit. Let light never be lacking. The light is something we keep alive for one another: showing up, sharing what we know, helping each other forward, and carrying the Way on.

The common thread is not that these traditions are identical. It is that many very different traditions take practice, humility, relationship, disciplined attention, service, and lifelong learning seriously.
The religious, spiritual, philosophical, and cultural references above describe ideas I study and influences I find useful. They are not belief requirements for students. Students are not expected to adopt, reject, defend, or disclose a religious, spiritual, Indigenous, philosophical, or non-religious belief. Classroom reflection can remain secular and can use interests, projects, community, culture, technical work, or another non-sensitive point of reference. Agreement with a belief is never assessed.

This site is partly an attempt to continue a tradition I benefited from long before I became a teacher: educators making useful material available to people they may never meet.
Michael Franzen maintained a site that was extremely useful to me during teachers college. That site is now offline, but the example stayed with me: a teacher could put useful technical material on the open web and someone outside their classroom could learn from it.
Peter Beens has likewise shared a substantial body of educational and technical material through peter.beens.ca, beens.org, and Beens Consulting.
I also owe a great deal to the technology team at Westdale Secondary School, who shared an enormous amount of material, experience, and practical advice:

Taylor Wilson: computer and transportation technology
Dave Kipp: construction and woodworking
David Christie: mathematics, science, and general technology
Craig Ramsden: construction and woodworking
Rejean Royer: transportation technology
Principal Brian Goodram

The wooden MR. ANDRADE name tag shown in this project was made and gifted to me by teachers at Westdale. Rejean also shared with me parts of his Indigenous heritage and his practice of smudging as part of his daily life. I am grateful for the trust involved in sharing both technical knowledge and personal tradition.
This project is meant to carry that spirit forward: take what is useful, credit the people who helped, improve it where you can, and leave something behind for the next person.



This project currently reflects my classroom work and the people whose ideas, feedback, and resources have influenced it. As others contribute directly to the site, contributor bios will be added here.
LinkedIn · GitHub · Personal site



Technological Education Resources is built for teaching at Port Credit Secondary School, and its visual identity deliberately connects to the school without trying to replace the school’s own identity.
Port Credit’s secondary-school history reaches back to 1919, when a continuation school opened in the community. The PCSS Alumni Association preserves school history, yearbooks, memorabilia, and stories while supporting scholarships and selected school projects.
The Regional SciTech Program launched in September 2005. Alumni material describes it as an integrated science and technology program intended for both inquiry-oriented academic learners and hands-on learners interested in college, apprenticeships, skilled trades, and industry.
The school motto, Lux numquam desit, is a natural fit for a visual system built around the Port Credit lighthouse, learning, and the idea of carrying useful knowledge forward.
Technological Education Resources also recognizes the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation and the Indigenous history and continuing stewardship connected to this place. Purple and orange are included in the working palette as community and reflection accents that can be used thoughtfully in Indigenous learning and reconciliation contexts. They are project colours, not presented as official colours of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation.

Mindfulness and well-being activities on this site are educational classroom practices, not therapy, counselling, diagnosis, or mental-health treatment. They may appear as brief start-up activities, pauses, check-ins, or reflections that support attention, self-regulation, readiness to learn, reflection, and awareness of physical, mental, spiritual, and emotional well-being. They sit alongside and around the curriculum as part of the learning environment rather than as therapeutic assignments.
These activities fit the promotion end of PDSB’s tiered mental-health model. PDSB’s 2026-2029 Mental Health and Addictions Strategy describes Tier 1 as positive mental-health and well-being promotion for all students through inclusive learning environments, social-emotional learning, and stigma reduction. Specialized consultation, assessment, family support, and therapeutic services sit at Tier 3 with appropriate mental-health professionals. The public PDSB Mental Health and Well-Being page is the starting point for current board resources and pathways to care.
Students are not asked to diagnose themselves or others, disclose private mental-health information, or participate in therapy as coursework. Personal disclosure, emotional intensity, or the private details of a student’s life are not a basis for assessment. Where reflection is assessed, the evidence is the curriculum learning or observable learning process identified in the task, not a student’s mental-health status or willingness to reveal personal information.


If a student asks for mental-health help, or a concern moves beyond ordinary classroom support, the role moves from classroom learning to connection and referral. Depending on the situation, that pathway can include Guidance or Student Services, school administration, the School Support Team, PDSB social work or psychology services, parents or caregivers, and community or regulated health professionals. PDSB’s current strategy calls for clear pathways to both school and community supports.
The teacher’s role is to notice, listen, respond appropriately, maintain professional boundaries, reduce stigma, and connect students with the people whose role and training fit the concern. It does not include diagnosing a condition or providing treatment. This reflects the Ontario College of Teachers’ Supporting Students’ Mental Health advisory, including its direction to observe, listen, inform, and involve others rather than counsel outside the educator’s role and training.
Students are not promised absolute confidentiality. When safety, suspected abuse or neglect, self-harm, threats, or another reporting obligation is involved, applicable school and board procedures, emergency protocols, and the OCT Duty to Report advisory govern the response. Professional relationships and communications also follow the OCT Professional Boundaries advisory and the Professional Standards.




AI can be used as an iterative learning partner for activities such as brainstorming, inquiry, coding, accessibility, drafting, feedback, and reflection on process when the task permits it. It does not replace professional judgement or reliable evidence of student learning. Assignment-specific directions identify what AI assistance is permitted and how it is attributed. Students may be asked to retain prompts and relevant outputs as evidence of process, while keeping personal and sensitive information out of those prompts.
Confidential or sensitive student information is not entered into public or unapproved AI tools. This includes student names or numbers, school account information, identifiable student work, grades, IEP or accommodation information, health or mental-health information, family circumstances, images or recordings, and other personal information. Student-facing third-party software use follows current PDSB approval, privacy, age, notice, and consent requirements.
PDSB’s published 2023 interim guidance on Artificial Intelligence in Education emphasizes transparency, privacy, verification of AI output, attribution, protection of confidential student data, and caution with AI-detection tools. Because AI tools, approvals, and board requirements change, current PDSB approved-tool, privacy, and instructional requirements take precedence over that interim document. The PDSB Privacy and Terms page provides the board’s public privacy information. Ontario’s O. Reg. 52/26, in force July 1, 2026, also requires school-board notice when student personal digital information is disclosed to qualifying third-party software applications.
AI-generated or AI-assisted educational material is reviewed for factual accuracy, context, bias, accessibility, privacy, and copyright before use. AI-detection output is not treated as proof by itself.



This site publishes generic teaching resources, not student records or routine student submissions. Student names, student numbers, contact information, grades, IEP or accommodation information, health information, and other private student data remain in board-approved systems. Identifiable student work, images, stories, or recordings are published only when the applicable permission, consent, and board requirements have been addressed.



Documents on this site are not safety documentation and are not to be used as a substitute for safety instruction, safety procedures, certification, supervision, authorization, or official safety requirements. I intend to avoid publishing stand-alone safety procedures here.
For safety documentation and procedures, use current authoritative sources appropriate to the actual activity and equipment. These include the Ontario Council for Technology Education (OCTE) Safety resources, your own school board and school safety procedures, employer requirements where applicable, manufacturer manuals and instructions, safety data sheets, applicable legislation and standards, and other official resources required for the setting.
Where a task involves tools, machinery, electrical systems, batteries, vehicles, lifting, fabrication, chemicals, heat, or another hazard, the current official procedure for the actual equipment and environment governs.



Technological Education Resources is an independently maintained collection of teaching materials, not a substitute for official PDSB, school, Ministry of Education, Ontario College of Teachers, or legal requirements. Where a resource conflicts with a current official requirement, the current official requirement governs.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
I teach and learn Technological Education at Port Credit Secondary School. Teaching is more than content: knowledge helps us build skill, judgement, and practical wisdom so we can grow in capability, live well, and learn through experience. This site shares lessons, assignments, slides, experiments, and revisions so others can adapt them, learn by doing, and follow the way in their own work.
The resources are organized around Ontario’s Technological Education curriculum, with connections to other curricular and co-curricular learning where they are useful. Across the courses, the resources also connect with Port Credit’s SciTech Regional Program and can support Ontario’s Specialist High Skills Major (SHSM) in Manufacturing, including sector-focused learning, certifications, experiential learning, career exploration, reach-ahead experiences, and sector-partnered experiences.
