title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
Before teaching at Port Credit, I worked at Palantir, ran a startup called PetroPredict, and completed internships at Facebook, Suncor, and several smaller technology companies. Earlier, while I was still in high school, I worked as a lifeguard and deck supervisor with the City of Mississauga and in a machine shop after a co-op placement.
Outside work and school, I was a sponsored kiteboarder for Switch Kites and have been an avid box lacrosse player. Kiteboarding was a major part of my life and shaped how I think about practice, judgement, risk, feedback, equipment, weather, failure, and learning from people who have different skills, knowledge, and wisdom from you.



After moving back to Mississauga following time living abroad, kiteboarding became something I could realistically do only a few times a year. I needed other ways to keep learning with people, contributing to communities, and doing things that require practice.
I now volunteer, guest speak, and run workshops with a variety of organizations, but I spend the most time contributing to my local parish in Mississauga. I am of Goan Catholic heritage, and I have helped with children’s programs including First Holy Communion and with liturgy involving exceptional individuals.
I take my own beliefs seriously while also trying to study other philosophies and religious traditions with respect. That helps me understand more of the people I teach and work with, and gives me more ways to think about learning, discipline, community, service, attention, and human well-being. More recently, I have been training in Gong Fu and Qigong with the Chung Wah Kung Fu International System and the Human Wellness and Recuperation Centre.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
The goal is simple: useful teaching and learning material is open-source, free to access, and easy to adapt. Learners, educators, and anyone else who can use it can access basic knowledge without a paywall or dependence on a single classroom, platform, or account.
This approach is influenced by open education projects such as Tony R. Kuphaldt’s Socratic Electronics, which emphasizes learning through questions, research, discussion, explaining ideas to others, and developing the ability to teach yourself.
The material here is meant to be used, questioned, adapted, improved, and shared again.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
Many religions and philosophies contain ideas that can sound similar, much as versions of the Golden Rule appear across different traditions. Similarity does not make them identical. I do not want to flatten distinct histories, beliefs, languages, or practices into one system. These are short ideas I find useful to keep nearby when thinking about teaching, learning, practice, and community.

The Way: I use the Way here in a broad, non-doctrinal sense: being present with things as they are, without judgement, and letting the path become clearer through practice. The focus is on being rather than constantly reaching for the next outcome: doing one thing mindfully, acting effectively, accepting what is present, and working without attachment to a particular result. This also connects to well-being as something lived and practised across the physical, mental, spiritual, and emotional parts of a person. Different traditions use the idea of a way or path differently, and those differences matter.
Spirit: Spirit can describe something carried within a person, but also something strengthened between people: school spirit, team spirit, community spirit. It can grow through belonging, responsibility, shared effort, service, and the feeling that your work is connected to something larger than yourself.
Paul Cormier / Indigenous learning methodology: Kinoo’amaadawaad Megwaa Doodamawaad, translated by Cormier as “they are learning with each other while they are doing.” I want that idea to shape these notes: students learn with one another while doing real work, and the documentation grows from that work.
Confucianism: learn something, then practise it. Learning is not complete when something has merely been heard or read.
Daoism: a long journey begins beneath your feet. Large work starts from what is small and present, and care at the end matters as much as enthusiasm at the beginning.
Stoicism: Epictetus treats education as more than book knowledge; character and judgement are developed through repeated practice and self-correction.
Epicureanism: Epicurus places unusual weight on friendship as part of a good life. Learning is easier to sustain when people enjoy doing worthwhile things together.
Hindu tradition: the Bhagavad Gita 2:47 distinguishes action from attachment to its results: do the work carefully without letting the outcome become the only reason for doing it.
Buddhism: the Dhammapada 76 compares a wise person who points out your faults to someone revealing hidden treasure. Good correction can be a gift.
Jewish tradition: Pirkei Avot 4:1 asks, “Who is wise?” and answers: the person who learns from every person.
Christian tradition: “Iron sharpens iron” is a useful image for people improving one another through honest contact, practice, challenge, and care.
Islamic learning tradition: “Seek knowledge from the cradle to the grave” is a widely repeated educational maxim. It is worth carrying for its meaning, while being careful not to present it as a verified Prophetic hadith. The Qur’an also gives the concise prayer, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge”.
Ubuntu: “A person is a person through other persons.” The idea of umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu keeps learning connected to relationship, dignity, and community.
“Each one, teach one.” Knowledge becomes more useful when it moves through people instead of stopping with the first person who receives it.
OSSTF/FEESO: “Let us not take thought for our separate interests, but let us help one another.”
Port Credit: Lux numquam desit. Let light never be lacking. The light is something we keep alive for one another: showing up, sharing what we know, helping each other forward, and carrying the Way on.

The common thread is not that these traditions are identical. It is that many very different traditions take practice, humility, relationship, disciplined attention, service, and lifelong learning seriously.
The religious, spiritual, philosophical, and cultural references above describe ideas I study and influences I find useful. They are not belief requirements for students. Students are not expected to adopt, reject, defend, or disclose a religious, spiritual, Indigenous, philosophical, or non-religious belief. Classroom reflection can remain secular and can use interests, projects, community, culture, technical work, or another non-sensitive point of reference. Agreement with a belief is never assessed.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
This site is partly an attempt to continue a tradition I benefited from long before I became a teacher: educators making useful material available to people they may never meet.
Michael Franzen maintained a site that was extremely useful to me during teachers college. That site is now offline, but the example stayed with me: a teacher could put useful technical material on the open web and someone outside their classroom could learn from it.
Peter Beens has likewise shared a substantial body of educational and technical material through peter.beens.ca, beens.org, and Beens Consulting.
I also owe a great deal to the technology team at Westdale Secondary School, who shared an enormous amount of material, experience, and practical advice:

Taylor Wilson: computer and transportation technology
Dave Kipp: construction and woodworking
David Christie: mathematics, science, and general technology
Craig Ramsden: construction and woodworking
Rejean Royer: transportation technology
Principal Brian Goodram

The wooden MR. ANDRADE name tag shown in this project was made and gifted to me by teachers at Westdale. Rejean also shared with me parts of his Indigenous heritage and his practice of smudging as part of his daily life. I am grateful for the trust involved in sharing both technical knowledge and personal tradition.
This project is meant to carry that spirit forward: take what is useful, credit the people who helped, improve it where you can, and leave something behind for the next person.

title: About Technological Education Resources
text:
Technological Education Resources is built for teaching at Port Credit Secondary School, and its visual identity deliberately connects to the school without trying to replace the school’s own identity.
Port Credit’s secondary-school history reaches back to 1919, when a continuation school opened in the community. The PCSS Alumni Association preserves school history, yearbooks, memorabilia, and stories while supporting scholarships and selected school projects.
The Regional SciTech Program launched in September 2005. Alumni material describes it as an integrated science and technology program intended for both inquiry-oriented academic learners and hands-on learners interested in college, apprenticeships, skilled trades, and industry.
The school motto, Lux numquam desit, is a natural fit for a visual system built around the Port Credit lighthouse, learning, and the idea of carrying useful knowledge forward.
Technological Education Resources also recognizes the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation and the Indigenous history and continuing stewardship connected to this place. Purple and orange are included in the working palette as community and reflection accents that can be used thoughtfully in Indigenous learning and reconciliation contexts. They are project colours, not presented as official colours of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation.

title: References
text:
Citation style
References use stable numbering based on the IEEE Reference Guide. A page can cite a whole source as [1] or a specific location as [1, Ch. 3, p. 76] or [1, Ch. 3, pp. 76–84].
For classroom use, this site modifies the usual IEEE locator by including the textbook chapter number whenever it is known. Chapter numbers make the cited material easier for students to find when they buy or use an edition whose page numbers differ.
As additional sources are added, their reference numbers remain stable so existing citations do not need to be rewritten.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
In the Anishinaabe teaching resources used here, Grandmother Moon helps mark time through changes in the land, water, plants, animals, weather, and community life.
The lunar calendar on a turtle’s back. Image and explanation from Ontario Parks. © King’s Printer for Ontario, 2018. Reproduced unchanged for non-commercial educational use.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
Start with community
Moon teachings are not identical across First Nations. Names, spellings, timing, and meanings change with language, territory, family, and community.
The sequence below comes from a Matawa Education and Care Centre resource, which identifies these as the 13 Moons of the Mississaugas of the Credit. Port Credit Secondary School stands within the traditional territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation.
The local sources use Grandmother Moon, rather than Mother Moon. A Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation notice names her Tibik Giizis Nookmissmaan and connects Grandmother Moon with water, cleansing, gratitude, and intention. See page 11 of the November 2019 Eaglepress.






Note



This page is a starting point, not a replacement for an Elder, Knowledge Keeper, language speaker, or community teacher.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
Read the turtle’s back





A common snapping turtle swimming at Toronto’s Evergreen Brick Works.


A living turtle. Photograph by Maxquijano at Toronto’s Evergreen Brick Works, 2011, CC BY-SA 3.0.





A photographed turtle-shell calendar display with 13 large centre sections.


A material example. Iroquoian turtle-shell calendar display at the Droulers-Tsiionhiakwatha archaeological site. Photograph by Pierre5018, 2020, CC BY-SA 4.0. The photographed edge has 25 visible small sections, which is why this page treats the numbers as a teaching pattern rather than a universal anatomy test.



What to notice


13large centre sectionsthe Grandmother Moons


28small edge marksdays in the teaching cycle


The Oneida Language and Cultural Centre explains the same 13-and-28 relationship. A Mississaugas of the Credit classroom story describes children counting 13 spots and connecting them to the 13 Moons. See page 14 of the May 2026 Eaglepress.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
The 13 Grandmother Moons
These compact meanings summarize the Mississaugas of the Credit sequence in the Matawa resource. Gregorian months are approximate guides, not fixed start and end dates.


1 · January

Mnido Giizis


Spirit Moon

quiet reflection


2 · February

Makwa Giizis


Bear Moon

birth and reflection


3 · March

Ziissbaakdoke Giizis


Sugar Moon

maple sap runs


4 · April

Namebine Giizis


Sucker Moon

fish return and sustain


5 · May

Waawaaskone Giizis


Flower Moon

flowers and medicines grow


6 · June

Odemin Giizis


Strawberry Moon

healing and reconciliation


7 · July

Mskomini Giizis


Raspberry Moon

gentleness and kindness


8 · July to August

Datkaamin Giizis


Blackberry or Thimbleberry Moon

a less frequent harvest


9 · August

Mdaamiin Giizis


Corn Moon

future generations


10 · September

Biinaakwe Giizis


Falling Leaves Moon

Creation gives back


11 · October

Mshkawji Giizis


Freezing Moon

prepare for winter


12 · November

Mnidoons Giizis Oonhg


Little Spirit Moon

healing and a good path


13 · December

Mnidoons Giizis


Blue or Big Spirit Moon

purification and healing


Other Anishinaabe communities may use different names, spellings, orders, or teachings because the land and community are different.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
New Moon and Old Moon


🌘

Old Moon


The thin waning crescent shortly before New Moon. This is an informal sky-watching name, not one of the 13 Grandmother Moon names.



🌑

New Moon


An astronomical phase when the lit side faces mostly away from Earth. The visible crescent grows afterward.



See NASA’s Moon phases guide for the complete astronomical sequence.

title: Grandmother Moon, the Seasons, and the Turtle’s Back
text:
Keep the two measures clear


13Grandmother Moonsa seasonal teaching round


28teaching daysshown around the shell


29.5astronomical daysabout one New Moon to the next


The turtle-shell teaching carries relationship, memory, and seasonal meaning. Astronomical measurement describes orbital timing. NASA gives about 27.3 days for one orbit around Earth and 29.5 days from one New Moon to the next.

title: Iteration 1: Robert Abraham and the CNC Lathe
text:
Mr. Knowles used to joke that my cohort was “Iteration 1”, the first group through the program. Many of us went on to engineering at Waterloo, U of T, and elsewhere.
This year, my own Iteration 1 has graduated and started university. I want to record some of what they accomplished, especially for anyone looking for co-op students, interns, or part-time technical help.
The important context for these stories is that this was not simply the assigned course work. These students did the regular work, did it to a high standard, and then chose problems that interested them and went much further. The best description is probably an impressive engineering side quest: the main quest was already complete.

title: Iteration 1: Robert Abraham and the CNC Lathe
text:
Robert Abraham
Introducing Robert Abraham, now studying Computer Engineering at the University of Toronto. You can find more about him and his projects at robert-abraham.com/projects.
Our school offers a Specialist High Skills Major (SHSM) in Manufacturing, and Computer Engineering is one of the elective courses students can take as part of that program. One of the goals is to connect those two worlds more deliberately: electronics, controls, programming, and Linux meeting machining, fabrication, and real manufacturing systems.
In Grade 11 Computer Engineering, Robert took the initiative to work on an old Lab-Volt CNC lathe that another high school was going to throw out. Restoring it was not an assigned project. He saw a difficult, open-ended problem and decided to take it on. Before Christmas, we were already machining our first part: a Christmas tree. Here is how it happened.



Disassembling the old Lab-Volt CNC lathe as we worked through its mechanical problems.


When we opened the electronics cabinet, the wiring was difficult to trace and did not consistently follow convention, including black being used as positive on part of the DC circuit.



Inside the CNC lathe electronics cabinet while we traced the existing system and planned the retrofit.


Robert researched a replacement controller compatible with the existing Gecko drives, and we worked through the electrical and mechanical problems. The mechanical work meant disassembling parts of the machine, cleaning them, resolving issues, and putting everything back together.
The broken controller was the only component we had to replace. Everything else was done using what we already had, open-source software, or software available free through student educational access.
We ran the machine with LinuxCNC, so part of the retrofit meant setting up and configuring our own Linux-based controller computer and operating system. LinuxCNC gave us an open-source machine-control platform without needing to buy proprietary CNC control software.



The rebuilt lathe running from our LinuxCNC controller computer.


We did not have another Mastercam licence available either. Robert learned Autodesk Inventor through educational access, generated the G-code, and kept pushing until the machine ran a program.



The finished CNC lathe after the retrofit and rebuild.


That project is a good example of what I want computer engineering to be: not just following instructions, but inheriting a broken system, researching what you do not know, and making it work. The impressive part was not that Robert completed an assignment. It was that he chose to go well beyond one.
Posted with Robert’s permission. If you are looking for an intern, co-op student, or someone for part-time technical work, consider reaching out to him.
Robert Abraham’s projects: robert-abraham.com/projects

text: I can separate what must be true from what would simply make the design better.

title: Necessities & Nice-to-Haves
text:
Sort the criteria

Requirement: something the solution should accomplish.
Restriction: a limit the design must work within.
Necessity: a requirement or restriction that must be satisfied. Score it 10/10.
Nice-to-have: a useful improvement that is not required. Score it 1-9/10.

A necessity is not just something you strongly prefer. If it is missing, the design fails or cannot be used safely and appropriately.

title: Necessities & Nice-to-Haves
text:
Quick test
For each criterion, ask: Would the design still work without this? If yes, it is probably a nice-to-have.
Sort the criteria in the N.I.C.E. Needs Worksheet.

title: Situation & Opportunity
text:
I can understand the situation and identify an opportunity to make it better.



Figure 1. Understand the situation, then look for an opportunity to improve it.

title: Situation & Opportunity
text:
I can understand the situation and identify an opportunity to make it better.



Figure 1. Understand the situation, then look for an opportunity to improve it.

title: Situation & Opportunity
text:
Break down the situation

Fact: something observed, measured, or supported by evidence.
Assumption: something that may be true but still needs to be checked.
Interpretation: the meaning or explanation attached to the facts.

Example: “Three students asked where the tools go” is a fact. “Everyone finds the storage confusing” is an assumption. “The labels are the problem” is an interpretation.

title: Situation & Opportunity
text:
Spot the opportunity
An opportunity is a change that could make the situation better for someone.

title: Situation & Opportunity
text:
Check before continuing
Write one sentence for each category. Then ask: What improvement could make a meaningful difference?
Open the N.I.C.E. Needs Worksheet.

title: Anger
text:
Back to all emotions
Anger gives us energy to confront a problem, defend ourselves, or protect a boundary.

title: Anger
section: It can give us the urge to
text:
It can give us the urge to

confront;
defend; or
push back.

title: Anger
text:
It may be telling us

a goal is blocked;
something feels unfair; or
a boundary was crossed.

title: Anger
text:
What can help

Pause.
Check the facts.
State the boundary.
Choose repair or useful action.

title: Anger
text:
Design connection
Heavy, angular lettering can create force, urgency, and defiance.
Examples: Riot Games, Fortnite, and Call of Duty.
Previous: Fear and anxiety | Next: Disgust

title: Envy
text:
Back to all emotions
Envy is about wanting something that someone else has.

title: Envy
section: It can give us the urge to
text:
It can give us the urge to

compare;
compete; or
get what someone else has.

title: Envy
text:
It may be telling us

someone has something we want;
a goal matters to us; or
we feel behind.

title: Envy
text:
What can help

Name what you want.
Turn comparison into a healthy goal.
Learn from others.
Notice your own progress and what you already have.

title: Envy
text:
Design connection
Gold, classic type, and achievement symbols can suggest status and aspiration.
Examples: Rolex, Jordan, and Coach.
Previous: Disgust | Next: Jealousy

title: Guilt
text:
Back to all emotions
Guilt can help us notice when our behaviour does not match our values.

title: Guilt
section: It can give us the urge to
text:
It can give us the urge to

apologize;
repair; or
make amends.

title: Guilt
text:
It may be telling us

our behaviour may not match our values;
someone may have been hurt; or
a correction may be needed.

title: Guilt
text:
What can help

Check the facts.
Acknowledge what happened.
Repair the harm.
Change the behaviour, then let go.

title: Guilt
text:
Design connection
Natural imagery, grounded type, and reuse symbols can communicate responsibility and repair.
Examples: Patagonia, Depop, and thredUP.
Previous: Jealousy | Next: Shame

title: What Do Emotions Do?
text:
Emotions give us information and energy. They are signals, not commands.
You never need to share private details to take part in this lesson.

title: What Do Emotions Do?
text:
What do emotions do?

1. They motivate us
Emotions prepare us to act.


2. They communicate to us
They point to what matters, what feels unsafe, or what needs attention.


3. They communicate to others
People read our face, voice, posture, and actions. Design communicates in similar ways through colour, type, images, shapes, spacing, and contrast.

title: What Do Emotions Do?
section: Don’t let the feed farm you
text:
Don’t let the feed farm you
The feed picks what you see.
It makes money when you keep scrolling.
Look up. Name what you feel. Pick your own move.

title: What Do Emotions Do?
text:
Explore an emotion
Brand examples may evoke the emotion, respond to it, or help shift it.



Emotion
What it does
What we can do
Brand examples




Fear and anxiety
Warns us about danger or uncertainty and prepares us to escape, avoid, or freeze.
Get safe, check the facts, ask for support, then take one brave step if it is safe.
Volvo, Headspace, Calm


Anger
Gives us energy when a goal is blocked, something feels unfair, or a boundary is crossed.
Pause, check the facts, state the boundary, and choose useful action or repair.
Riot Games, Fortnite, Call of Duty


Disgust
Pushes us away from something that may be unsafe, harmful, or against our values.
Name the problem, check the evidence, step back, and reject harm without attacking a person.
Mr. Clean, CeraVe, Lush


Envy
Shows us something another person has that we may want for ourselves.
Name what you want and turn comparison into a healthy goal.
Rolex, Jordan, Coach


Jealousy
Warns us that we may lose a relationship, role, place, or attention.
Check the facts, ask directly, name what you need, and build trust.
Snapchat, Discord


Guilt
Tells us our behaviour may not match our values or may have hurt someone.
Acknowledge it, repair the harm, change the behaviour, and let go.
Patagonia, Depop, thredUP


Shame
Makes us want to hide when we feel exposed, rejected, or wrong as a person.
Check the facts, separate the action from your identity, repair if needed, and talk to someone safe.
Always #LikeAGirl, Rare Beauty, Dove


Happiness
Draws us toward people and actions that feel rewarding, meaningful, or successful.
Notice the win, enjoy it, share it, and keep doing what works.
LEGO, Nintendo, Crocs


Love
Connects us to people, places, ideas, values, and communities that matter.
Show care, respect boundaries, offer useful support, and let others care for you.
Hallmark, Sanrio, Build-A-Bear


Sadness
Slows us down when something is lost, ends, or matters deeply.
Name the loss, rest, reach out, and take one small action when ready.
Kleenex, Pixar, Build-A-Bear

title: What Do Emotions Do?
section: What can we do with an emotion?
text:
What can we do with an emotion?

Name it to tame it. What am I feeling?
Feel it to heal it. Notice the feeling without acting right away.
Check the facts. What is happening? What does the emotion make me want to do?
Choose the next action. What response will help?

title: What Do Emotions Do?
text:
Use emotions in your design
Choose three emotions you want people to feel when they see your personal brand.
For each emotion, choose one design move using colour, type, images, shapes, spacing, or contrast.
Open the Three Emotions worksheet Make a worksheet copy
Continue with the Personal Brand Graphic in Photopea.

text:

Rounded symbols, friendly characters, and handwritten forms can create warmth and affection.

title: Shame
text:
Back to all emotions
Shame says, “Something is wrong with me.” That is different from guilt, which focuses on an action.

title: Shame
section: It can give us the urge to
text:
It can give us the urge to

hide;
disappear; or
avoid eye contact.

title: Shame
text:
It may be telling us

we fear rejection;
we believe we failed a value; or
we feel exposed.

title: Shame
text:
What can help

Check the facts.
Separate the action from your identity.
Repair the action if needed.
Talk to a safe person.

title: Shame
text:
Design connection
Soft forms and calm colour can move a message from shame toward confidence and self-acceptance.
Examples: Always #LikeAGirl, Rare Beauty, and Dove.
Previous: Guilt | Next: Happiness

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
By the end of this lesson:

I can trace a sketch with separate vector shapes.
I can name each layer so I know what it contains.
I can colour each part without changing the other parts.
I can save a PSD and export an SVG with separate parts.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
Why this is useful
Most hand-drawn logos have more than one part. A separate graphics layer for each part makes the logo easier to fix, colour, move, and animate.
An SVG can also guide a laser cutter, embroidery machine, vinyl cutter, or other machine. Clean paths and clear names make the file easier to use later.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
What you will make
You will rebuild a small landscape logo. The two mountain peaks also look like the letters AA. The finished SVG has four separate parts:

SUN
LEFT-A
RIGHT-A
RIVER



Your browser cannot play this video. Use the screenshots and steps below. 
Open the lesson video in a new tab.






NoteLevel 3 example



This is a simple Level 3 example, below 75%. It shows the required tracing and layer skills, but it is not a highly styled final design.
After the trace works, improve the shapes, spacing, colours, and style. Make your own logo look more polished and original.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
1. Fade and lock the sketch

Open the sketch in Photopea.
Rename the image layer REFERENCE.
Lower its Opacity to about 30%.
Lock the layer.

The sketch should be light enough that new black shapes are easy to see.



A faded landscape sketch on Photopea’s transparent canvas with the reference layer visible in the Layers panel.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
2. Make the sun

Choose the Ellipse Tool.
Set the tool to Shape mode.
Use a solid black fill and set the stroke to None.
Drag a circle over the sun.
Rename the new layer SUN.

Hold Shift while dragging if you want a perfect circle.



A black vector circle placed over the faded sun with a separate SUN layer in the Layers panel.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
3. Make two mountain shapes
The two peaks are separate pieces. Do not trace the whole mountain as one shape.

Choose the Pen Tool.
Choose Shape in the top bar.
Click anchor points at the bottom-left corner, the top of the first peak, and the centre valley.
Click the first anchor point again to make a closed path.
Rename the layer LEFT-A.
Start a new shape layer.
Trace the second peak and rename it RIGHT-A.

Use only a few points. Fewer points make a cleaner shape.



Two black triangular mountain shapes over the faded sketch with separate LEFT-A and RIGHT-A layers.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
4. Make the river
The river is a thin closed shape, not a brush line.

Start another new shape layer.
Click several points along the top edge of the river.
Click back along the bottom edge.
Close the path by clicking the first point.
Rename the layer RIVER.

For a smoother river, drag while placing an anchor point to make a Bézier curve. A few well-placed anchor points usually look smoother than many small ones.
Keep the shape simple. The curve does not need many points.



A thin black river shape traced below the two mountain shapes with the RIVER layer selected.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
section: 5. Hide the sketch and check the shapes
text:
5. Hide the sketch and check the shapes
Click the eye beside REFERENCE to hide the sketch.
Check the logo in black before adding colour. Black makes uneven shapes, gaps, and unwanted overlaps easier to see.



The black sun, two mountain peaks, and river on a transparent background with five clearly named layers.



Check your layers
The Layers panel should show:

RIVER
RIGHT-A
LEFT-A
SUN
REFERENCE, hidden and locked

These names become useful labels inside the SVG. In the next assignment, you can animate the sun, each peak, and the river separately.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
7. Add colour at the end

Double-click the shape thumbnail beside SUN.
Choose a colour and select OK.
Repeat for LEFT-A, RIGHT-A, and RIVER.
Use a small set of colours that are easy to tell apart.

Colour comes last because the black version makes shape problems easier to find.



The finished logo with a gold sun, two green mountain peaks, and a blue river on a transparent background.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
8. Save the editable PSD
Choose File > Save More > Save PSD/PSB. Keep PSD selected. Name the file studentnumber-lastname-layered-logo.psd, then choose Save.
The Photoshop Document (PSD) keeps the reference and all four editable shape layers.



Photopea’s Save PSD or PSB window over the finished coloured logo.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
9. Export the SVG

Keep REFERENCE hidden.
Choose File > Export as > SVG.
Name the file studentnumber-lastname-layered-logo.svg.
Leave add raster graphics off.
Leave add hidden layers off.
Choose Save.

The empty background keeps its transparency, so the SVG does not gain a white rectangle.



Photopea’s SVG export window with raster graphics and hidden layers turned off.


Open the finished four-part SVG to compare it with your file.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
Submit
Submit:

studentnumber-lastname-layered-logo.psd
studentnumber-lastname-layered-logo.svg

Every filename must begin with your student number, followed by your last name. Replace studentnumber and lastname with your own information. Example: 123456789-Smith-layered-logo.psd.






TipRename a downloaded file



If Photopea downloads a file with the wrong name, rename it before you submit it. Keep the file ending, such as .psd, .png, or .svg.

ChromebookWindowsLinux



Open the Launcher, then open Files.
Open Downloads.
Select the file.
Press Ctrl+Enter.
Type the required filename, then press Enter.




Open File Explorer with Windows+E.
Open Downloads.
Select the file, then press F2.
Type the required filename, then press Enter.




Open Files.
Open Downloads.
Select the file, then press F2. If that does not work, right-click the file and choose Rename.
Type the required filename, then press Enter.




Do not remove or change the letters after the final dot. For example, an SVG filename must still end in .svg.
Official help: Chromebook Files, Windows File Explorer, and Ubuntu Files.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
Common issues

Everything is on one layer: undo the last shape, make a new layer, and draw that part again.
The Pen Tool makes a line instead of a filled shape: choose Shape mode before you click points.
The shape has too many bumps: remove points. Use only the points needed to show the main form.
The sketch appears in the SVG: hide REFERENCE and export again with add raster graphics and add hidden layers off.
The parts cannot move separately: check that every part is on its own shape layer.
The colours look busy: use fewer colours and keep enough contrast between nearby parts.


Design curriculum: Builds vector drawing, layer organization, revision, SVG export, and animation preparation.

title: Lesson 2B: Trace a Multi-Layer Logo in Photopea
text:
Summary
You traced one simple sketch as four named vector shapes. You checked the black shapes first, added colour at the end, saved an editable PSD, and exported an SVG whose parts can be animated separately.
This Level 3 example is a starting point. Improve the styling and make the final design your own.
Previous: Lesson 2A: Warm-Up: Trace the AA Logo. Next: Lesson 3: Combine the Logo and Nameplate.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
Why this is useful
A clear nameplate is easier to read and easier to change. The empty space on the left gives the logo a planned place instead of squeezing it in later.
You will use this file again in Lesson 3.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
What you will make
You will make a transparent 11 × 4 inch nameplate. The left 4 × 4 inches stay empty. The name Andrade sits in the right part of the design.


Your browser cannot play this video. Use the screenshots and steps below.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
Before you start
Open Photopea in a browser.
You will use:

the Type Tool (T);
a vertical guide;
the Move Tool (V); and
the Layers panel.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
1. Make the canvas

Choose File > New.
Set Width to 11 inches.
Set Height to 4 inches.
Set DPI to 300.
Set Background to Transparent.
Choose Create.

Photopea will make a 3300 × 1200 pixel canvas. That is correct for 11 × 4 inches at 300 pixels per inch.



Photopea’s New Project window set to 11 inches wide, 4 inches high, and 300 pixels per inch.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
2. Mark the logo space
The logo space is a 4 × 4 inch square on the left.

Choose View > New Guide.
Choose a Vertical guide.
Enter 4 in. If Photopea asks for pixels, enter 1200 px.
Choose OK.

Everything left of the guide is for the logo. Keep the name to the right of it.



A vertical guide marks four inches from the left side of the transparent nameplate.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
3. Type the name

Select the Type Tool (T).
Click to the right of the guide.
Type Andrade.
Select the whole word before changing the font.




The name Andrade added to the right side of the nameplate.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
4. Try several fonts
Select the whole name. Try at least three fonts before choosing one. Change only the font at first. This makes the choices easier to compare.
Try:

a serif font;
a decorative or rounded font; and
a plain sans serif font.

A serif font has small finishing strokes on the letters. Serif fonts are common in printed books. A sans serif font does not have those strokes. Sans serif fonts are often a clearer starting point for signs and nameplates.
   
No font is always good or bad. The best font fits the job and stays easy to read.

Serif: try Georgia or Times New Roman for a printed-book look. Check the thin strokes.
Sans serif: try DejaVu Sans, Arial, Verdana, or Open Sans for clear letters.
Rounded or display: try Nunito, Montserrat, or Impact for personality. Check for crowding.
Script or decorative: use joined or detailed letters with care. They can be hard to read and engrave.

Font names may vary. Choose a similar font if one is unavailable.



Andrade shown in a serif font while the student compares font choices.


Ask these questions:

Can I read the name quickly?
Can I tell similar characters apart, such as I, l, and 1?
Are the lines thick enough to engrave?
Do the spaces inside a, e, and o stay open?

Read the name from an arm’s length away. If you need extra time to recognize it, try a simpler font.
Zoom out until the whole nameplate fits on the screen. Compare the fonts again at the smaller view. The Accessible Design guide shows why this test matters.
The example ends with DejaVu Sans Book at about 300 px. Another clear sans serif font is also fine.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
5. Place the name

Select the Move Tool (V).
Keep the name inside the right 7 inches.
Centre it from top to bottom.
Leave a clear margin on the right.
Check that the name does not cross the 4 inch guide.

Use your eyes as well as the numbers. The empty space above and below the name should look even.



Andrade in a balanced sans serif font with room for a logo on the left.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
6. Save and export
Save three files.
Every filename must begin with your student number, followed by your last name. Replace studentnumber and lastname below with your own information.

Choose File > Save as PSD. Name it studentnumber-lastname-nameplate.psd.
Choose File > Export as > PNG. Name it studentnumber-lastname-nameplate.png.
Choose File > Export as > SVG. Name it studentnumber-lastname-nameplate.svg.

Example: 123456789-Smith-nameplate.psd
Keep add raster graphics off when you export the SVG. The checkerboard means the background is transparent. It will not appear in the saved image.



Photopea’s Export as menu with PNG and SVG choices visible.








TipRename a downloaded file



If Photopea downloads a file with the wrong name, rename it before you submit it. Keep the file ending, such as .psd, .png, or .svg.

Type the required filename, then press Enter.




Do not remove or change the letters after the final dot. For example, an SVG filename must still end in .svg.

title: Lesson 1: Build the Nameplate Text in Photopea
text:
Common issues

The canvas has a white box: make a new file with Background: Transparent.
The name is in the logo space: move it to the right of the 4 inch guide.
The name looks too small: make the type larger, but keep a clear right margin.
The name is hard to read: choose a simple sans serif font with open letter shapes.

title: Lesson 2A: Warm-Up: Trace the AA Logo in Photopea

A blue hand-drawn AA logo opened as a reference image in Photopea.

Choose Shape in the top bar.

Photopea makes a new shape layer. A shape line stays sharp when it is resized.

The traced AA logo by itself on Photopea’s transparent checkerboard.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
Why this is useful
The wrong file can look blurry or behave badly in another program. Knowing how the file works helps you choose the right image for a screen, an engraving, or a cut line. It also helps you send clear instructions to tools such as a laser cutter, vinyl cutter, embroidery machine, or CNC router.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
section: Two ways to describe an image
text:
Two ways to describe an image
A raster image is made from a grid of tiny squares called pixels. Raster images work well for photos, painted textures, and shading. A raster image can look blocky when it is made too large.
Each pixel stores one small piece of the image.
A vector image is made from shapes and paths. Its points, curves, fills, and lines can be edited. It stays sharp when it is made larger or smaller. Vector files are useful for logos, diagrams, score lines, and cut lines.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
Same logo, two different files
At normal size, the PNG and SVG versions of this logo look almost the same. The difference becomes clear when you zoom in.



PNG: a grid of pixels



The PNG stores the logo as a grid of coloured squares. Those squares are called pixels.



When the PNG is enlarged, the square pixels make a stair-step edge.





SVG: shapes and paths



The SVG stores the logo as shapes and paths. The small points on a path are called nodes. Move a node to change the shape.



When the SVG is enlarged, the edge stays smooth. The blue line shows the path and the squares show editable nodes.











TipTry it



Open the PNG and SVG in your design program. Zoom in as far as you can. Look for square pixels in the PNG. Select the SVG with a path-selection tool and look for nodes.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
What a machine sees
A machine path is the route that a tool follows. A laser, blade, pen, needle, or router can use vector geometry to plan that route.








File
What it stores
A good use




PNG
A grid of pixels
Photos, shading, websites, and laser engraving


SVG
Shapes, paths, and nodes
Laser cutting or scoring, vinyl cutting, pen plotting, and CNC paths



An embroidery design can begin with an SVG because its clean shapes are easy to trace and size. Embroidery software must then turn those shapes into stitches and save a machine file such as DST or PES. The embroidery machine follows the stitch file, not usually the SVG itself.

title: Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
Raster, Vector & SVG | Digital Design Foundations
text:
Sort by intended operation

Raster image: use when engraved tone or photographic detail is intentional.
Filled vector shape: useful for clean engraved artwork.
Open or closed vector path: useful for scoring or cutting when the machine workflow recognizes it.

Make the same symbol in three forms: a low-quality raster image, a filled vector shape, and an outline path. Make each one larger. Check the edges. Decide how a laser program may read each one.

title: Teacher Guide: Bring Your Brand to Life
text:
Before the assignment

Materials and access

Each student needs an existing logo as a layered PSD, a clean PNG, or another file the selected tool can import.
Test smooth.video on the student network and device image. It needs a current browser and WebGL.
Keep Photopea available as an equal-status fallback.
Have students create one local folder for the project, draft exports, and final export.
No account, music, voice-over, or stock media is required.



Teacher demonstration files

Captioned smooth.video screencast
Animated AA example
Advanced Technology Commons emblem example
Python source for the advanced emblem generator
Editable smooth.video starter
Original four-part AA SVG
Before-and-after comparison

The AA logo is an inspection model. Ask students to identify the order, timing changes, hold, and ending before showing the editor.
The Technology Commons emblem is an optional teacher or coding extension. It is not part of the required student path. It shows that the same timeline skills can support a more complex transformation when the artwork is prepared as separate elements first. Emphasize that smooth.video can animate imported layers, but it does not automatically split a flattened PNG into the arrow halves, lighthouse supports, roots, waves, or hands. Three to five well-timed parts are enough for a successful student submission.

title: Teacher Guide: Bring Your Brand to Life
text:
Learning evidence
Look for four kinds of evidence:

Motion design: at least two intentional changes across the logo or its parts.
Timing: varied speed, a readable hold, and a complete 5–8 second sequence.
Brand clarity: motion supports a named emotion and the logo remains legible.
Process: version 1, feedback, one visible improvement, editable project when supported, final export, and one design sentence.

title: Teacher Guide: Bring Your Brand to Life
text:
Suggested launch demonstration
Keep the launch under 12 minutes so students can start making.

Play the finished AA example once without explanation.
Ask students to identify the beginning, middle, ending, and emotion.
Open smooth.video and use Add media to import the existing logo.
Show Animate > in and compare two effects.
Drag an animation point on the timeline to change its duration.
Stagger two parts, then add a readable hold.
Show Menu > Save project and Export > MP4 or GIF.
Reopen the exported result.

The student page begins with a real, captioned screencast that has pause, replay, and full-screen controls. It then follows one six-step path: watch, make a complete draft, add a keyframe change, match the feeling, test, and export. The compact project-launch deck mirrors this sequence without turning the assignment into four lectures.

title: Teacher Guide: Bring Your Brand to Life
text:
Four-day sequence

Day 1: Learn the editor and choose an emotion
Mini-lesson: intent, timing, beginning-middle-end, and the difference between an entrance preset and a keyframe.
Student work: import the existing logo, try three entrance effects, choose one direction and emotion, and build a rough motion test.
Checkpoint: every student can play something from start to finish. Ask: “What should the audience feel, and which motion choice causes that feeling?”


Day 2: Build the first complete draft
Mini-lesson: staggering elements, using contrast in speed, and holding the completed logo long enough to read.
Student work: build a 5–8 second beginning, middle, and ending with at least two intentional changes.
Checkpoint: students export and keep version 1. Check duration before discussing polish.


Day 3: Test and improve
Mini-lesson: critique the motion, not the person. Use three prompts: intended feeling, strongest readable moment, and one timing problem.
Student work: peer test once without explanation, record feedback, and make one visible improvement.
Checkpoint: compare version 1 and version 2. The improvement should solve a named problem.


Day 4: Finalize and submit
Mini-lesson: export choices, file naming, and the reopen test.
Student work: peer test, make final fixes, save the editable project, export MP4 or GIF, reopen it, and submit manually in Google Classroom.
Checkpoint: verify the final animation, editable project when supported, and design-choice sentence.

Differentiation and accessibility

Let students animate one whole-logo PNG if layer separation creates too much setup work.
Give the editable .smooth starter to students who need a functioning timeline to inspect.
Let students use Photopea for a frame-by-frame GIF without penalty.
Encourage keyboard preview with the space bar and short work-test-save cycles.
Pair the controllable screencast with the short written steps and screenshots; avoid requiring students to learn from video alone.
Let students choose low-motion fades or short slides when energetic motion is uncomfortable.
The web example swaps its animated GIF for a still frame when the device requests reduced motion.
Do not require audio. It is not assessed and can create access, copyright, and classroom-noise barriers.
Keep a copy of the two-page handout available in print or as a local PDF.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Investigate alternatives
Do not give every student one finished stand file. Compare triangular legs, straight or angled legs, curved legs, T-feet, cross-feet, slot bases, easel backs, and two-leg systems. Ask what each solution changes about the footprint, material use, assembly, viewing angle, and centre of gravity.
The project-components library provides starting geometry for investigation. Students remain responsible for adapting dimensions, selecting a concept, testing it, and documenting why it works.
Use the focused standing-name-tag component set to compare a triangle leg, T-foot, cross-foot and easel back. Copy a concept into a new file; do not submit the palette sheet as the project. Complete the fabrication planning worksheet and follow Paper to Inkscape.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Easel reference set
The external FreePatternsArea easel set shows four variations on the same structural idea. Each uses a wide A-shaped front frame, one or more crosspieces, and a rear leg or kickstand. The variations change the ledge, hinge pieces, rear-leg adjustment and decorative openings rather than changing the basic load path.
The source describes a 5.51 in high, 3.70 in wide easel for 0.118 in material (140 × 94 mm, using 3 mm stock). It suggests scaling the complete design by \(4/3 = 1.333\) for 0.157 in (4 mm) material, which produces an easel about 7.35 in high and 4.92 in wide (187 × 125 mm). That preserves every proportion, including the slots. It is not the best method when you want to change the display height without changing the material thickness. In that case, resize the structure and reset every slot from the measured material instead.






WarningReference, not a verified cutting file



The SVG declares a numerical viewBox but does not declare a physical unit. Import it using a known reference dimension, confirm the intended 5.51 in (140 mm) assembled height, and measure every slot before cutting. The files have not been physically verified by Technology Commons.
The source currently identifies the design as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for personal, non-commercial use. Preserve the FreePatternsArea credit and check the current licence terms before using or sharing the files. These external files are not covered by the Technology Commons CC BY-SA licence.


Reference formats: SVG, DXF, DWG, CDR, PDF, and PNG preview.

How to read the flat reference files
The six downloads above are alternate formats of the same reference sheet. For the Technology Commons workflow, open the SVG in Inkscape. Use the PDF or PNG only to look at or print the design. DXF and DWG are for CAD/CAM software, and CDR is for CorelDRAW.
The outlines are flat parts, not a picture of the assembled easel. In the cropped example, the large A-shaped outline is the front frame and the large T-shaped outline is the wide single rear support. That T-shaped part is the large single leg: its wide top provides an attachment or hinge zone and its broad centre reaches the table. It does not stand by itself. The complete design still needs the front frame, an attachment between the parts, and a stop or tether that controls the opening angle.
The source sheet does not label every part or provide a verified step-by-step assembly sequence. Keep each apparent group together, prototype it in cardboard, and do not guess the purpose of an isolated small outline. For a clearer original starting point, choose Wide single easel back · like the reference in the Leg & Support Builder; the tool now shows both the flat cut part and a coloured assembled view.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
What the legs actually do



Front and side force diagrams for a three-legged A-frame easel



Two splayed front legs
The two front legs carry most of the vertical load. Their feet are farther apart than their tops, so the front support width is large without making the top bulky. The load should travel mostly along the plane of the sheet and down the legs as compression. Sheet material is much stiffer in its own plane than it is when pushed sideways out of plane.
The space between the legs is not only decorative. Removing low-demand material reduces mass while leaving a deep outer frame. The remaining rail width must still resist cracking at slots, grain defects and narrow corners.


Rear kickstand
The rear leg changes the frame from a nearly flat object into a triangle. In side view, the front feet and rear foot form a support footprint. The stand remains stable while the vertical projection of the combined centre of mass stays inside that footprint.
Moving the rear foot farther back increases the tipping margin and usually reduces the force needed to balance the display. It also creates a longer, more slender leg. A loose pivot or a sideways bump can then make the leg bend or buckle. The rear leg works best when its top pivot and bottom contact keep the main force close to the leg’s centreline, so the part carries compression instead of acting like a long cantilever.


Cross rail and ledge
The cross rail ties the two front legs together. It resists racking, where the frame changes from a symmetric A shape into a skewed shape, and splaying, where the feet move apart. The ledge carries the displayed object and transfers that load into both front legs. A ledge attached at only one small tab creates a concentrated bending force; two separated tabs or a continuous shoulder distribute the load more effectively.


Pivot, tabs and slots
The pivot carries shear between the front frame and rear leg while allowing the angle to change. A larger hole removes more of the leg’s net section, and a hole close to an edge can split the remaining material. Keep useful material around the hole, use a washer or smooth spacer where appropriate, and test repeated opening and closing.
Tabs and slots locate parts and transfer shear through bearing on their faces. The shoulder, not the fragile tip of a tab, should stop the part at its final position. Make the slot from measured thickness plus a tested fit adjustment; do not assume nominal plywood thickness is exact.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Bending force and size
The basic bending moment is:
\[M = F L\]
where \(F\) is the applied force and \(L\) is the perpendicular distance to the section being checked. Doubling the display load or doubling the lever arm doubles the bending moment.
For a long member behaving roughly like a cantilever, deflection changes approximately with:
\[\delta \propto \frac{F L^3}{E I}\]
This explains why a leg that is merely twice as long can feel about eight times more flexible when its cross-section is unchanged. \(E\) describes the material stiffness and \(I\) describes how the material is distributed around the bending axis.
For a rectangular strip bending out of the sheet plane, \(I\) includes the material thickness cubed. Increasing thickness from 0.118 in to 0.157 in (3 to 4 mm) can therefore increase weak-axis bending stiffness by roughly \((4/3)^3 = 2.37\) when the other dimension stays the same. Increasing thickness from 0.118 in to 0.236 in (3 to 6 mm) gives roughly \(2^3 = 8\) times the weak-axis stiffness. Real plywood varies by species, ply quality, grain direction, voids, moisture and cut quality, so these ratios explain trends rather than certify a load.
The most effective design move is not simply making every leg thick. Keep forces in plane, use a triangular footprint, shorten unsupported lengths, tie the front legs together, and avoid eccentric joints that twist the sheet.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Starting proportions to investigate
These are prototype starting points for a light display easel, not structural ratings:








Feature
Starting relationship
Why it matters




Front footprint width
about 0.6 to 0.75 of easel height
improves side-to-side tipping resistance


Rear-foot distance
about 0.35 to 0.5 of easel height
improves front-to-back tipping resistance


Front leg or frame-rail width
at least 4 to 6 material thicknesses
leaves a useful net section around cutouts and slots


Cross-rail depth
at least 4 material thicknesses
helps resist racking and leg splay


Tab length along an edge
at least 4 material thicknesses
distributes bearing instead of concentrating it at one small tab


Material beside a slot
at least 2 material thicknesses as a first check
reduces splitting at the slot end



For 0.118 in (3 mm) stock, those starting relationships suggest front rails around 0.47 to 0.71 in wide, a cross rail at least about 0.47 in deep, and a tab at least about 0.47 in long. These are hypotheses to test with the actual stock, not guaranteed minimums.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Worked example: 11 × 4 inch name plate
Assume the plaque is 11 inches wide, 4 inches high and nominally 1/8 inch thick. Measure the actual material rather than entering exactly 0.125 inch automatically. Define the viewing angle from the tabletop: 75 degrees is 15 degrees back from vertical, while 80 degrees is 10 degrees back from vertical.









Viewing angle
Top moves behind the bottom
Vertical rise
Centre-of-mass projection behind the bottom




75°
1.04 in
3.86 in
0.52 in


80°
0.69 in
3.94 in
0.35 in



The centre-of-mass values assume a uniform plaque without a heavy attachment. The support footprint must extend behind that projected point, with additional margin for bumps and material variation.

Stronger, quieter option: two high supports

Put two triangular cheeks or rear legs about 1.5 to 2 inches in from each end of the 11-inch plaque.
Attach each support about 3 to 3.5 inches above the bottom edge.
Start with the rear contact about 1.5 to 1.75 inches behind the plaque’s bottom contact.
A rear member from a 3.25-inch-high attachment to that footprint is about 3.2 to 3.4 inches long at the proposed angles.

The pair distributes load across the plaque and resists twisting. The higher attachment gives the support more leverage to resist rotation, but the longer member needs enough width to prevent sideways bending. A triangular cheek is usually stiffer than a narrow stick because it shortens the unsupported load path.


Sleeker option: one low centre support
A single centred support can attach about 1.25 inches above the bottom, place its rear contact about 1.25 inches behind the bottom, and use a member about 1.5 to 1.6 inches long. This is compact and visually quiet, but the smaller vertical spacing creates greater force at the joint for the same overturning moment. One central support also provides less resistance to twisting across an 11-inch-wide plaque.
Use two separated bottom locating points or a continuous ledge even if there is only one rear leg. They stop the plaque from rotating around the centre support. Widening the concealed base of the centre support also improves side-to-side stability without making the visible leg taller.


Prototype sequence

Draw both side profiles full size on half a sheet of paper or cardboard.
Test 75 degrees and 80 degrees. Choose the smallest tilt that still reads well under the expected viewing height.
Test the two-support version first as the reference design.
Remove material or move toward a single centre support only after the reference design passes the push tests.
Measure the real 1/8-inch stock and cut a slot coupon. Set the slot from measured thickness plus the tested fit adjustment.
Push at both ends and at the top centre. Watch for tipping, plaque twist, slot splitting and out-of-plane leg bending.

title: Make It Stand | Optional Laser-Cutting Extension
text:
Stability checks

Locate the combined centre of mass approximately over the support area.
Increase the support footprint where tipping is likely.
Consider plaque height, thickness, angle, and the direction of expected bumps.
Test front-to-back and side-to-side stability.
Push lightly from both sides and watch for out-of-plane leg bending or pivot twist.
Check whether the cross rail prevents the front legs from spreading.
Check whether slots weaken a narrow region or create fragile grain directions.
Inspect the net material around every pivot hole and slot end.
Record what changed between versions.
Label the load path and the interface that locates the engraved blank.
Test the stand with the actual blank rather than a guessed rectangle.

Use cardboard or scrap material for a quick geometry prototype before cutting the full design. A stand that works only on a perfectly still surface needs another iteration.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Supports TIJ1O and TDJ2O design-process learning through alternatives, modelling, stability, constraints, testing, feedback, and iteration. Construction and manufacturing contexts may connect to TCJ2O and TMJ2O.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text: Calibration is not one magic kerf value. It is a short, recorded test that connects this sheet, this machine condition, this geometry, and this intended fit.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
Operating procedure or material calibration?



Operating procedure


Machine-specific setup, safety instruction, assessments, and authorization are not provided on this public website. Follow your school board’s safety guidelines and the course-specific instruction provided by your teacher. Students in Mr. Andrade’s classes can find that information in Google Classroom.




Material calibration


Measure how one stock-and-setting combination changes size and fit. This is about the result of the process.



Actual thickness and batch are recorded.


A known drawing dimension imports at 100%.


Cut width and finished dimensions are measured.


Slots and holes are tested against the real mating object.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
1 · Measure the actual sheet
Plywood sold as 1/4 inch may not measure 6.35 mm. Measure at several locations with callipers, including near a visibly damaged edge but not on it. Record the minimum, maximum and the value used to design the test.

Material thicknessRecord a measured range, not a catalogue assumption. Ruler / scale checkConfirm millimetres and 100% import before cutting. Dimension verificationCompare a known drawing dimension to the finished result.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
2 · Understand what kerf changes
The beam removes a narrow band centred on the path. With the path drawn on the intended boundary, an outside part tends to finish smaller and an inside opening tends to finish larger. The magnitude varies, so do not copy a universal number.



Kerf diagram showing the cut band around a vector path, a smaller outside part and a larger inside opening.


BRM’s current kerf and kerf-compensation explanation is a useful process reference. BRM also hosts a free kerf gauge SVG, credited there to Nameek and Elplatt, and explicitly tells users to check scale after import. Use it as another test method, not as a pre-approved local setting.
Ponoko’s 2011 article, Figuring out kerf for precision parts, is included only as a historical/conceptual example of test-and-revise thinking. Do not copy its old settings or service-specific assumptions.

Kerf testMeasure a repeated cut rather than guessing from one edge. Tab fitTest the male feature and its orientation. Slot fitStart from measured thickness, then compare a small series. Four-fit seriesName the function: loose, sliding, snug or press. Hole fitTest the actual bottle, dowel or fastener, not only a calliper.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
3 · Cut, measure and decide

Open one test SVG in Inkscape and confirm document units, viewBox scale and a known dimension.
Label the coupon with material, batch, date, machine and revision before cutting.
Use the course-specific process provided by your teacher.
Let the coupon cool and measure it consistently; do not force a calliper into a soft or angled edge.
Test the real mating object in every candidate feature.
Select the fit that serves the function. A press fit is not automatically “more accurate” than a sliding fit.
Update the source dimension, save the record and repeat only the smallest necessary test.







Warning



Kerf compensation changes geometry; it does not correct a machine-condition problem, warped stock, or an incorrectly scaled import. Resolve unexpected machine behaviour through the course-specific process before interpreting the coupon.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
A laser cutter makes accurate flat parts. The finished object also depends on how those parts locate one another, how loads move through the joints, how much surface is available for bonding, and how the edges and faces are finished.






ImportantScope of this lesson



This lesson explains design and material choices. It is not safety information or equipment authorization. Use your school board’s requirements, teacher instruction, professional experience and judgement, and the current manufacturer information for every machine, adhesive and finish.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
A laser cutter makes accurate flat parts. The finished object also depends on how those parts locate one another, how loads move through the joints, how much surface is available for bonding, and how the edges and faces are finished.






ImportantScope of this lesson



This lesson explains design and material choices. It is not safety information or equipment authorization. Use your school board’s requirements, teacher instruction, professional experience and judgement, and the current manufacturer information for every machine, adhesive and finish.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
Adhesive choices








Adhesive
Typical design use
Design consideration




Wood glue
Close-fitting wood, plywood or MDF joints
Works best when the mating surfaces fit well and provide useful bonded area. Select the exact product for the material and environment.


White glue
Paper, cardboard, light wood and general porous-material assemblies
Useful for classroom models and lighter work, but do not assume it has the same strength or moisture resistance as a purpose-selected wood glue.


Epoxy
Mixed materials, small gaps, repairs or assemblies that need a rigid bond
A two-part system can bond several material types and fill space, but the specific product determines cure, gap and finish behaviour.


Super glue (cyanoacrylate)
Small, close-fitting parts that need a quick bond
Fast setting leaves little repositioning time. Test it on the real material because appearance and bond behaviour vary.


Glue stick
A temporary adhesion or separation layer on a compatible 3D-printer build plate
This is not a structural adhesive and is not for a laser-cutter bed. Follow the printer and filament guidance for the exact build surface.



Adhesive should support a good joint, not hide a poor fit. Keep glue away from visible surfaces that will be stained because sealed patches can absorb colour differently.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
section: Joint geometry, surface area and strength
text:
Joint geometry, surface area and strength

Butt joint: simple, but it offers little alignment and may have limited bonded area.
Lap or half-lap: overlaps material to increase contact area and resist sliding.
Tab-and-slot joint: locates parts and can transfer force when the tab, slot and material thickness match.
Finger or box joint: repeats interlocking fingers to increase bonded area and create a visible pattern.
Mortise-and-tenon form: uses a projecting part and a receiving opening to locate an assembly.
Keyed, wedged or interlocking joint: uses geometry or a separate key to hold parts in position.
Layered or laminated joint: stacks cut profiles to create thickness, relief or a stronger local feature.

More bonded surface area can spread a load, but area alone does not guarantee strength. Also consider grain direction, sheet thickness, fit, leverage, notches, stress concentration, material quality and the selected adhesive.

Learn from Japanese joinery
Japanese joinery can inspire precise shoulders, keys, wedges and interlocking forms. Study how the geometry locates parts and manages force, then adapt the principle to sheet material and the project’s actual loads. A laser-cut imitation of a traditional joint is not automatically strong, so test fit and performance in the real material.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
section: Design the appearance of the joint

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
Cleanup and shaping tools







Tool
Useful for




File or needle file
Refining tabs, slots, straight edges and small openings with control.


Rasp
Removing wood quickly and shaping larger outside profiles.


Sanding block
Keeping broad faces and straight edges flat while smoothing them.


Belt sander
Faster material removal on accessible outside edges and surfaces.


Oscillating spindle sander
Smoothing inside curves, openings and concave edges.


Coping saw
Trimming notches or internal shapes before final filing and sanding.


Fine abrasive paper
Final smoothing and easing exposed corners without removing too much material.



Cleanup must preserve the dimensions that make a joint work. Keep a locating shoulder square when the assembly depends on it, while easing exposed corners when that improves touch and appearance.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
Sanding and staining wood
Sanding can remove residue, level faces, soften exposed corners and prepare a consistent surface. Do not sand away the fit of tabs, slots or calibrated edges. Move from shaping to finer finishing only as much as the material and intended appearance require.
Stain changes colour and can emphasize grain, but laser-cut edges, glue residue and different sheet layers may absorb it unevenly. Test the complete combination on an offcut: cut edge, sanded face, adhesive and stain. Decide whether the project benefits from preserving the dark cut edge, sanding it lighter, or making every edge treatment consistent.

title: Laser-Cut Assembly, Adhesives & Finishing
text:
Assembly and finish check

Do the joints locate the parts without forcing them?
Is there enough well-fitted bonded area for the intended load?
Are high-stress notches, thin tabs or long lever arms creating a weak point?
Does the cleanup method preserve critical dimensions?
Are visible joints, grain, edges and stain part of one aesthetic decision?
Has the material, adhesive and finish combination been tested on an offcut?

title: Laser Cutting for Technology Education | SVG, Kerf, Fits & Fabrication
text:
Testing and iteration in practice
Small tests lead to better builds. Compare, record and revise.




Power and line-quality tests. The bears are repeated test samples: their purpose is to make differences in engraving and cutting easy to see, not to prescribe a finished design.





Cut and fit prototype. Repeating interlocking geometry exposes incomplete cuts, excessive burning and pieces that fit too loosely or tightly.





Engraving plus cut geometry. One sample can test whether the image remains readable after puzzle lines, kerf and handling are introduced.





Compare alternatives. Different faces, symbols and mechanisms make design choices visible so evidence can guide the next version.





Functional prototype. Layered plates, slots, fasteners, wiring and moving parts shift testing from appearance to assembly, access and operation.





Refined display model. A developed build still depends on earlier tests of scale, joint fit, alignment, support and finish.



Use the material-fit calibration workflow to plan controlled tests, then use Evaluate, Improve & Repeat to turn observations into a specific next decision.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text: Build the design from measurements and named parts. Do not redraw every primitive by eye. Keep the editable master; make a separate fabrication copy only when the local machine workflow requires converted text or flattened artwork.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Before the screen

Complete the fabrication planning worksheet.
Draw front, top and side views. Mark the datum: the edge or centre from which important dimensions are located.
Measure the real object and sheet. Record ranges when objects vary.
Decide whether each circle means a hole or a circle part.
Identify one critical feature to test before the complete cut.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Set up Inkscape

Open File → Document Properties.
Set display units and document units to mm.
Set the page to the intended physical output size.
Save immediately as project-name_v01_master.svg.
Turn on snapping only when it supports the intended datum and alignment; do not let snapping replace entered dimensions.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Bring in building blocks
If the project begins as a plate with a row, grid, radial or perimeter hole pattern, use the Fabrication Plate Builder first. Its output is intentionally plain: CUT_OUTER, CUT_HOLES and an optional GUIDES group. Inkscape remains the place to add labels, slots, custom profiles and manufacturing intent.

Open the relevant component palette.
Select the named component group and copy it into the master file.
Use the toolbar or Object → Transform to enter exact width, height and position.
Rename the group by purpose: top-shelf, bottle-hole-01, left-gusset.
Duplicate repeated parts from one checked original. Use Object → Align and Distribute for centres and spacing.

Avoid advanced node editing in the first sequence. If a shape requires many uncontrolled node moves, return to simpler parts or revise the paper plan.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Separate manufacturing intent
Use clearly named groups or layers for CUT, SCORE and ENGRAVE. The library uses red, blue and black as a communication convention, but the machine operator confirms the local mapping. A colour alone is never approval to cut.
For the first name-tag engraving, set the page to the measured pre-cut blank, keep artwork inside the safe margin, hide/delete guides, and export the page as PNG at the instructor-set resolution. Reopen the PNG and confirm pixel dimensions, crop and orientation before it enters the laser workflow.

Every critical dimension matches the paper plan.
One controlled original was used for duplicates.
No duplicate paths, stray objects, hidden output or critical external fonts remain.
The machine preview contains the expected count of cuts and engraves.

The filename shows project and version; obsolete versions are not sent accidentally.
