title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
Choose an existing tool holder, organizer, fixture, or storage product as a precedent. Study what it does well, identify a real opportunity, then create an original design that improves the experience for a defined user and context.
The goal is not to make a copy. The goal is to learn from a good idea, explain how it works, and produce a better response to the problem using your own measurements, geometry, testing, and documentation.
Your evidence should justify each criterion, make every trade-off visible, and show at least one iteration.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
Choose an existing tool holder, organizer, fixture, or storage product as a precedent. Study what it does well, identify a real opportunity, then create an original design that improves the experience for a defined user and context.
The goal is not to make a copy. The goal is to learn from a good idea, explain how it works, and produce a better response to the problem using your own measurements, geometry, testing, and documentation.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
The design challenge
Develop a tool holder or organizer that improves at least three of these qualities:

Faster: quicker to fabricate, assemble, install, use, inspect, clean, or return tools to.
Cheaper: less material, fewer parts, common hardware, shorter machine time, or lower replacement cost.
Better looking: clearer proportions, stronger visual hierarchy, intentional colour and form, or a better fit with its setting.
More ergonomic: easier reach, a safer grip, better visibility, comfortable clearances, and one-hand use where appropriate.
More positive: creates calm, confidence, pride, delight, belonging, or satisfaction instead of clutter and frustration.
More useful: holds the right objects, supports a wider range, or solves a problem the precedent misses.
More durable or serviceable: stronger load path, replaceable wear parts, accessible fasteners, or easier repair.
More responsible: less waste, fewer mixed materials, efficient sheet layout, or parts that can be reused.

Every gain has a possible trade-off. A cheaper design may take longer to assemble. A smaller design may make tools harder to grasp. State what improved, what did not, and what evidence supports the claim.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
1. Find precedents
Collect at least three references from two different source types. Include one commercial product and one build, model, or assembly that reveals how parts might work together.

Product and laser-project ideas

Etsy tool-holder results: compare use cases, forms, prices, claims, and recurring themes in public reviews. Do not copy seller photos, artwork, or files.
Glowforge Catalog: study laser-cut construction, layer strategies, visual language, and product categories. Catalog access does not grant permission to redistribute or recreate a paid design.
Instructables tool-organizer search: look for build sequences, material choices, mistakes, tests, and revisions.



Mechanisms and fabrication ideas

Printables tool-holder search: inspect mounting, retention, modularity, print orientation, user makes, ratings, and comments.
Thingiverse tool-holder and organization group: compare holders for specific tools with broader workshop systems.
MakerWorld tool-holder collection: study adjustable, magnetic, modular, and low-support approaches.



Assemblies and form studies

Onshape public documents: use the Public filter to study part relationships, assemblies, parameters, and drawings.
Sketchfab tool-holder models: rotate models to inspect form, access, and assembly. Check the licence on each model before downloading or reusing anything.



Graphics and visual language

Openverse, Openclipart, and Noun Project: investigate symbols, silhouettes, and graphic styles for labels. Check the individual licence and attribution requirement before use.

Start locally too: browse the Laser Fabrication Library, purpose-built holder kits, five organizer reference assemblies, and Tool Organizer Gallery.
For more starting points, use the public libraries above and add teacher-reviewed references on inclusive design, repair, CAD, graphics, museum scans, electronics, and sustainability. A teacher must review each entry before classroom use.






ImportantPublicly visible does not mean free to copy



Record the creator or seller, page title, URL, access date, and stated licence for every reference. You may analyze publicly observable functions, interfaces, proportions, mechanisms, and user feedback. Do not trace product photographs, reproduce logos or distinctive decoration, download files without permission, bypass payment, or present another person’s work as your own. Reuse a file only when its licence clearly permits your intended use, and provide the required attribution.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
section: 2. Reverse engineer the problem, not the artwork
text:
2. Reverse engineer the problem, not the artwork
For each precedent, make an evidence table.







Question
Evidence to record




Who is it for?
User, setting, tools, reach zone, and likely routine


What problem does it solve?
Need, current frustration, and desired result


How does it work?
Support, retention, mounting, labels, load path, and assembly


What looks successful?
Features supported by photographs, specifications, build notes, or repeated review themes


What could improve?
Specific issue, affected user, and evidence rather than a guess


What cannot be confirmed online?
Hidden dimensions, material grade, strength, comfort, fit, or long-term durability



Treat reviews as clues, not facts. Look for repeated observations, separate shipping or seller issues from product-design issues, and verify what you can with direct measurement and testing.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
3. Write an improvement brief
Use this sentence frame:

Design an original [product] for [user and setting] that [solves the need]. It must [three measurable criteria] while respecting [material, machine, time, safety, and cost constraints].

Turn broad intentions into testable criteria.







Intention
Testable version




Faster
A user can identify, remove, and return the selected tool in 10 seconds or less.


Cheaper
The design fits within the assigned sheet area and uses no more than two purchased fastener types.


Better looking
Three users can identify the intended tool group and describe the visual hierarchy without prompting.


More ergonomic
The target tools can be removed with one hand without pinching neighbouring tools or twisting the wrist sharply.


More positive
User feedback includes a chosen feeling, such as calm or confidence, and identifies the feature that created it.


More serviceable
A damaged holder component can be replaced without discarding the backer or removing unrelated tools.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
4. Generate and select concepts

Measure the real tools, mounting area, stock, and critical hand clearances.
Sketch at least three meaningfully different concepts. Changing only decoration does not create a new concept.
Annotate the support method, retention method, mounting interface, assembly order, and expected load path.
Score each concept against the criteria using a decision matrix.
Explain the selected concept and one trade-off you accepted.

title: 3D Printing Slicing | Layer Height, Walls, Infill, Orientation & Supports
text:
Settings with consequences

Layer height: changes vertical detail, surface texture, time, and the number of layer interfaces.
Walls/perimeters: strongly affect shell strength and feature quality.
Infill: supports top surfaces and can change stiffness, mass, and time; more is not automatically better.
Top and bottom layers: close surfaces and distribute loads.
Orientation: changes overhangs, supports, surface finish, dimensional behaviour, and the direction of layer weakness.
Supports: make some overhangs possible but add material, time, cleanup, and surface evidence.

title: 3D Printing Slicing | Layer Height, Walls, Infill, Orientation & Supports
text:
Orientation comparison
Choose a bracket or hook and compare at least three orientations. For each, record support volume, estimated time, contact area, critical surface quality, likely load direction, and risk of failure. Select an orientation against the actual requirements rather than the most attractive preview.

Before printing

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
section: Choose the support by the force path
text:
Choose the support by the force path

Straight tabbed pair: locates two members in the front plane. It still needs a separate base that provides front-to-back depth.
Angled tabbed pair: spreads the feet sideways in the front view. It still needs a separate base or rear support for front-to-back stability.
Triangular side cheeks: can carry a plaque between two side panels, but this generator does not create the required joints.
Wide single easel back: generates a T-shaped support plus optional mating-slot geometry. A fixed slot connection is not the same as a hinge.
Narrow hinged rear strut: is one component of a picture-frame-style easel. It needs a front plaque, pivot hardware and a tether or stop.
Interlocking X-base: generates two half-slotted base bars only. The upright and plaque connection must be designed separately.

The purple coupon tests the chosen tab length and calculated slot width. Blue slot rectangles are mating geometry to position in the holder plate, not separate finished parts.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
text:
Before cutting

Measure the actual sheet thickness in several places.
Cut the fit coupon before the complete legs.
Open the SVG in Inkscape and confirm its physical dimensions at 100% scale.
Place matching slots in the holder plate and check that each slot has enough material around it.
Prototype in cardboard or scrap stock.
Assemble the real holder and test front-to-back and side-to-side tipping.

Use the Tool Organizer Gallery and design criteria to plan and test the complete build. Use the Fabrication Plate Builder for the holder plate and repeated holes.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
section: Which reference file do I use?
text:
Which reference file do I use?
The SVG, DXF, DWG, CDR, PDF and PNG in the reference folder are different formats of the same template set. Do not combine all six files.

Use SVG in Inkscape. This is the easiest editable version for the laser workflow.
Use DXF or DWG in CAD/CAM software when that program handles those formats better.
Use CDR only in CorelDRAW.
Use PDF or PNG to look at or print the design. They are reference views, not the preferred editable cut file.

The external sheet contains several easel concepts. Select one complete matching group of parts, move that group into a new document, confirm the scale, and resize every slot for the measured sheet thickness. The reference was drawn around 0.118-inch material, which is slightly thinner than nominal 1/8-inch material. Always test one joint first.

title: Portable Utility-Knife Organizer
text: ← All finished organizers

title: Portable Utility-Knife Organizer
text:
Read the finished organizer

  
    
    1
    2
    3
  
  Finished prototype. The numbered markers connect the physical features to the design decisions below. Open the shared project photo.



  1Visible and easy to useAll five handles face the user. Each can be seen, counted and gripped without moving a neighbouring knife. An empty position would be obvious.
  2Portable as one objectThe tool face, side supports and base form one self-contained organizer. It can be moved to another bench without installing a permanent wall system. A carry test should still confirm that the tools remain secure while it is moved.
  3Stands on its ownThe wide base and triangular side braces create a larger footprint than the upright tool face. That support geometry helps the organizer resist tipping when a knife is removed.

title: Portable Utility-Knife Organizer
text:
Why the spacing works
Ergonomic spacing is based on the real tool and the way a person reaches for it, not only on equal distances. Each handle remains visible, the grip areas do not overlap and the outside knives have clearance from the supports. The photograph is evidence that the layout was checked with the actual utility knives.
A future test should record whether different users can remove the centre and outside knives comfortably with one hand and whether the organizer remains stable when an outside knife is removed first.

title: Portable Utility-Knife Organizer
text:
A one-sided wall version

Keep one tool face; replace the freestanding base with a French-cleat interface
If the organizer only needed tools on one side, a later version could remove the second working face and the bench base. A solid backer on the remaining tool face could engage a continuous French cleat fixed to the wall. A lower spacer would keep the organizer parallel to the wall, and an anti-lift feature would prevent it from being knocked upward during use.
This is a design direction, not a tested claim. The cleat, backer, wall, fasteners, tool load and removal forces must be built and load-tested together. Mounting hardware must suit the actual wall and load.
Browse French-cleat starting points in the Laser-Cut Gallery

text:
I can explain how a design choice can include or exclude people.
I can decide whether an image is informative, functional, complex, or decorative.

Note

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
I can explain how a design choice can include or exclude people.
I can decide whether an image is informative, functional, complex, or decorative.
I can write alt text that communicates what the image contributes.







Note



This lesson applies the BBC guidance for visually and hearing impaired audiences and the current W3C image decision tree.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Why this is useful
People are not the problem. A design becomes disabling when it depends on one way of seeing, reading, hearing, or operating it. Accessible design gives the same idea more than one reliable path.
For images, that second path is often text. The description should carry the image’s purpose, not list every visible object.

title: Access & Alt Text
section: Decide what kind of image it is
text:
Decide what kind of image it is


Informative
The image adds a useful fact or relationship. Write a short description of what the learner needs to notice.


Complex
The image is a chart, diagram, or detailed process. Use brief alt text and explain the important data or relationships in nearby text.


Functional
The image is a button or link. Describe the action or destination, not the way the icon looks.


Decorative
The image adds no information. Use empty alt text so a screen reader can skip it.

title: Access & Alt Text
section: Use the guide’s Google Docs example
text:
Use the guide’s Google Docs example




Google Docs with an image selected and the Image options panel open to Alt Text. The animation shows the right-click method and the Ctrl plus Alt plus Y shortcut.




The original guide demonstrates two ways to open the Alt Text control in Google Docs: right-click the image and choose Alt text, or select it and press Ctrl + Alt + Y.

Alt text is not the visible caption. A caption helps everyone understand the figure. Alt text gives an equivalent purpose or meaning when the image is unavailable.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Write for purpose, not pixels


Too literal
“A screenshot with a white panel, a blue square, black text, menus, and a toolbar.”


Useful
“Google Docs Image options panel open to Alt Text for a selected image.”


The useful version identifies the tool, the control, and the reason the screenshot is present. It avoids details that do not help someone complete the task.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Try it
Choose one instructional image from a lesson or handout.

Write one sentence stating its purpose.
Name the relationship, result, or action the learner must notice.
Remove details that do not change the meaning.
If the image is complex, add a nearby explanation that carries the full information.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Check your work

The description makes sense without “image of” or “picture of.”
Text shown only inside the image is available in the alt text or nearby text.
A decorative image has empty alt text.
A linked image describes where the link goes or what it does.
A complex figure has more than a one-line description somewhere on the page.

title: Access & Alt Text
text:
Summary
First decide what job the image performs. Then write the shortest text that performs the same job. Continue to Fonts & Text Effects.
Sources: W3C Images Tutorial and Harvard Digital Accessibility: Write helpful image descriptions.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
I can compare fonts at the size people will actually see.
I can judge whether a background, outline, shadow, or 3D effect improves readability.
I can keep style without letting effects hide the letter shapes.







Note

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
I can compare fonts at the size people will actually see.
I can judge whether a background, outline, shadow, or 3D effect improves readability.
I can keep style without letting effects hide the letter shapes.







Note

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Why this is useful
Type can look clear while you are zoomed in and fail at the actual size. Letter shape, spacing, line thickness, background, and output method all affect readability.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Give text a reliable background




A presentation slide called Sew, Sew, Sew, Your Boat. The body text sits on a pale solid rectangle instead of directly on the changing background photograph.




The solid panel keeps the paragraph readable even when the photograph changes behind it. Example retained from the original guide.

Text placed directly on a photograph has many backgrounds at once. A solid or nearly solid panel is the most dependable fix. A shadow or outline may help a short title, but it should not be asked to rescue a paragraph.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
section: Compare effects by what they do to the letters
text:
Compare effects by what they do to the letters





Four text samples compare a thin stroke, a proper outline, an overly thick stroke, and an overly thick outline. Thick effects close spaces inside the letters.



Outline with restraint
A thin halo can separate text from a changing background. Thick effects fill counters and merge neighbouring letters. Source example.






The script word Hustle in white with a black outline and a large black drop shadow.



Shadow can separate
The outline and shadow add separation, but the script letter shapes still take longer to recognize. Style does not cancel the need to test.






The words Check it use blue 3D depth, dark outlines, highlights, curved internal strokes, and a shadow.



Effects can compete
Depth, highlights, outlines, and internal strokes all compete with the letters. Use this treatment for display only, not instructions or small labels. Source video.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Try it
Set the same short word in three fonts. Keep the size and colour identical.

View the words at 100%.
Step back or reduce the design to its final output size.
Compare the thinnest lines and the open spaces inside letters.
Add one effect at a time. Keep it only if recognition becomes faster.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Check your work

The type remains clear at the final size.
Important text does not depend on a photograph staying light or dark.
An outline does not close the spaces inside letters.
A shadow separates text without becoming a second word.
Decorative or 3D type is limited to short display text.

title: Fonts & Text Effects
text:
Summary
Choose the font by testing the real output, then add the least effect needed. Continue to Understanding Colour.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
I can describe colour using hue, saturation, and value.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
I can describe colour using hue, saturation, and value.
I can explain the difference between RGB screens and CMYK printing.
I can explain how opacity changes the result.







Note



The lesson uses the BBC guidance for visually and hearing impaired audiences as its accessibility reference and keeps only the diagrams needed to explain each decision.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Why this is useful
Colour is easier to control when you separate what kind of colour it is from how intense and how light it is. The same model helps with screens, print, paint, and accessibility checks.

title: Understanding Colour
section: How the eye receives colour information
text:
How the eye receives colour information




A simplified eye points to the retina and optic nerve, then labels long, medium, and short wavelength cones plus rods.



Four receptor types
The guide simplifies the retina into three kinds of cone cells for colour and rod cells that are especially useful in low light.






A graph plots the overlapping response ranges of short, medium, and long wavelength cones and rods from 400 to 700 nanometres.



Overlapping responses
The curves overlap. The brain interprets a pattern of signals rather than receiving a single red, green, or blue value. Source noted in the guide.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Separate hue, saturation, and value




Three vertical scales show hue changing through the spectrum, red losing saturation toward grey, and value changing from white to black.



Hue, saturation, value
Hue identifies the colour family. Saturation describes intensity or greyness. Value describes lightness or darkness. Source.






A colour wheel appears beside a greyscale copy. Yellow becomes very light while several blue, green, and purple hues become similar dark greys.



Different hue, similar value
Strongly different colours can have nearly the same lightness. This is why a monochrome check can reveal weak contrast. Source.

title: Understanding Colour
section: Connect the model to design software
text:
Connect the model to design software





A rainbow comparison labelled RGB on the left and CMYK on the right. The CMYK side is duller in several regions.



RGB screen, CMYK print
Screens mix emitted red, green, and blue light. Many printing systems use cyan, magenta, yellow, and black inks. A bright screen colour may reproduce with less intensity in print.






Two white rectangles cover a pink flower photograph. The high-opacity rectangle hides the flower and the low-opacity rectangle allows it to show through.



Opacity controls what shows through
High opacity blocks more of the layer below. Low opacity allows more of it to affect the result. Source noted in the guide.





Go deeper: the Munsell colour solid





A three-dimensional Munsell colour solid places value on a vertical black-to-white axis, hue around the axis, and chroma moving outward.




The Munsell system organizes colour in three dimensions: value moves vertically, hue moves around the centre, and chroma moves outward. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Try it
Choose one hue in your design tool.

Make a vivid and a muted version by changing saturation.
Make a light and a dark version by changing value.
Convert the set to greyscale.
Record which differences remain visible without hue.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Check your work

You can name whether you changed hue, saturation, value, or opacity.
Important colours still separate in greyscale.
You previewed a screen design on the target screen or a print design in print.
Opacity does not create an unpredictable background for text.

title: Understanding Colour
text:
Summary
Hue tells you the colour family, saturation tells you its intensity, and value tells you its lightness. Value is the most direct bridge to readable contrast. Continue to Contrast, Emphasis & Output.

text: Follow the sections in order. Use the sidebar for lessons, references, labs, projects, and optional enhancements.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:

0. Orientation, Safety, and Design
1. Numbers, Units, and Calculator Skills

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
0. Orientation, Safety, and Design







What students learn
Why it matters




Work safely, follow a design process, and document decisions and sources.
Safe, documented work is the foundation for every build, investigation, and engineering decision.



Subsections: Safety; design process; documentation; privacy and attribution
Coming out of this section, students can: Work safely, document decisions, cite sources, and keep a usable design record.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
1. Numbers, Units, and Calculator Skills







What students learn
Why it matters




Use number systems, units, engineering notation, estimates, and a scientific calculator.
Units, scale, estimation, and calculator fluency make technical results understandable and trustworthy.



Subsections: Number systems; units; significant figures; engineering notation; calculator workflow
Coming out of this section, students can: Convert technical quantities, use engineering notation, estimate results, and present calculations clearly.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
2. Electrical Fundamentals







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain and calculate charge, voltage, current, resistance, sources, and loads.
These quantities explain how sources, conductors, and loads behave in a complete circuit.



Subsections: Charge; voltage; current; resistance; sources and loads; AC and DC
Coming out of this section, students can: Explain and calculate charge, voltage, current, resistance, opens, shorts, and source behaviour.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
3. DC Circuit Analysis







What students learn
Why it matters




Analyze direct-current networks, solve their equations, and connect electrical energy to useful work.
Circuit analysis predicts electrical behaviour; an energy-conversion lab shows what that behaviour accomplishes in a real device.



Subsections: Ohm's law; series circuits; parallel circuits; mixed networks; Kirchhoff's laws; linear systems; work, energy, power, and efficiency; dividers; troubleshooting
Coming out of this section, students can: Solve and verify series, parallel, and mixed networks, use linear equations, and compare electrical energy with mechanical work.
Collaboration: The Engineering Preparation Track collaboration map connects this work with TEJ3M/TEJ4M, SPH3U physics, SCH4U chemistry, and SBI4U biology.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
4. Building, Schematics, and Measurement







What students learn
Why it matters




Build readable circuits and compare calculated, simulated, and measured results.
Readable schematics, careful construction, and correct measurement make troubleshooting possible.



Subsections: Breadboards; schematics; simulation; multimeter use; measurement uncertainty
Coming out of this section, students can: Build from a schematic, measure safely, compare predicted and measured values, and locate wiring errors.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
5. Components and Applied Circuits







What students learn
Why it matters




Select and apply common components in useful low-voltage circuits.
Component knowledge lets students select, connect, protect, and test useful electronic circuits.



Subsections: Sensors; batteries; capacitors; diodes; transistors; timers; motors and relays
Coming out of this section, students can: Design and test sensor, timing, switching, power-supply, and actuator-interface circuits.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
6. Digital Logic and Inputs







What students learn
Why it matters




Create stable digital inputs and analyze combinational and sequential logic.
Stable inputs and Boolean logic connect physical switches and sensors to dependable digital decisions.



Subsections: Logic levels; pull-ups and pull-downs; debouncing; logic gates; truth tables; state
Coming out of this section, students can: Build stable switch inputs, complete truth tables, analyze logic, and create a small digital system.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
7. Fabrication and PCBs







What students learn
Why it matters




Turn a tested prototype into a durable fabricated or manufactured result.
Fabrication turns a tested design into a durable, repeatable physical product.



Subsections: Soldering; connectors; PCB design; manufacturing files; enclosures and fabrication
Coming out of this section, students can: Prepare a manufacturable design and produce a soldered, printed, laser-cut, or machined result.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
8. Computer Systems







What students learn
Why it matters




Assemble, commission, maintain, upgrade, and troubleshoot computer hardware.
Computer hardware work connects electrical principles to real systems, maintenance, repair, and reuse.



Subsections: Components; power; assembly; startup; Linux installation; upgrades and troubleshooting
Coming out of this section, students can: Identify, assemble, commission, benchmark, troubleshoot, upgrade, and document a computer.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
section: 9. Linux, Operating Systems and Basic Networking
text:
9. Linux, Operating Systems and Basic Networking







What students learn
Why it matters




Use and administer a Linux system safely from the desktop and command line.
Operating-system knowledge gives students control over files, software, permissions, and system behaviour.



Subsections: Desktop use; files and permissions; command line; software; basic networking; services; backup and recovery
Coming out of this section, students can: Install and use Linux, manage files and permissions, run commands, check basic network settings and connectivity, and complete basic administration.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
10. Programming







What students learn
Why it matters




Write, test, debug, and document programs for calculations, data, and control.
Programming turns a process or calculation into a repeatable tool that can handle inputs and errors.



Subsections: Algorithms; variables; conditions; loops; functions; files; testing and debugging
Coming out of this section, students can: Write, test, debug, and document programs that calculate, model, process data, or control a task.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
11. Microcontrollers







What students learn
Why it matters




Connect code to protected sensors, inputs, outputs, communication, and actuators.
Physical computing joins code, sensors, outputs, timing, and electrical protection in one system.



Subsections: Inputs and outputs; sensors; timing; communication; actuators; state machines; data logging
Coming out of this section, students can: Create a protected sensor-and-actuator system using a microcontroller or single-board computer.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
12. Networking and Administration







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain networks and operate small classroom services using defensive practices.
Networking explains how devices communicate and how small services are operated safely.



Subsections: Addresses; protocols; diagnostics; secure remote access; services; users and backups
Coming out of this section, students can: Configure and diagnose a small network or classroom service using defensive administration practices.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
13. Data Science and Machine Learning







What students learn
Why it matters




Prepare, visualize, model, and evaluate non-personal data responsibly.
Data science helps students turn measurements into evidence while recognizing uncertainty and bias.



Subsections: Data preparation; visualization; regression; classification; model evaluation; responsible use
Coming out of this section, students can: Clean, visualize, model, and evaluate a non-personal dataset and explain the limits of the result.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
14. Language Models and Applied AI







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain, use, ground, and evaluate small language-model applications responsibly.
Understanding language models helps students use, test, and evaluate artificial intelligence responsibly.



Subsections: Tokens; prediction; small models; prompting; grounding; evaluation; responsible use
Coming out of this section, students can: Build or evaluate a small grounded artificial-intelligence application with documented tests and limits.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
15. Culminating Projects







What students learn
Why it matters




Plan, build or simulate, test, revise, and explain an integrated technology project.
A culminating project combines design, construction, programming, testing, revision, and communication.



Subsections: Requirements; design; build or simulation; testing; revision; technical communication
Coming out of this section, students can: Deliver a working or simulated technology project supported by evidence, revision, and a technical explanation.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
16. Control Systems and CNC







What students learn
Why it matters




Model or build systems that use sensing, decisions, feedback, and safe states.
Control systems show how sensing, decisions, and feedback produce safe, useful machine behaviour.



Subsections: Open and closed loop control; hysteresis; proportional control; PID; interlocks; motion and CNC
Coming out of this section, students can: Model or build a feedback-controlled system with safe states, interlocks, and measured response.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
You will apply Kirchhoff’s current law at a node and Kirchhoff’s voltage law around a loop. These laws let you write equations for a circuit that cannot be reduced by inspection.
Used in college or university: Nodal analysis, mesh analysis, electronics, power systems, and control hardware. [1, Ch. 9]
Where you see it: In a car wiring harness, current splits between lights and control modules. In a robot, it splits between the controller, sensors, and motors.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Class materials

Teaching slides
Assignment: From Two Loops to a Matrix
Printable two-loop-to-matrix guide
Make a copy of the current student problem set
TEJ Electronics Quick Reference
Make a copy of the General Schematic and GUESS handout

ElectroBOOM101-008: Lumped Model, Kirchhoff Circuit Laws
Teacher answers: restricted







TipMonday: theory, discussion, and a live Jupyter demonstration



Watch ElectroBOOM101-008 together as the unit capstone rather than restarting the completed assignment. While watching, record one statement about the lumped-circuit model, one KCL statement, and one KVL statement. The teacher will then use the completed Question 4 equations to introduce standard form, the matrix equation \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\), numpy.linalg.solve, negative-current interpretation, and residual verification. Predict each result before the live code runs. Monday is for explanation, prediction, and questions; the independent lab is Tuesday.



Tuesday: derive two loops, build the matrix, and solve two ways
Open the complete student assignment and submission instructions, use the printable two-loop guide, and download Notebook 3A. Use the completed Question 4 circuit and its released answer. This is not another KCL/KVL worksheet. It teaches the missing bridge from loop traversal to standard form and a matrix.

Define \(I_1\), \(I_2\), and the shared current \(I_3=I_1-I_2\).
Walk around Loop 1 and explain every KVL sign before rearranging Equation 1.
Walk around Loop 2 and explain why the shared-resistor sign changes before rearranging Equation 2.
State the variable order and units, build \(A\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), and read both matrix rows back as equations.
Solve numerically with numpy.linalg.solve and report the residual vector.
Solve symbolically with sympy.solve, preserve the exact fractions, and calculate \(I_3\).
Compare the original, released, numerical, and symbolic results, then complete the reflection.

Tuesday submission: one completed .ipynb file containing both full loop derivations, the matrix, NumPy results and residuals, SymPy exact results, the comparison table, and the assigned reflection. No physical lab or new circuit topology is required while the regular teacher is absent.






NoteLater debugging lessons



Do not compress the debugging ladder into Tuesday. Notebook 3 later uses a keyword error, a non-square numpy.linalg.solve input, and a silent factor-of-1000 unit bug. The parameter sweep is also later. Tomorrow is only the two-loop derivation, matrix, numerical solution, symbolic solution, and verification.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Kirchhoff’s current law



Figure 1. At a square junction node, total current entering equals total current leaving. #


\[
\sum I_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum I_{\mathrm{out}}
\tag{1}\]
A negative answer means the real current is opposite the arrow you selected.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Kirchhoff’s voltage law



Figure 2. Two loops share one resistor and create two simultaneous equations. #


\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\Delta V_k = 0
\tag{2}\]
Choose one loop direction and keep the signs consistent. A source rise is positive; a resistor drop in the current direction is negative.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Workflow

Mark the essential nodes and independent loops.
Choose and label unknown current directions.
Write current-law and voltage-law equations.
Replace resistor voltage with \(V=IR\).
Solve without rounding, then check every original node and loop equation.
Build the same network in Tinkercad and compare the simulated values.

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
text:
Worked solutions






NoteQuestion 2: Missing loop voltage





Kirchhoff’s voltage law requires the source rise to equal the voltage drops:
\[
V_3=12.0\,\mathrm{V}-2.4\,\mathrm{V}-4.1\,\mathrm{V}=5.5\,\mathrm{V}.
\tag{3}\]
Check: \(12.0-2.4-4.1-5.5=0.0\,\mathrm{V}\).









NoteQuestion 4: Two loops with two sources





The two loop equations are
\[
5I_1-2I_2=10
\tag{4}\]
\[
-2I_1+7I_2=6.
\tag{5}\]
Solving them gives \(I_1=2.645161\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}\) and \(I_2=1.612903\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}\).
The shared-branch current is
\[
I_3=I_1-I_2=1.032258\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}.
\tag{6}\]
Final answers: \(I_1=2.65\,\mathrm{mA}\), \(I_2=1.61\,\mathrm{mA}\), and \(I_3=1.03\,\mathrm{mA}\).

title: Kirchhoff’s Laws
section: Practical pathway: test the node and loops
text:
Practical pathway: test the node and loops
Core learning: derive the node and loop equations by hand before using a simulator or solver. Follow Define Variables → Write Equations → Standard Form or Matrix → Solve → Verify.
Guided practice: if Tinkercad can represent the same sources and passive components faithfully, build the two-loop network with the Tinkercad tutorial. Otherwise, use the teacher-approved physical circuit or simulator and identify the substitution. Measure the currents needed for one KCL check and voltages needed for one KVL check.



Check
Predicted total
Simulated or measured total
Residual




Current entering minus leaving (mA)
0




Left-loop voltage sum (V)
0




Right-loop voltage sum (V)
0





Independent challenge: deliberately reverse one current arrow without changing the circuit. Rewrite the affected signs, solve again, and explain why a negative result is meaningful rather than automatically wrong.






TipProgressive hints






Keep one chosen loop direction from start to finish.
Compare every matrix row with its original KCL or KVL equation.
A residual near zero checks the entered equations; compare signs and units with the schematic to check the model.




Use Notebook 3 only after deriving the equations. Record the coefficient order and verify by substitution.
Reflection: What did the residual establish, and what mistake could still produce a near-zero residual?

title: Parallel Circuits
text:
You will identify parallel branches and calculate equivalent resistance, source current, branch current, and power. This explains how several loads can operate independently from one source.
Used in college or university: Circuit analysis, electrical distribution, instrumentation, and electronics.
Where you see it: A car connects lights and control modules in parallel so each receives battery voltage. A robot does the same when several sensors share one supply.

title: Parallel Circuits
text:
General parallel rules
The source current is the sum of the branch currents:
\[
I_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} I_k
\tag{2}\]
The equivalent resistance is
\[
\frac{1}{R_T} = \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{R_k}
\tag{3}\]
For exactly two parallel resistors, the product-over-sum shortcut is
\[
R_T = \frac{R_aR_b}{R_a+R_b}
\tag{4}\]
Calculate any branch current with Ohm’s law:
\[
I_k = \frac{V_T}{R_k}
\tag{5}\]
Total power equals the sum of the branch powers:
\[
P_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n}P_k = V_T I_T
\tag{6}\]

How sigma notation works
\[
I_T=\sum_{k=1}^{n}I_k=I_1+I_2+\cdots+I_n
\tag{7}\]
\[
\frac{1}{R_T}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{R_k}
=\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{R_n}
\tag{8}\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(R_T\) or \(R_{eq}\)
total or equivalent resistance


\(R_k\) or \(I_k\)
the value at position \(k\)


\(k\)
the index variable; it changes through \(1,2,3,\ldots,n\)


\(n\)
the fixed last index; the sum stops here



\(\Sigma\) means add each term while \(k\) runs from \(1\) to \(n\). The final expanded term uses \(n\).

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n} I_k \overset{?}{=} I_T
\tag{9}\]
Equation Equation 9 checks the branch currents. The equivalent resistance from Equation Equation 3 must be smaller than the smallest branch resistance.

title: Series-Parallel Combination Circuits, Part A
text:
Assignment 1.4
You will identify series and parallel groups, reduce a mixed circuit one group at a time, calculate the total values, and then work back to each resistor. This is useful when one protected power source feeds several loads in a robot, vehicle, computer, or sensor system.
Used in college or university: circuit laboratories, electronics, robotics, instrumentation, and preparation for Kirchhoff’s laws. The same circuit pattern lets cars and robots power several loads from one protected source.
Where you see it: A car uses a fuse and switch to feed parallel lamps or control modules. A robot uses one protected supply for sensors, indicators, and control boards.

title: Series-Parallel Combination Circuits, Part A
text:
Start with a real system
A robot may have a fuse, switch, and current-limiting resistor in series with several parallel loads. A vehicle uses the same pattern when one protected supply feeds lamps, sensors, or control modules. The series parts affect every load; each parallel branch still receives the same branch voltage.
For an engaging introduction, watch ElectroBOOM101-005, then use The Organic Chemistry Tutor’s series and parallel explanation or Khan Academy’s resistor-network review for the calculation steps.

title: Series-Parallel Combination Circuits, Part A
text:
Identify the connections
Components are in series when the same current must pass through them. Components are in parallel when both ends connect to the same two nodes. Trace nodes and current paths; do not decide from visual appearance alone.



Figure 1. Series has one current path; parallel has branches connected to the same two nodes. #

title: Series-Parallel Combination Circuits, Part A
text:
Rules and equations
For a series group, current is common, voltage drops add, and resistance adds:
\[
I_T=I_1=I_2=\cdots
\tag{1}\]
\[
V_T=\sum_{k=1}^{n}V_k
\tag{2}\]
\[
R_{\mathrm{series}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}R_k
\tag{3}\]
For a parallel group, voltage is common, branch currents add, and reciprocal resistance adds:
\[
V_T=V_1=V_2=\cdots
\tag{4}\]
\[
I_T=\sum_{k=1}^{n}I_k
\tag{5}\]
\[
\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{parallel}}}
=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{R_k}
\tag{6}\]
For exactly two parallel resistors:
\[
R_{\mathrm{parallel}}=\frac{R_aR_b}{R_a+R_b}
\tag{7}\]
For any resistor, use Ohm’s law and power:
\[
V_k=I_kR_k
\tag{8}\]
\[
P_k=V_kI_k=I_k^2R_k=\frac{V_k^2}{R_k}
\tag{9}\]

How sigma notation works
\[
R_T=R_{eq}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}R_k=R_1+R_2+\cdots+R_n
\tag{10}\]
\[
V_T=\sum_{k=1}^{n}V_k=V_1+V_2+\cdots+V_n
\tag{11}\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(R_T\) or \(R_{eq}\)
total or equivalent resistance


\(R_k\) or \(V_k\)
the value at position \(k\)


\(k\)
the index variable; it changes through \(1,2,3,\ldots,n\)


\(n\)
the fixed last index; the sum stops here



\(\Sigma\) means add each term while \(k\) runs from \(1\) to \(n\). The final expanded term is \(R_n\) or \(V_n\).

title: Series-Parallel Combination Circuits, Part A
text:
Reduce, solve, expand, and check

Mark one true series or parallel group.
Replace it with an equivalent resistance and redraw the whole circuit.
Repeat until only total resistance remains.
Solve the equivalent circuit with \(I_T=V_T/R_T\).
Work backward. Use common current for series parts and common voltage for parallel branches.
Check that branch currents add, voltage drops add around a path, and component powers add to total power.




Figure 2. The common mixed-network pattern used in Questions 1, 2, and 4. #

title: Series-Parallel Combination Circuits, Part A
text:
Question 1 worked example
A \(12.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series with \(R_2=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in parallel. This is the complete model for the questions that follow.
Given
\[
V_T=12.0\,\mathrm{V},\qquad
R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega},\qquad
R_2=R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
\tag{12}\]
Unknowns
\[
R_{23},\ R_T,\ I_T,\ V_1,\ V_{23},\ I_2,\ I_3,\ P_T
\tag{13}\]
General equations
\[
R_{\mathrm{parallel}}=\frac{R_aR_b}{R_a+R_b},\qquad
R_{\mathrm{series}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}R_k,\qquad
I=\frac{V}{R}
\tag{14}\]
\[
V=IR,\qquad
P=VI
\tag{15}\]
Circuit-specific equations
\[
R_{23}=\frac{R_2R_3}{R_2+R_3},\qquad
R_T=R_1+R_{23},\qquad
I_T=\frac{V_T}{R_T}
\tag{16}\]
\[
V_1=I_TR_1,\qquad
V_{23}=V_T-V_1,\qquad
I_2=\frac{V_{23}}{R_2},\qquad
I_3=\frac{V_{23}}{R_3}
\tag{17}\]

Step 1: Equivalent resistance
\[
R_{23}=\frac{(2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega})(2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega})}
{2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}+2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}
=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
\tag{18}\]
\[
R_T=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}+1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
\tag{19}\]


Step 2: Total current and section voltages
\[
I_T=\frac{12.0\,\mathrm{V}}{2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}
=6.0\,\mathrm{mA}
\tag{20}\]
\[
V_1=(6.0\,\mathrm{mA})(1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega})=6.0\,\mathrm{V}
\tag{21}\]
\[
V_{23}=12.0\,\mathrm{V}-6.0\,\mathrm{V}=6.0\,\mathrm{V}
\tag{22}\]


Step 3: Branch currents and power
\[
I_2=I_3=\frac{6.0\,\mathrm{V}}{2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}
=3.0\,\mathrm{mA}
\tag{23}\]
\[
P_T=V_TI_T=(12.0\,\mathrm{V})(6.0\,\mathrm{mA})
=72\,\mathrm{mW}
\tag{24}\]
Calculator entries
(2 EXP 3 × 2 EXP 3) ÷ (2 EXP 3 + 2 EXP 3)
12 ÷ (2 EXP 3)
6 ÷ (2 EXP 3)


Step 4: Check
\[
I_2+I_3=3.0\,\mathrm{mA}+3.0\,\mathrm{mA}=6.0\,\mathrm{mA}=I_T
\tag{25}\]
\[
V_1+V_{23}=6.0\,\mathrm{V}+6.0\,\mathrm{V}=12.0\,\mathrm{V}=V_T
\tag{26}\]


Final answers

\(I_3\)
\(P_T\)

title: Series-Parallel Combination Circuits, Part A
text:
Student questions
Use the student handout for the fillable GUESS tables and work space.

Question 1: worked model
Review the complete Question 1 solution, then use the same sequence for the remaining questions.


Question 2: unequal parallel branches
An \(18.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_1=3.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series with \(R_2=6.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_3=3.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in parallel. Find \(R_{23}\), \(R_T\), \(I_T\), \(V_1\), \(V_{23}\), \(I_2\), \(I_3\), and \(P_T\). Check current and voltage.


Question 3: two series branches in parallel
A \(24.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source is connected across two branches. Branch A has \(R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_2=3.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series. Branch B has \(R_3=2.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_4=4.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series. Find the branch resistances and currents, every resistor voltage, total current, equivalent resistance, and total power.



Figure 3. Question 3 has two series branches connected in parallel. #




Question 4: find an unknown branch resistor
A \(20.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_1=1.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) in series with a parallel group. One branch is \(R_2=2.4\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and the other is an unknown \(R_3\). The source current is \(10.0\,\mathrm{mA}\). Find \(V_1\), \(V_{23}\), \(I_2\), \(I_3\), \(R_3\), and \(R_T\).


Question 5: current-limit design
A \(12.0\,\mathrm{V}\) source supplies \(R_S\), \(R_1=330\,\mathrm{\Omega}\), and a parallel load made from \(R_2=680\,\mathrm{\Omega}\) and \(R_3=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\). Find the minimum \(R_S\) that keeps source current at or below \(15.0\,\mathrm{mA}\). Select the next safe standard 5% value, then calculate current, load voltage, branch currents, resistor powers, and suitable power ratings.



Figure 4. Question 5 turns the analysis process into a current-limit design. #

title: Computational Engineering
text:
Use this pathway after the normal electronics teaching and problem set. The notebooks support the circuit model; they do not replace deriving equations, building safely, or measuring a real system.






NoteCurrent class position



Basic schematics and the five KCL/KVL questions are complete. Before circuit linear algebra, students begin with a zero-experience Python notebook, then learn NumPy, plotting, documentation lookup, and evidence-based help requests. The bridge is run one line → variables and types → lists → one small array → NumPy investigation → Kirchhoff equations → matrix model. Capacitors and RC response follow this bridge.








ImportantBrowser start: open JupyterLite



JupyterLite is the browser program that runs the downloaded notebook. Click OPEN JUPYTERLITE NOW, use Upload Files, and double-click the downloaded .ipynb file. Use the step-by-step JupyterLite instructions if this is your first notebook.



Read the step-by-step JupyterLite instructions: download a notebook, open JupyterLite, upload the file, run a cell, and preserve the finished work.
Play and mod Circuit Quest: add a team name, change a colour, rotate circuit tiles, and power two branches.
Complete Python First Steps: print one line, use calculator operations, store variables, recognize types, select list items, and use one small NumPy array.
Run Python and Jupyter on your own computer: use a virtual environment in WSL, native Windows, macOS, or Linux instead of depending on JupyterLite.
Complete Python and NumPy Foundations: practise loops, functions, arrays, filters, checks, plotting, and one documentation-driven repair.
Find documentation and ask for programming help: reproduce an issue, search Python, NumPy, pandas, and Stack Overflow, and write a complete technical help request.
Complete the two-loops-to-matrix assignment: derive each loop equation step by step, build the matrix, and compare NumPy with an exact SymPy solution.
Work through the Jupyter Electronics Lab: apply the skills across KCL/KVL, graphs, data, investigation, RC, op-amps, and the calculus bridge.
Complete the Life Checkpoint Upgrade: digitize and correct the checkpoint, solve it with NumPy, and verify the same circuit in Tinkercad.
Continue to Python measurement logging and analysis and curve fitting when the investigation needs repeated measurements or a fitted model.







ImportantCurrent assignment



Begin with Circuit Quest: change the team name and one colour, then finish three levels. Next, use the Life Checkpoint Upgrade: Jupyter + Tinkercad notebook on Monday and Tuesday. The Tinkercad build is the Life Checkpoint two-loop circuit, not the game board. Submit the notebook, Tinkercad URL, screenshot, and any missing course work through the assigned Classroom posts.








NoteCore workflow



Understand → Calculate → Build → Simulate → Measure → Verify → Investigate → Document → Share
Most introductory notebook activities take about 15–30 minutes after the electronics calculation is complete. The Jupyter Electronics Lab also defines multi-day investigations that can carry the electronics course while students wait for components, instruments, or soldered kits.


The browser route does not require a local installation or a new account, but the school browser must allow JupyterLite and WebAssembly. Download work before leaving the browser.
Hardware remains valuable, but it is not assumed to be simultaneously available to every student. A simulation-first submission is complete when it meets the stated modelling outcomes and labels its evidence honestly. Measurements can be added later as a separate validation stage.

3. If you see a red message
Stop and read the last line.

SyntaxError often means a quotation mark or bracket is missing.

title: Run Python and Jupyter on Your Own Computer
text:
Route A: Windows with WSL
WSL is the Windows Subsystem for Linux. It provides a Linux command line and filesystem while Windows continues to supply the desktop and browser.

A1. Check or install WSL
Open PowerShell and check the installed distributions:
wsl --status
wsl --list --verbose
If WSL is not installed and this is your own computer, follow the official Microsoft WSL installation guide. The normal installation command is run from an administrator PowerShell window:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
Restart if requested. Launch Ubuntu, wait for its first-time setup, and create the Linux username and password when prompted. This Linux password is separate from the Windows sign-in and is used when an authorized system change requires sudo.


A2. Install Python support in Ubuntu
In the Ubuntu terminal, check Python first:
python3 --version
python3 -m venv --help
If venv or pip is unavailable, install the Ubuntu packages on a computer where you have permission:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip
Do not use sudo pip install. System packages belong to Ubuntu; course packages belong inside the virtual environment created below.


A3. Put the course folder in the Linux filesystem
Keep a Linux-run project under /home, not permanently under /mnt/c, for better performance and fewer cross-filesystem permission problems.
From Ubuntu, open your Linux home folder in Windows File Explorer:
cd ~
explorer.exe .
Extract the course ZIP and copy the tej-computational-engineering folder into that window. The result should contain:
~/tej-computational-engineering/
├── data/
├── notebooks/
├── README.txt
└── requirements-jupyter.txt
Windows can also reach the same location through a path such as:
\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\your-linux-username\tej-computational-engineering


A4. Create and activate the virtual environment
In Ubuntu:
cd ~/tej-computational-engineering
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements-jupyter.txt
The prompt normally begins with (.venv) after activation. Verify that Python and pip come from the project:
which python
python -m pip --version
Both paths should point inside ~/tej-computational-engineering/.venv.


A5. Start Jupyter in WSL and use the Windows browser
Keep the Ubuntu terminal open and run:
python -m jupyter lab --no-browser
Jupyter prints one or more local URLs. Copy the complete URL containing the token, for example:
http://localhost:8888/lab?token=...
Paste that URL into Chrome, Edge, or Firefox in Windows. WSL normally forwards Linux services to localhost on Windows, so the Windows browser can display the Jupyter server running inside Ubuntu. Do not share the token or bind the class server to a public network address.
Open notebooks/03a-two-loop-to-matrix-bridge.ipynb, confirm that the selected kernel belongs to .venv, and run the working cells before completing the student scaffold.
To stop Jupyter, return to Ubuntu and press Ctrl+C. Confirm shutdown if asked. Then leave the environment with:
deactivate


A6. Start it again later
cd ~/tej-computational-engineering
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m jupyter lab --no-browser
If the Windows browser cannot connect, keep the Ubuntu terminal running and try these checks before changing firewall or network settings:
python -m jupyter server list

Copy the exact current URL instead of reusing an old token.
Try the printed 127.0.0.1 URL if the printed localhost URL does not open, or the reverse.
Confirm that Jupyter is still running and did not exit with an error.
Confirm that the URL is opened on the same Windows computer running WSL.
Ask before changing firewall, WSL networking, or server binding settings.

Microsoft documents that Windows applications can normally reach a service running in WSL through localhost.

B2. Create the environment

source .venv/bin/activate

title: Run Python and Jupyter on Your Own Computer
text:
Route D: native Windows PowerShell
Use this route if WSL is unavailable and a normal per-user Python installation is permitted. It works, but it is not the recommended course route because Windows paths, activation, and command-line behaviour differ from the WSL and Linux instructions used elsewhere in the course.
py --version
Set-Location "$HOME\tej-computational-engineering"
py -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --upgrade pip
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements-jupyter.txt
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m jupyter lab
Using the direct .venv interpreter works even when PowerShell activation scripts are blocked. Do not weaken the computer-wide execution policy for this course.

title: Run Python and Jupyter on Your Own Computer
text:
Route E: Google Colab
Open Google Colab when you cannot install Python or Jupyter locally.

Sign in with an approved Google account.
Choose File > Upload notebook and upload the required .ipynb file from the complete notebook bundle.
Upload any required CSV or other data file into the Colab session.
Run the notebook from the top and download the finished .ipynb before ending the session.

Colab is convenient because there is no local setup, but the code runs in a temporary cloud virtual machine. The runtime can disconnect or be replaced, local files are not automatically available, and free resources are neither guaranteed nor unlimited. For these small course notebooks, startup, uploads, Google Drive access, and network delay can make Colab feel slower than a prepared local environment. It also gives you less control over Python versions, installed packages, USB devices, serial ports, and measurement hardware. Use local Jupyter for repeatable engineering work whenever possible. See the official Google Colab FAQ for current runtime and resource limitations.

text:

title: Build a Technical Portfolio
text:
1. Tell the engineering story
Use these headings in this order:

The problem: What need, fault, or question were you addressing? What would success look like?
Initial design or prediction: Show the first idea and predict an outcome before testing.
Calculations: Include units, significant figures, equations, assumptions, and an independent check.
Circuit schematic or system diagram: Use the course drawing conventions and useful alt text.
Simulation or experimental evidence: Include a labelled table, graph, photograph, or measurement record.
Python analysis: Link or summarize the notebook when computation adds value. Do not add code only for decoration.
Mistakes and revisions: Explain one meaningful stumbling block, the evidence that exposed it, and what changed.
Final conclusion: State whether the evidence meets the original success criteria and identify limitations.
What I learned: Explain the transferable skill and how you got unstuck.

The starter uses Quarto’s native grid listing, category filters, text filter, sorting, responsive layout, and site search. It does not require an external data service or custom JavaScript after publishing.

The problem
Another student can see the final result but cannot tell why your design changed or whether the evidence supports your conclusion.
The essential skill: connect every claim to a calculation, test, observation, source, or limitation.
The challenge: add one complete project, one new category, and one revision that materially changed the outcome. Then change the listing order using a documented Quarto option.
The stumbling block: a broken image or link may work in the editor but fail in the rendered site because its relative path starts from the wrong source file.
The investigation: use the official Quarto websites, listings, and navigation documentation. Search the exact option name and read the YAML example.






TipHint 1: concept clue

TipHint 3: technical clue





For an image stored at assets/example.svg, a page in projects/ uses ../assets/example.svg. The project list can use sort: "date desc" and sort-ui: [date, title].

title: Capacitors 1: Capacitors from Zero
text: This is the first lesson in the capacitor sequence. Start here even if the hardware is not available.

title: Capacitors 1: Capacitors from Zero
text:
What you will learn

A capacitor has two conductors separated by an insulating dielectric.
Capacitance is measured in farads.
Many capacitors use microfarads, nanofarads, or picofarads.
A polarized capacitor must be connected the correct way.
The voltage rating must be greater than the circuit voltage.

title: Capacitors 1: Capacitors from Zero
text:
Look inside a capacitor



Figure 1. Charge does not pass straight through the dielectric. The separated charge creates an electric field.

title: Capacitors 1: Capacitors from Zero
text:
Symbols and polarity



Figure 2. Check polarity before connecting an electrolytic capacitor.

title: Capacitors 1: Capacitors from Zero
text:
Units
\[
1\,\mathrm{F}=10^6\,\mu\mathrm{F},\qquad
1\,\mu\mathrm{F}=10^3\,\mathrm{nF},\qquad
1\,\mathrm{nF}=10^3\,\mathrm{pF}
\]
Example:
\[
220\,\mathrm{nF}\left(\frac{1\,\mu\mathrm{F}}{1000\,\mathrm{nF}}\right)=0.220\,\mu\mathrm{F}
\]
The unit you do not want cancels.

title: Capacitors 1: Capacitors from Zero
section: Read the part before connecting it
text:
Read the part before connecting it



Figure 3. Check capacitance, voltage rating, polarity, and physical fit.

title: Capacitors 1: Capacitors from Zero
text:
Charge and energy
The charge stored by an ideal capacitor is:
\[
Q=CV
\]
The stored energy is:
\[
E=\frac{1}{2}CV^2
\]
Use farads for \(C\), volts for \(V\), coulombs for \(Q\), and joules for \(E\).






WarningSafe handling



Disconnect power, discharge through a suitable resistor, and verify the voltage before handling a capacitor. Do not short a charged capacitor with a screwdriver.

title: Capacitors 1: Capacitors from Zero
text:
Worked example using GUESS
A \(68\,\mu\mathrm{F}\) capacitor is charged to \(9.0\,\mathrm{V}\). Find the stored charge.
Given
\[C=68\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F},\qquad V=9.0\,\mathrm{V}\]
Unknown
\[Q=?\]
Equation
\[Q=CV\]
Substitute and solve
\[
Q=(68\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F})(9.0\,\mathrm{V})
=612\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}
\]
Statement
The capacitor stores \(612\,\mu\mathrm{C}\) of charge.

The XL741 pathway is an optional extension after capacitors, diodes, and transistor fundamentals. title: Capacitors 2: RC Charging and Discharging
text: This lesson uses a resistor to control how quickly a capacitor charges or discharges.

title: Capacitors 2: RC Charging and Discharging
text:
Charging



Figure 1. When the switch closes, current flows through the resistor and charge builds on the capacitor.


At the instant the switch closes for an ideal uncharged capacitor:
\[
v_C(0)=0\,\mathrm{V},\qquad i(0)=\frac{V_S}{R}
\]
The current is largest at the start. As the capacitor voltage rises, the resistor voltage and current fall.
After a long time:
\[
v_C(\infty)=V_S,\qquad i(\infty)=0\,\mathrm{A}
\]
The charged capacitor behaves like an open circuit for steady DC in this ideal model.

title: Capacitors 2: RC Charging and Discharging
text:
Discharging



Figure 2. The source is removed. Stored energy leaves the capacitor through the resistor.


The capacitor voltage cannot jump instantly in the ideal model. It falls from its starting value toward \(0\,\mathrm{V}\).

title: Capacitors 2: RC Charging and Discharging
text:
Read the graph



Figure 3. At one time constant, charging is about 63.2% complete and discharging has about 36.8% remaining. At five time constants, use the practical final value.


For charging toward a source voltage \(V_S\):
\[
v_C(\tau)\approx0.632V_S,\qquad v_C(5\tau)\approx0.993V_S
\]
For discharging from \(V_0\):
\[
v_C(\tau)\approx0.368V_0,\qquad v_C(5\tau)\approx0.0067V_0
\]

title: Capacitors 2: RC Charging and Discharging
text:
Worked example using GUESS
A capacitor charges toward \(12.0\,\mathrm{V}\). Estimate its voltage after one time constant and after five time constants.
Given
\[V_S=12.0\,\mathrm{V},\qquad t=\tau\text{ and }5\tau\]
Unknown
\[v_C(\tau),\qquad v_C(5\tau)\]
Equations
\[v_C(\tau)\approx0.632V_S,qquad v_C(5\tau)\approx0.993V_S\]
Substitute and solve
\[
v_C(\tau)=0.632(12.0\,\mathrm{V})=7.58\,\mathrm{V}
\]
\[
v_C(5\tau)=0.993(12.0\,\mathrm{V})=11.9\,\mathrm{V}
\]
Statement
The capacitor is about \(7.58\,\mathrm{V}\) after one time constant and \(11.9\,\mathrm{V}\) after five time constants.

title: Capacitors 2: RC Charging and Discharging
text:
Tinkercad check

Calculate the expected starting, one-time-constant, and five-time-constant values first.
Build the source, switch, resistor, and capacitor in one loop.
Use red for positive, black for \(0\,\mathrm{V}\), and another colour for the capacitor signal node.
Place the voltmeter across the capacitor.
Start the simulation, close the switch, and record the capacitor voltage.
Share the Tinkercad circuit link.

Use the step-by-step Tinkercad circuit guide if you need the controls and screenshots.

title: Capacitors 2: RC Charging and Discharging
text:
Complete the work

Complete all five questions using GUESS.
Label \(0\), \(\tau\), and \(5\tau\) on the graph.
Use the notebook to check the estimates.
Build one charging circuit in Tinkercad.
Submit the sheet, notebook, and Tinkercad link.

title: Component Foundations 2: Resistors

title: Component Foundations 2: Resistors
Component Foundations 2: Resistors
text:
What is inside?
Common through-hole resistors use a resistive film formed around an insulating body, with metal end caps and leads. The material and geometry determine resistance. Open Circuits can be used in class to inspect truthful internal construction; public notes use original descriptions rather than copied cutaways. [2]

title: Component Foundations 2: Resistors
text:
Value, tolerance, and power
A resistor description such as 4.7 kΩ, ±5%, 0.25 W contains three different limits:

4.7 kΩ is nominal resistance;
±5% is the permitted manufacturing range;
0.25 W is the maximum power rating under stated conditions.

For 4.7 kΩ at ±5%, the resistance can reasonably fall between \(4.465\,\text{k}\Omega\) and \(4.935\,\text{k}\Omega\).
The common four-band colour code for 4.7 kΩ ±5% is yellow, violet, red, gold. Always confirm unfamiliar codes with the course reference or a meter.

title: Component Foundations 2: Resistors
text:
Equations
Ohm’s law connects voltage, current, and resistance:
\[V=IR\]
Resistor power can be checked with:
\[P=VI=I^2R=\frac{V^2}{R}\]
Choose a resistor rating comfortably above the expected operating power. A calculated value below the printed rating is not permission to ignore temperature, enclosure, ventilation, pulses, or manufacturer derating.

title: Component Foundations 2: Resistors
text:
Example: LED current limiting
For a 5.0 V source and an LED with an approximate 2.0 V forward drop, a 330 Ω series resistor has about 3.0 V across it:
\[I\approx\frac{5.0\,\text{V}-2.0\,\text{V}}{330\,\Omega}=9.09\,\text{mA}\]
The resistor power is about:
\[P_R=I^2R\approx27.3\,\text{mW}\]
This simplified calculation is a design estimate. The real LED forward voltage and resistor value vary.

title: Component Foundations 2: Resistors
text:
Five-question starter

Explain the difference between resistance and a resistor.
State the nominal value, tolerance, and power rating of a 2.2 kΩ, ±5%, 0.25 W resistor.
Calculate the possible resistance range of a 1.0 kΩ ±5% resistor.
A 9.0 V source is connected across 1.0 kΩ. Calculate current and resistor power.
A student selects a 100 Ω resistor for a 5.0 V LED circuit with a 2.0 V LED drop. Calculate the estimated current and resistor power, then explain what else must be checked before building.

title: Component Foundations 5: Transistors
Component Foundations 5: Transistors
text:
A first switching circuit



Figure 1. The input controls base current through \(R_B\); the transistor controls the load path.


For a beginner switching model:

off: base drive is absent, so collector current is approximately zero;
on: sufficient base drive allows load current, subject to the load, source, transistor ratings, and saturation voltage.

This model is useful but incomplete. Transistor gain varies, and a switch design must provide adequate drive without exceeding base, collector, voltage, power, or temperature limits.

title: Component Foundations 5: Transistors
section: Package shape is not a pinout
text:
Package shape is not a pinout
Two transistors in similar packages may arrange base, collector, and emitter differently. Verify the exact manufacturer datasheet and the board marking. Installing a transistor backwards is a common kit fault.
The XL741 v2.0 uses thirteen 2N3904 NPN transistors and seven 2N3906 PNP transistors. The quantity itself is a useful lesson: an op-amp symbol can represent a system built from many individual devices.

title: Component Foundations 5: Transistors
text:
Five-question starter

Name the three BJT terminals and state the role of each.
Explain why NPN and PNP transistors are not interchangeable.
Trace the load-current path in Figure 1 when Q1 is on.
Explain why both \(R_B\) and the LED load resistor are required.
A transistor matches the package drawing but the circuit fails. Write a diagnostic sequence that checks part number, pinout, orientation, supply polarity, base drive, and current limiting without immediately replacing the part.

title: Component Foundations 5: Transistors
text:
Jupyter and lab pathway
Start with an ideal two-state model in Jupyter or a circuit simulator. Sweep the input condition and predict load current from the source, LED model, and load resistor. Clearly label this as a model: it does not prove the selected transistor has adequate drive, safe power dissipation, or the expected pinout.
Physical testing uses a protected low-voltage supply and current limiting. The XL741 build comes later, after students can identify diode and transistor orientation and inspect solder joints.
Textbook support: Grob transistor and switching chapters, used with the matching Problems and Experiments Manual sections. [1, Chs. 28-30] Open Circuits provides classroom visual context for semiconductor construction. [2]

Power off. Unplug. Control static. Then look inside.
Figure 1. The whole system first. Open image source and licence.
crumbs: 1. Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts

title: Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts
text:
What is inside?


Motherboard
The main circuit board. It connects the CPU, RAM, storage, power, ports, and expansion cards.


CPU
Runs program instructions. A heat sink and fan usually cover it.


RAM
Fast working memory for programs in use now. It clears when power is removed.


Power supply
Converts wall AC to the low-voltage DC used by the computer. Inspect only the outside, cables, and label.


Cooling
Fans, heat sinks, vents, and thermal material move heat away from chips.


Expansion parts
Graphics, Wi-Fi, network, and sound cards add functions. Not every computer has every part.
crumbs: 1. Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts

title: Open a Computer Safely and Identify the Parts
text:
SSD or spinning hard disk?





A hard disk drive beside a solid-state drive.



HDD: spinning disk
Magnetic platters spin under a moving read/write head. Usually cheaper per terabyte, but slower, noisier, and easier to damage while spinning.
Figure 2. HDD and SSD. Open source and licence.






M.2 solid-state drive circuit board.



SSD: flash storage
Stores data in electronic flash memory. No moving parts. Usually faster, silent, lower-power, and more resistant to bumps.
Figure 3. M.2 SSD. Open source and licence.

How storage connects





The data and power connectors on a SATA solid-state drive.



SATA drive: two connections
SATA data is the narrow 7-pin path to the motherboard. SATA power is the wider 15-pin path to the power supply.
Figure 4. SATA connectors. Open source and licence.






M.2 storage board ready to mount in a motherboard slot.



M.2 drive: mounts on the board
M.2 describes the shape. The drive may use SATA or NVMe/PCIe. The drive and motherboard slot must support the same type.

A repeatable benchmark and improvement loop.








WarningDraft assignment

Define what best means for the assigned user before final testing. Record hardware, operating system, benchmark version, run conditions, units, and baseline results. Use evidence to identify a bottleneck and propose an approved compatible change.

title: Ethernet Cable Categories and Speeds
text:
The category printed on the cable describes tested cabling performance. The slowest port, cable path, or device sets the link speed.





Numbered contacts on an 8P8C modular plug.



8P8C, often called RJ45
Eight positions and eight contacts. Keep the pairs twisted close to the plug. Do not judge cable category by colour.
Figure 1. Open source and licence.






Close view of a twisted-pair Ethernet cable and modular plug.



Read the jacket
Look for the category, conductor type, and certification printed along the cable jacket.
Figure 2. Open source and licence.





Cat5e1 Gbps to 100 m. 2.5 or 5 Gbps may work when the equipment and cable meet the standard.


Cat61 Gbps to 100 m. 10 Gbps on shorter runs, commonly up to 55 m in suitable conditions.


Cat6A10 Gbps to 100 m. Thicker and often less flexible.


Cat825 or 40 Gbps to 30 m. Mainly data centres, not a normal classroom patch cable.








NoteWhat about Cat7?



Cat7 appears in retail listings, but it is not the normal ANSI/TIA category choice for a standard RJ45 classroom cable. Prefer a correctly made Cat6 or Cat6A cable for a known requirement.


Class choice: use the cable and plug specified by the teacher. Match the plug to solid or stranded conductors and to the cable diameter.

title: Set Up Your Accounts and Explore Linux
text:
The main goal of this lesson is simple: have fun with Linux and make the computer useful. The website is your lesson and reference. Each Google Doc below is a separate submission artifact.
Complete the assignments in this order: 3.1 Computer Detective, 3.2 Bashcrawl, then 3.3 Sleek Out Linux Mint. The first two can be completed at home on Windows, Mac, Chromebook, Linux, or, with more difficulty, a phone. They also work offline in class from an installed Linux Mint system or the live USB. Assignment 3.3 requires Linux Mint Xfce, either installed or running from the live USB.
